16024-the-great-round-world-and-what-is-:
Harison's weekly paper for boys and girls, number forty-six, dated September 23, 1897, now under the Great Round World Publishing Company. News, science, and stories fill the paper in words young readers could follow. This number leads with India, where news runs encouraging. The paper kept children abreast of empire and war.

Britain's plan to send a strong force against rebellious tribes has had a good effect, the paper reports. The Afridis held a council of war and chose to return home and gather their harvests. Head men of the tribe, who made a strong stand, own the decision. Seen now, the issue shows how 1897 children learned of frontier war: brief, confident, and from London's side.
28532-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
January 1846 brought number 363 of Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, volume 59, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London. Its lead piece mourns Sir William Follett, dead in his forty-seventh year while Attorney-General and head of the British Bar. The bar felt his loss at Michaelmas term, when his voice and figure were suddenly absent.

Other contents include The Last Hours of a Reign, A Campaign in Texas, The Greek and Romantic Drama, and My College Friends. The Student of Salamanca, Sicilian sketches, aesthetics of dress, a Christmas carol, and The Crisis complete the number. Together they show a monthly miscellany at full Victorian range.
29858-blackwoods-edinburgh-magazine-volu:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 365, volume 59, is dated March 1846. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The contents open with the twenty-fourth book of Homer's Iliad, attempted in English hexameters. The writer admits the risk, noting that even Southey seldom held the measure, though his happy lines show real progress.

The Student of Salamanca continues in part five, and Moses and Son offers a didactic tale. Vichyana, It's All for the Best in conclusion, and The Roman Campagna follow. Mr. Brooke of Borneo, The Smuggler's Leap in the Pyrenees, and Ministerial Measures close the number. The issue shows Blackwood's range: verse, fiction, travel, and politics in one monthly bundle.
29883-blackwoods-edinburgh-magazine-volu:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine, number 366, volume 59, is dated April 1846. William Blackwood and Sons printed it in Edinburgh and London. The contents open with The Marquess Wellesley, a piece on noble recollection, great actions, and national character. The writer asks why Eastern kingdoms perished without reverence, while Greece and republican Rome still draw homage.

A letter to Eusebius and part six of The Student of Salamanca follow. How They Manage Matters in The Model Republic, Antonio Perez, and Recollections of a Lover of Society add variety. The Old Player, The Crusades, and The Burden of Sion by Delta close the literary side. Rhymed hexameters and The Surveyor's Tale end a full monthly number.
30388-blackwood-s-edinburgh-magazine-vol:
Blackwood's Edinburgh Magazine for May 1846, number 367, volume 59, comes from William Blackwood and Sons. Its Edinburgh address is 45 George Street, and its London address 37 Paternoster Row, printed by Ballantyne and Hughes and sold by all booksellers in the United Kingdom. The Student of Salamanca, part the last, leads, followed by Shakespeare and the drama, Birboniana on Italian antiquaries and antichità, and The Americans and the Aborigines, part one.

The state of Ireland, its condition, the life and property bill, the debate, and the famine follow. The Modern Pilgrim's Progress, the Iliad of Homer, book the first, in English hexameters, a prospectus, Truth and Beauty, and The Campaign of the Sutlej follow. The Student of Salamanca opens amid crowd and clamour in Pampeluna's principal coffee-house, on a July evening just after Don Baltasar escaped the town.
548-project-trinity-1945-1946:
Carl Maag and Steve Rohrer compile this Defense Nuclear Agency review of the first atomic test, Project Trinity, in 1945 and 1946. The report covers the Alamogordo site, its organization, and its military and civilian hands. Preshot work, the detonation of 16 July 1945, and postshot surveys fill the core chapters.

Later sections treat radiation safety, site and offsite monitoring, and film-badge doses for participants. Figures show the shot tower, shelters, base camp, and Jumbo after the blast. The volume serves as a sober, factual record of a test that changed war, science, and the lives of all who stood near it.
612-the-constitution-of-japan-1946:
Japan's postwar constitution, promulgated in November 1946 and in force from May 1947, opens this short text. The Japanese people, through the National Diet, declare sovereign power resides with the people and renounce war forever. Government is called a sacred trust, its powers drawn from the people and used for their benefit.

Articles that follow set out rights, the Diet, the cabinet, courts, and local rule in plain, grave language. The text marks a sharp break from the 1889 imperial charter. It serves as a founding document of modern Japan, where peace, liberty, and popular rule replace empire and war.
all-s-well-that-ends-well-pg2246: Helena's daring drives this edition: she cures the King, claims Bertram, and wins him through the bed-trick and the impossible tasks. "All's well that ends well" is tested by a heroine who refuses to lose. The problem comedy at its most provocative.
an-exposition-of-dr-cobb-s-art-of-discov: An Exposition of Dr Cobb's Art of Discovering the Faculties of the Human Mind and Bodily Infirmities is a short American pamphlet of 1846, thirty-two pages long. Its subject is a method, credited to a Dr Cobb, for reading a person's mental faculties and bodily weaknesses, in the spirit of the character-reading sciences then popular. The piece is credited to Enos Cobb. It survives as a small specimen of the 1840s trade in practical mind reading.
arxiv-2509-00846:
Woon Yee Ng, with three co-authors, proposes Causal SHAP for explaining model predictions. SHAP is a widely used method that scores each feature. It tells how much each feature counts for a prediction. But it cannot separate cause from mere correlation. It can thus give wrong credit when features move together.

Causal SHAP weaves causal links into the scores it gives. It keeps many good traits of the original SHAP. The method combines the Peter-Clark algorithm, which finds causal graphs. It also uses the IDA algorithm to measure causal strength. Tests use both synthetic and real-world data. Scores fall for features that are merely linked to the target. The gain is clearest in high-stakes fields such as healthcare.
arxiv-2509-01346:
Ozan Hur studies a robust finance question: what is the worst-case chance that an asset Y beats a benchmark X, when Y's distribution is only known to lie near the benchmark's? Nearness is measured by Kullback-Leibler divergence, a standard gauge of how far one probability law sits from another. The problem takes a max-min form over ways of coupling the two outcomes.

Hur shows that problem has a tractable dual, reached through optimal transport, and its solution tilts the benchmark law exponentially. The answer forms a one-parameter family, with the parameter acting as a budget for the allowed information shift. As it grows, probability mass moves steadily from lower to higher outcomes. Because the method needs only the baseline distribution, Hur offers it as a tool for wide scenario generation and robust performance testing.
arxiv-2509-01446:
Ireland's population will shift over the coming decades, and planners need local detail, not just national totals. Sean Caulfield Curley, Karl Mason, and Patrick Mannion present a dynamic microsimulation model for Ireland running from 2022 to 2057. The model follows individuals through four main events: births, deaths, internal migration, and international migration.

Each simulated person carries seven traits, including age, sex, marital status, citizenship, education, and economic status. Those traits change over time by chance, using transition rates drawn from Irish data. People are placed at the fine Electoral Division level, allowing close local analysis. Curley and the team offer the model as a tool for academic study and for testing how demographic change and policy choices might play out across Ireland's regions.
arxiv-2509-01546:
Testing solid-state sensors for particle physics needs a way to excite charge at a precise point inside the material. Enoch Ejopu, with nine co-authors, commissions a femtosecond laser system whose wavelength can be tuned across a very wide range, from ultraviolet to deep infrared. Two-photon absorption in the sensor gives three-dimensional resolution for creating electron-hole pairs at a chosen spot.

The system pairs a commercial laser with an optical amplifier unit that tunes the output. Beam measurements set the focused spot's size and its Rayleigh length, the span over which the beam stays tight. First tests on silicon and diamond samples show the expected quadratic rise of signal with pulse energy, and models explain extra signal from reflections. The silicon results match a one-dimensional model well, marking the facility ready for detector work.
arxiv-2509-01646: Mohammad Adarbeh and Mohammad Saleh introduce a new notion in module theory. It is uniform S-projectivity relative to a module, or u-S-projectivity for short. A module P has this trait when maps out of it respect a class of surjections tied to a set S. The dual notion, relative u-S-injectivity, is defined alongside it. The pair discusses traits of both notions. They give characterizations of u-S-semisimple modules through them. Quasi forms of both notions are also introduced and studied.
arxiv-2509-01846:
Takashi Onaka, Itsuki Sakon, Takashi Shimonishi, and Mitsuhiko Honda hunt for missing oxygen hidden in large ice grains between the stars. At least a quarter of oxygen in thin space clouds sits in no known form. Ice marks in near infrared light hint that a fifth of the missing share lies in big water ice grains. But those marks weaken and tangle for the largest grains, so they cannot settle the count.

Far infrared ice marks at two longer wavelengths can pin down crystal ice up to larger sizes. Reading them over a bright background needs a sensitive tool like the PRIMA spectrograph. Broad marks need only modest sharpness but very accurate calibration. Solving the oxygen gap matters for cloud chemistry and star birth studies.
arxiv-2509-01946:
Aarsh Shah, Cleyton Magalhaes, Kiev Gama, and Ronnie de Souza Santos present Tether, a desktop aid for software engineers with ADHD. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder can hinder focus, task starts, and self regulation at work. Few tools target those hurdles inside coding workflows, despite growing awareness of neurodiversity in the field. Tether uses a large language model to give adaptive, context aware support.

The app tracks system activity locally to prompt engagement at the right moments. Its chatbot draws on ADHD specific resources through retrieval, so replies stay relevant. Games style rewards add motivation for steady work. Early self use showed sharper context accuracy after prompt and retrieval tuning. User trials with the target group remain future work.
arxiv-2509-02046:
Kaiyue Wen, David Hall, Tengyu Ma, and Percy Liang benchmark pretraining optimizers fairly and find smaller speedups than often claimed. Optimizers steer model training by updating weights from gradients. AdamW has long dominated language model pretraining despite rivals claiming large speed gains. The team blames unequal tuning and narrow evaluation setups for the confusion.

Ten optimizers are tested across four model scales and varied data to model ratios with rigorous tuning. Rankings can flip mid training, so only end of training scores count. Real speedups shrink with scale, falling to a modest edge at the largest size tested. The fastest methods all use matrix preconditioners rather than per entry scaling. Careful methodology, the authors argue, is the real bottleneck.
arxiv-2509-02546:
Nathan R. Sandford and sixteen co-authors, with the S5 Collaboration, present a 2025 astronomy paper on Boötes I, an ultra-faint dwarf galaxy orbiting the Milky Way. New survey spectra are merged with about fifteen years of archived data.

The combined sample is the largest of its kind for such a galaxy, with well over a hundred confirmed members reaching far from the centre. It includes new members, binary candidates, pulsating stars, and many iron abundance measures. Correcting for perspective rotation for the first time in this setting reveals a velocity gradient aligned with the galaxy's orbit, hinting at tidal stretching. Metal content falls with radius. A Jeans model of the motions mildly favours a cusped dark matter profile, and chemical modelling suggests rapid, wasteful star formation with strong outflows.
arxiv-2509-02646:
Shivam Kumar Mishra, Jackson Levi Said, and B. Mishra present a 2025 cosmology paper working out how small disturbances evolve in a modified gravity theory. The theory is teleparallel gravity extended with the Gauss-Bonnet invariant, a curvature quantity with deep geometric roots.

Background expansion alone cannot judge such models; perturbations test their stability and health. The authors take a gauge invariant approach, so results do not depend on coordinate choices, then illustrate popular gauge options. They derive the equations of motion for every perturbative mode. New contributions from the Gauss-Bonnet coupling are interpreted physically, mode by mode. The work supplies a needed check for whether these cosmologies can match structure formation data without hidden instabilities.
arxiv-2509-02746:
Saarang Panchavati, Corey Arnold, and William Speier present a 2025 biomedical AI paper exploring foundation models for EEG, the brain wave recordings used to diagnose epilepsy and other disorders. EEG data is noisy, high-dimensional, and strongly nonlinear, which limits older automated methods.

Their model uses a Mamba architecture, a selective state space design built for long sequences. Training first teaches the model to reconstruct masked EEG in a self-supervised way, then tunes it for seizure detection on a large set of seizure and non-seizure recordings. Ranking accuracy on test data held out from training was solid but not spectacular. The authors frame the work as a step toward large, clinically usable EEG foundation models, rather than a finished diagnostic tool, with scale and generality as the main goals.
arxiv-2509-02846:
Siddharth Mansingh and twelve co-authors wrote a 2025 scientific computing paper. It brings test-time thinking to foundation models for partial differential equations. Those equations sit behind most physics simulation. Such models falter on long rollouts and unfamiliar cases. They also demand huge training sets.

Inspired by language model reasoning tricks, the authors spend extra computation at inference time instead. Reward models grade candidate predictions for spatio-temporal consistency. They guide a stochastic base model toward better trajectories. Tests use compressible Euler simulations from the PDEGym benchmark. Test-time computing improved predictions over standard autoregressive rollout. It did so with smaller models and fewer training samples. The authors frame it as a first step toward fuller reasoning algorithms for physics workflows.
arxiv-2509-03046:
Divyansh Agrawal, Venkateswaran P. Krishnan, and Vladimir A. Sharafutdinov worked in 2025 on describing which outputs a ray transform can produce. The transform adds up a tensor field, a grid of directional quantities, along every straight line. Knowing its range, the set of reachable outputs, is key to undoing it in imaging problems.

Earlier work settled the question in three or more dimensions on weighted smoothness spaces. The two-dimensional case behaves very differently, and the authors handle it in higher order versions of those spaces. Their main tool is a formula named after Reshetnyak that equates the sizes of a field and its transform. They treat fields with no net source, called solenoidal. The result sharpens inverse problem theory for planar tensor data.
arxiv-2509-03446:
Niteesh Midlagajni and Constantin A. Rothkopf taught a graph neural network in 2025 to simulate liquids being manipulated by moving rigid bodies. Faithful fluid simulation matters for design, graphics, and robotics, yet learned models usually cover only static free-fall scenes or simple primitive objects. Real tasks involve containers and tools that move and collide with the liquid.

In their framework, particles become graph nodes and collisions with objects are handled through surface representations accelerated by a bounding volume hierarchy, a tree that speeds up contact checks. Training covered single-object manipulation tasks only. The model still generalized to new objects and new manipulation tasks, and it also worked as a plain free-fall simulator. Its learned dynamics could then drive control through gradient-based optimization.
arxiv-2509-03646:
How reinforcement learning builds reasoning in large language models, layer by layer, is the question in a 2025 research paper by Haozhe Wang and five co-authors. Reinforcement learning clearly improves complex reasoning, but the mechanism behind the gains stayed unclear. Odd phenomena reported by others, like sudden aha moments and shifting entropy, are treated here as clues to one underlying pattern.

Their analysis finds an emergent hierarchy resembling human cognition, where high-level strategy sits above low-level procedure. Early training is bottlenecked by procedural correctness, so models first sharpen basic execution skills. Later the bottleneck moves upward, and gains come from exploring and mastering strategic planning. Standard algorithms like GRPO push on all tokens equally, diluting the learning signal. Their method, HICRA, concentrates credit on high-impact planning tokens instead. Many experiments show it beats strong baselines by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-03746:
A 2025 research paper by Anushya Subbiah and five co-authors focuses on giving each product its own single token inside a large language model recommender. Recommendation systems built on language models gain broad world knowledge, but real catalogues hold millions of items. The field's standard view held that item identifiers must be split into several tokens, which slows real-time serving badly.

The authors challenge that practice and treat item IDs as full members of the model instead. Simple changes to training and inference allow one-token representations per item and single-step decoding of a recommendation. On Amazon shopping datasets, recommendation quality improves over existing techniques on recall and ranking measures. Inference also runs many times faster, between five and fourteen times in their tests. The work opens a different route for integrating huge identifier sets into language models, with code released for others to build on.
arxiv-2509-04446:
Kiymet Akdemir and four co-authors present a framework for drawing and then polishing multi-frame stories with image generators in a 2025 research paper. Text-to-image diffusion models paint detailed scenes from words, and story visualization strings those scenes into narratives. Creators need to revise frames afterward, though, without breaking consistency of characters, style, or plot across panels. Existing tools rarely allow both fine and coarse edits while holding a story together.

Their zero-shot framework, Plot'n Polish, needs no task-specific training. It generates consistent story frames and supports disentangled editing, meaning one aspect can change while others stay fixed. Writers and illustrators gain a drafting partner that accepts revision instead of forcing a fresh start.
arxiv-2509-04646:
Health simulations can inform policy, yet their complexity often shuts out the people they should help. Philippe J. Giabbanelli and one co-author address that gap in a 2025 mixed-methods paper on personalised explanations. Stakeholders include clinicians, policymakers, patients, caregivers, and health advocates, each with different needs.

The authors present a step-by-step framework to identify what each group needs from an explanation. The framework then guides large language models in producing tailored summaries of simulation outputs and model design. Their aim is to replace one-size-fits-all summaries with explanations matched to audience and purpose.
arxiv-2509-04746:
The Efimov effect, where three particles show a repeating pattern across scales, appears as a limit cycle in renormalisation group language. Langxuan Chen, lead author with five co-authors, ask whether its mathematical form stays universal across regulators in a 2025 paper. Regulators are tools that tame short-range behaviour in calculations.

Working through two classic three-body equations, they derive a universal functional form for general separable regulators. The form follows from a real Möbius transformation with three parameters. Numerical checks confirm the shape across regulators, although the parameter values depend on the regulator. The result broadens understanding of three-body renormalisation.
arxiv-2509-05046:
The internal quark structure of the spin-1 deuteron includes tensor-polarised distributions that experiments are only beginning to reach. S. Kumano and one co-author calculate one such twist-3 distribution in a 2025 paper. They use relations modelled on classic spin-half results, together with known twist-2 distributions of the same type.

The resulting curve has a shape similar to its twist-2 counterpart and a comparable size. Because the energy scale at a current facility is not far above the hadronic scale, higher-twist effects could be sizable there. The authors argue upcoming experiments at several facilities could measure these curves directly.
arxiv-2509-05146:
Translating text inside a photograph is harder than translating clean documents, because real images have messy backgrounds and varied fonts. Yanzhi Tian, lead author with six co-authors, tackle that practical setting in a 2025 paper on in-image multilingual machine translation. Existing research relies on synthetic data that cannot reflect real conditions.

The team annotate a dataset of real captured one-line text images with complex backgrounds, diverse fonts and positions, and many translation directions. Their end-to-end model processes visual text and background separately, aiming for better translation quality and visual effect. Experiments show gains over other models in their tests, and code and data are public.
arxiv-2509-05446:
Shrinking deep image networks in one pass, without a slow search, is proposed by Iftekhar Haider Chowdhury and three co-authors in a 2025 paper on filter pruning. Large convolutional networks perform well but cost too much memory and computing for many devices.

Their method scores each filter by fusing three importance measures: gradient sensitivity, a first-order Taylor estimate, and how activation patterns shift. Filters whose scores disagree across measures are scaled up in importance ranking as unstable or less critical candidates. In tests cutting half to seventy percent of filters, the method removed most floating point operations while keeping nearly all baseline accuracy at the deepest cut. It needs only one forward and backward pass.
arxiv-2509-05646:
Stable states that follow a slowly changing field can survive energy loss in three-level quantum systems, Emil A. Gazazyan, Gayane G. Grigoryan, and Vanush Paturyan show in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Adiabatic states support gentle transfer methods used in atomic control.

The authors derive the needed stability conditions, both necessary and sufficient, and check them in numbers across setups held at exact two-photon resonance. In every scheme the state's lifetime is set by the dephasing time between levels not linked by an allowed transition. They also show efficient transfer through a middle state at room temperature despite slow relaxation. They match one special state's lifetime to the dark state's under large detuning.
arxiv-2509-05746:
Sharpening a photo should depend on how far away each part of the scene is, Tianhao Guo and three co-authors argue in a 2025 image processing paper. Standard super-resolution assumes one blur model everywhere, while real optics add distance effects like haze, focus falloff, and perspective distortion.

Their variational framework treats reconstruction as a spatially varying inverse problem with distance-dependent blur, giving theory for reconstruction limits by depth. A neural network implements the resulting energy flow with depth-aware convolution kernels and learned smoothness that adapts to local geometry. Spectral rules from atmospheric scattering theory guard far regions against noise blow-up. Across five benchmarks the method led on outdoor driving scenes at two scales.
arxiv-2509-06546:
Movement between regions in a network is rebuilt from basic physics by Hadrien Oliveri and two co-authors in a 2025 applied mathematics paper. Their cases range from infections between countries to toxic proteins between brain areas. Standard network models move quantities between nodes using a graph Laplacian, a rule based on connections alone. That shortcut ignores what happens inside each link.

Taking flow, reaction, and spreading along each link as the true mechanism, the authors derive the network-level transport rule from first principles. The resulting effective graph Laplacian is fully fixed by the small-scale physics inside the edges. They show the operator captures transport correctly and study how it scales when edges grow longer. The work gives network modelers a transport rule with a clear physical basis instead of a fitted guess.
arxiv-2509-06646:
Gravity emerging from a matrix model of string theory is the subject of a 2025 theoretical physics paper by Pei-Ming Ho and two co-authors. Matrix models define string theory without assuming spacetime; spacetime is supposed to arise from the matrices themselves. Fluctuations around that background should then represent both matter and gravity.

The authors focus on the IIB matrix model and ask how coordinate-change symmetry, called diffeomorphism invariance, appears, and how unitarity, the rule that probabilities behave sensibly, is guaranteed. They treat matrices as bilocal fields, objects living on pairs of points, and describe the Lorentz-invariant vacuum and its low-energy excitations in those terms. Conditions for unitarity are rewritten for bilocal fields. In the low-energy limit, they argue, the fields reduce to a finite set of massless local fields plus infinitely many massive ones, all consistent with unitarity.
arxiv-2509-06746:
A honeycomb magnet candidate for exotic quantum states is probed with X-rays by M. M. Ferreira-Carvalho and ten co-authors in a 2025 paper on condensed matter. The compound, a barium cobalt arsenate, is a possible host for Kitaev physics. Its cobalt atoms sit inside oxygen cages whose exact shape shapes the magnetism.

Absorption and magnetic circular dichroism readings at the cobalt edges used a fluorescence method fit for insulating samples. A strong linear dichroic signal showed a marked trigonal twist of the cages. Fitting the spectra with a full-multiplet cluster model showed the key hole density focused in one orbital, and sum rules gave the spin and orbital moments. The twist energy came out larger than the cobalt spin-orbit coupling, showing how local form drives this material's electronic and magnetic conduct.
arxiv-2509-06846:
A fresh map of how stars move in the Milky Way's central bulge is built by Carlos Quezada and nine co-authors in a 2025 astronomy paper. Bulge motion is complex, mixing several stellar components, and dust plus crowding leave the region near the galactic plane poorly measured. Better maps are needed to test dynamical models.

Radial velocities from the GIBS and APOGEE surveys were combined with published and new MUSE observations, including nine new fields close to the plane. The total came to fifty-seven fields and about twenty-three thousand measured velocities. A custom Python tool extracted spectra from the instrument's data cubes. Statistical sampling corrected for foreground contamination and produced new analytical fits. The updated maps confirm the bulge's cylindrical rotation and reveal a boxier shape in the velocity dispersion pattern, with its central peak preserved.
arxiv-2509-07346:
Itzhak Bars, writing alone in 2025, argues that the Higgs field does far more than give particles their masses. The Higgs boson is famous as a ripple on a universe-wide field whose background value fills all space. Bars claims that near singularities, the points where gravity becomes extreme inside black holes and at the universe's start, the field changes character completely.

In his account, the field there becomes strongly varying and builds new spacetime domains governed by antigravity beyond the singularities. Gravity and antigravity regions join through traversable singularities, making the whole spacetime geodesically complete, with no paths that simply end. Electroweak symmetry is restored at the singularities, he argues. He also claims the picture resolves the black hole information paradox in a manifestly unitary way. Detailed calculations sit in a companion paper, and these remain his claimed results.
arxiv-2509-07446:
Nikhil Yewale and 2 co-authors draw an analogy in 2025 between a standing wave on a pool of liquid and a mechanical oscillator. A standing wave sloshes in place rather than traveling, and its free oscillations are the motions it makes when left alone. The authors show the equations for the liquid surface and for the mechanical model share the same kinds of solutions.

Both systems admit quiet solutions and time-periodic ones with finite amplitude, and the periodic ones can turn linearly unstable depending on amplitude. A new Mathieu-like equation, derived by a simpler route, governs stability of the standing wave against a super-harmonic disturbance. Analytic predictions are checked against numerical solutions of the full nonlinear equations for both systems. Agreement is good in most cases, and the mismatches are analyzed to mark where the analogy breaks down.
arxiv-2509-07546:
Sungjun Eom and 1 co-author extend differential dynamic programming in 2025 to control problems whose target is an ellipsoid, a stretched ball region, rather than a single point. Many real tasks, such as parking a vehicle, accept any final state inside a safe region. Differential dynamic programming, or DDP, is an efficient optimal control method, but it needs smooth cost functions, and the ellipsoid version creates costs with kinks.

Their ETS-DDP reformulates the problem with an orthogonal projection operator and smooths the cost locally around the previous iteration's path. A statistical inference method designs the ellipsoid itself from target points shown in expert demonstrations. In an autonomous parking simulation, the method finds an admissible trajectory efficiently and runs much faster than a comparison point-target approach. Region targets could make optimal control fit real tasks more naturally.
arxiv-2509-07746:
Samvit Kumar and 3 co-authors test Lighthill's mechanism for concentrating vorticity near walls in turbulent flow in a 2025 paper. Vorticity measures local spinning in a fluid, and the logarithmic layer is the region of wall turbulence where average velocity grows with the log of distance from the wall. Lighthill proposed long ago how motion toward and away from the wall gathers spanwise vorticity there.

Using a channel flow database at high Reynolds number, the team computes flows conditioned on motion toward or away from the wall. The results support Lighthill's proposal across the whole logarithmic layer, extended by counterflows that explain an anti-correlation between two vorticity transport routes. Vorticity transport also looks like a cascade through a hierarchy of eddy scales. Townsend's attached hairpin eddies account for half the cascade; necklace-like shawl vortices wrapping turbulent sweeps supply the other half.
arxiv-2509-08746:
Ryan McGaughey and 2 co-authors challenge a core belief about defenses in federated learning in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model without pooling raw data. Robust aggregation tries to spot and exclude harmful client updates.

Their Chameleon Poisoning keeps harmful updates inside the main distribution, so they look normal. Feedback from aggregation tells the attacker whether its update was accepted. The attacker then balances a harmful part with a camouflage part. Across two datasets, attack success rises sharply against nine defenses. The result shows detection based on outliers alone is not enough.
arxiv-2509-08946:
Stellar evolution codes produce grids of thousands of star models, and mining those grids by hand is slow. D. Tarczay-Nehéz presents MESAlab in a 2025 research paper written alone. MESAlab is a Python pipeline for post-processing output from MESA, the standard open-source stellar evolution code. It is modular, so users can adapt the stages to their own grids.

The pipeline spots selected evolutionary features automatically. One example is the blue loop phase in the life of classical Cepheid stars. It can also prepare inputs for, and launch, two companion tools that compute how stars pulsate. Visualization tools draw evolutionary tracks on standard diagrams, including the Gaia color-magnitude diagram. For researchers running huge model grids, MESAlab turns weeks of file handling into a repeatable workflow. Pulsation analysis comes attached to the phases that matter.
arxiv-2509-09146:
Internet providers gain speed and control by peering directly with each other, but choosing partners is a slow, manual courtship. Md Ibrahim Ibne Alam and 4 co-authors automate that choice with machine learning in a 2025 research paper. Providers otherwise pay transit services to carry their traffic. Peering through exchange points is preferred, yet arranging it eats time and expertise.

The team assembled public data on providers from databases like PeeringDB and CAIDA. They compared tree-based, neural network, and transformer models at predicting which pairs should peer. Tree-based models won on both accuracy and efficiency. The best one predicted peering partners with very high accuracy and stayed robust across time, region, and missing data. The authors envision providers automating partner selection entirely, making the internet's connective tissue grow faster and with less friction.
arxiv-2509-09446:
Hazem Hassan's 2025 paper develops a p-adic tool aimed at conjectured objects called Stark-Heegner cycles. Heegner cycles are higher-weight relatives of Heegner points, and their intersection numbers show up inside modular forms. A proposal by Rotger and Seveso predicts matching cycles over real-quadratic fields, whose existence would follow from deep conjectures of Bloch and Beilinson.

Hassan lifts the rigid meromorphic cocycle theory of Darmon and Vonk into higher weight, building a pairing on the p-adic upper half-plane for divisors coming from real-quadratic fields. Values computed for principal cycles appear to land in abelian extensions of real-quadratic fields. That algebraic behaviour counts as indirect support for the predicted cycles actually existing.
arxiv-2509-09946:
Vu-Minh Le and 5 co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a way to lift ordinary two-dimensional multi-camera tracking into three dimensions. Tracking people across many cameras is key for large-scale surveillance, and depth data plus camera calibration can place each target in real space. Rebuilding a whole tracking system for 3D, though, is often not practical for teams with working 2D setups.

Their method keeps the 2D tracker, then uses depth to rebuild each target as a point cloud and recover its 3D box by clustering and heading correction. An improved matching step uses local identity consistency to assign global identities across frames. On the 2025 AI City Challenge 3D tracking data set, the system placed third on the leaderboard.
arxiv-2509-10146:
Mathijs van Noort and 2 co-authors show that a temporal logic can shed its best-known operators in a 2025 logic paper. It loses nothing by the cut. Reasoning over time often leans on negation. That habit suits closed data sets. It breaks down when data arrive late or never. Sensor networks and the Semantic Web face just that risk. Negation-free fragments keep reasoning monotone and scalable. They might be too weak, though, to say all that is needed.

The authors work inside negation-free metric temporal logic. They drop the always operators first. Once, since, and until carry the load instead. Then once is dropped as well. A fragment built only from until and since remains. Broad claims about all past or future time survive the cut. Such claims were long thought to need the muscle of negation.
arxiv-2509-10246:
Amir Bahador Javadi, Amin Kargarian, and Mort Naraghi-Pour use machine learning to lighten a heavy power-grid planning problem in this 2025 paper. Grid operators must commit power plants a day ahead while renewable output stays uncertain, a two-stage stochastic problem whose transmission constraints grow enormous.

Their idea replaces the flood of line-flow limits with a much smaller set learned by a support vector machine. The swap rests on the geometry of the feasible region under a standard DC power flow approximation, and training data comes from fast optimal power flow runs. On the IEEE 57-bus and 118-bus test systems, the learned constraints stayed highly accurate, planning ran about forty-six and thirty-one percent faster, and generation costs barely moved.
arxiv-2509-10446:
Rui Lu and 8 co-authors present DeepDive, a system that teaches language models to search deeply, in this 2025 paper. Browsing tools can turn a model into a research agent, but open models still reason poorly over long searches and lack hard training questions. The team attacked both problems together.

First, they generate tough, hard-to-find questions automatically from open knowledge graphs. Second, they train the model with multi-turn reinforcement learning, with a penalty that discourages asking the same query twice. Their 32-billion-parameter model set a new best among open systems on the BrowseComp benchmark, ahead of several named rivals. All data, models, and code were released in public.
arxiv-2509-10746:
Medical chatbots often sound emotionally flat, and Adarsh Srinivasan with five co-authors fix that openly with RECAP in this 2025 health AI paper. Their framework works at inference time, no retraining, and is grounded in cognitive appraisal theory, the psychology of how people evaluate events. A patient's message is decomposed into auditable stages: reflect, extract, calibrate, align, produce.

Across benchmarks and models from eight to one hundred twenty billion parameters, RECAP improved agreement with human judgments, with the biggest gains on the smallest models. Its intermediate steps expose a blind spot: models systematically underweight relational factors like social support. In blinded tests, oncology fellows preferred RECAP's responses over baselines in roughly three quarters to seven eighths of comparisons, suggesting careful prompting can raise emotional intelligence while keeping reasoning visible for clinicians.
arxiv-2509-11246:
Krystian Gajdzica, Bernhard Heim, and Markus Neuhauser classify a sign pattern in this 2025 number theory paper. Partitions count ways to break a whole number into pieces. The authors study counts from restricted infinite products. Some factors are left out by an exception set.

One quantity compares neighboring partition counts. Its sign shows local log-concavity or log-convexity. The simplest case gives regular partitions. There, no part is a multiple of a fixed number. The authors find that large-parameter signs follow a pattern. The pattern depends on the small numbers two through five. It depends on which of them are exceptions. It also depends on the remainder of n. A value set by the exception set fixes that remainder.
arxiv-2509-11346:
Connor Ligeikis, Heath Hofmann, and Jeff Scruggs built a self-powered vibration controller in this 2025 control engineering paper. The system harvests energy from the shaking it suppresses. The prototype works at a larger scale than earlier demos. It handles forces around a kilonewton. Power flows exceed a watt.

The hardware couples a linear ballscrew to a synchronous machine. That machine uses permanent magnets. A custom inverter steers power flow. A converter moves energy in and out of a storage capacitor. Real circuits waste some energy. The control law must meet a feasibility condition stricter than passivity. The authors give a workable design method respecting it. Hardware-in-the-loop tests used a stochastically shaken tuned absorber. The design behaved as intended.
arxiv-2509-11646:
Cristiano Spotti surveys a borderland between two fields in this 2025 discussion paper. Differential geometry is one side. Algebraic geometry is the other. His topic is Kähler-Einstein metrics. These are special curved geometries on complex spaces. What happens to them under limits and rescalings is the thread.

The discussion centers on moduli spaces. Those catalog all varieties of a kind. Singularities get equal weight. Those are points where spaces fail to be smooth. Spotti walks through basic examples and reviews recent results. Tentative conjectural pictures link the two sides. Rescaled metric limits mirror algebraic ways to complete moduli spaces. The paper maps an active frontier for readers who want the lay of the land.
arxiv-2509-11746:
Jian Cao and 9 co-authors simulate a newly seen exotic particle in a 2025 hadron physics paper. A detector team recently reported an axial-vector particle, X(2300), in a specific decay process. What the particle is made of is still unknown.

Using a parton and hadron cascade model, the authors simulate its making in electron-positron collisions. They propose candidate inner structures for the first time, among them four-quark states and a bound system of a strangeonium with a light hadron. Each candidate forms by coalescence steps in the simulated final states. They compute the particle's angular momentum in its rest frame and classify each candidate. Estimated rates differ by an order of magnitude between candidates, and their momentum spreads differ a lot, giving tests for experiments.
arxiv-2509-11946:
Vibrating beams stiffened with carbon nanotubes get a fast new analysis method from Maryam Jalili and one co-author in 2025. Their subject is the nonlinear free vibration of composite beams whose nanotube content can be spread evenly or graded through the thickness.

The authors build boundary-adapted Chebyshev functions that satisfy clamped and simply supported end conditions exactly, then apply a Ritz procedure with geometric nonlinearity included. Material properties come from a modified mixing rule, and the reduced model converges fast. With a dozen basis functions, the lowest frequency already sits within a tenth of a percent of published benchmarks. It also costs far less computing time than fine finite-element models. Raising the nanotube share lifts the frequency, they find, though the method still assumes a slender beam.
arxiv-2509-12846:
Junlin Song, Antoine Richard and Miguel Olivares-Mendez give in 2025 a fast way to align a motion sensor and a camera in space and time. Drones, phones, and robots need that match set in advance, or their sense of place drifts.

Most past methods use smooth curves over time, which are exact but slow. The new method uses step-by-step states instead and fixes the weak point of such states for time shifts. The gain is large at scale: saving one minute per device across a million devices saves thousands of work days. Code is shared openly so labs and firms can use and check it.
arxiv-2509-13046:
Eyal German, Daniel Samira and two co-authors attack fake table data in 2025 to test if rows leak their source. Diffusion makers can craft true-like tables for health and finance share. They may also store real rows and leak them.

Their MIA-EPT attack is black-box: it sees only fake output. It masks row fields, rebuilds them, and reads miss size as a member clue. Tests span three makers with fair leak scores. In a 2025 contest run it placed second in its track. The lesson is stark: fake data is not safe by default.
arxiv-2509-13246:
Samuel Escribano, Alfredo Levy Yeyati and Elsa Prada derive in 2025 a compact band model for III-V crystals under strain. Strain tunes electronic traits, but full band models cost too much for device-scale runs. Simple strain-aware forms for these quantum-grade materials lagged behind.

Starting from an eight-band model with corrections, they fold down to one band. Closed forms give mass, potential, spin coupling, and g-factor under strain. Small to mid strain matches full results. Wire and layered cases test the form. Spintronic and quantum designs gain a fast, trusted tool.
arxiv-2509-13546:
Nam Nguyen and five co-authors lay out a full cost analysis in a 2025 quantum computing paper for simulating the extended Jaynes-Cummings model. That model describes light interacting with matter across several modes and underlies technologies such as photon addition, but classical simulation becomes impossible for large systems.

The team develops explicit quantum algorithms and circuits for the model's time evolution, using first and second order product formulas in two different pictures of the dynamics. They prove closed-form error bounds, handle both pure and mixed states, and check their cost models numerically. Finally they compile the circuits for a surface-code fault-tolerant architecture, giving concrete estimates of physical qubits and run times for future machines.
arxiv-2509-13646:
Kexue Fu and six co-authors present Vistoria in a 2025 human-computer interaction paper, a writing system where text and images act as equal partners in fictional storytelling. Most writing tools are text-only, even though people naturally think and remember in pictures, which limits how authors plan and develop ideas.

A co-design study with ten writers, run in Wizard-of-Oz style, showed how sketches, images, and annotations drive ideation and organization. Vistoria supports operations borrowed from image editing, such as lasso selection, collage, filters, and perspective shifts, applied to narrative material. In a controlled study with twelve participants, co-editing improved expressiveness and immersion and strengthened feelings of authorship, though it also raised mental effort.
arxiv-2509-13846:
Puru Vaish and four co-authors challenge a quiet assumption in representation learning in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Self-supervised methods usually assume that loosely related views of the same scan are enough to teach a model useful structure. The team argue that meaningful structure in the hidden representation does not appear on its own; it has to be induced.

Their method, Consistent View Alignment, aligns representations from different views so complementary information lines up without creating false matches. Applied to foundation models for three-dimensional medical image segmentation, it improved downstream performance over standard self-supervised baselines. Entries using the method took first and second place in the MICCAI 2025 SSL3D challenge with two different backbone networks.
arxiv-2509-14346:
Muqaddar Abbas and three co-authors model a light effect in 2025 inside a tiny optical cavity holding a bilayer of graphene. The photonic spin Hall effect splits light by polarisation. Left and right circular parts shift sideways in opposite directions.

In their setup, pump and probe fields drive one mirror of the cavity. Radiation pressure sets the second mirror vibrating. The two polarisation parts of a probe beam then separate across the incidence plane. The split can be tuned with cavity fields, mechanical coupling and phonon links to electronic states. Phonons are quantised vibrations in the material. Results hold also for standard optomechanical systems without those extra links, widening where the tuned effect could be used.
arxiv-2509-14546:
Zhilun Zhou and six co-authors benchmark the rationality of large language models in 2025, across both thinking and acting. Models now simulate people and assist decisions widely, raising a plain question: do they reason and choose as rational agents should? Rationality has theoretical and practical sides.

Their benchmark is presented as the first omnibus test of model rationality across many domains. It probes consistency of beliefs, preference logic and decision quality under varied framings. Multiple leading models are compared on the same suite. Human like fluency can mask systematic irrationality, such as framing effects or inconsistent trade offs. A shared rationality scorecard helps buyers and researchers see where a model can be trusted as a simulated or advising agent.
arxiv-2509-15046:
Shu Yang, Konstantinos Zinelis, Sourojeet Chakraborty, and C. Ricardo Constante-Amores simulate a liquid thread breaking inside a yield-stress material in a 2025 fluid dynamics paper. A Newtonian thread drains and pinches off while surrounded by a viscoplastic medium, a material that flows only where stress passes a threshold. Such setups appear in embedded printing, where ink threads rest inside support gels.

Simulations and theory agree that breakup happens below a nearly universal threshold set by the balance of capillary force and yield stress. The viscosity contrast matters little at low Ohnesorge numbers, which compare viscous and capillary effects. Maps over the parameter plane reveal distinct regime boundaries, and a scaling law predicts the minimum thread radius accurately. Stress localization inside the viscoplastic surroundings emerges as the key mechanism.
arxiv-2509-15446:
Yahui Qu and Benedek Valkó study how points spread in a random pattern called the Sine beta process. This pattern is the large scale limit of a family of random tables used in physics and math. A key question is how likely two points are to sit at a given gap. That likelihood is the pair correlation function, the object of this paper.

The pair write that function through a random differential equation and through an endless system of such equations. They show the function varies smoothly with the key parameter and bound how fast it fades. For even values of the parameter, a finite set of equations pins it down, and they expand it as a series. Their formulas recover the known cases.
arxiv-2509-15546:
Ran Hong leads a team that boosts a video cutting tool guided by words. The task is to cut out, in each frame, the objects a text query names. A recent system joins a language model with a strong cutter. The team improve it with no extra training, using two added parts.

One part checks that the named subject and action truly appear in the video, which cuts false hits. The other part picks key frames with care, catching early views and long range context. On a known test set, the boosted system scores well and takes second place in a 2025 contest track. The work shows checks and frame choice can lift a strong base system.
arxiv-2509-15646:
Sharan Banagiri, Eric Thrane, and Paul Lasky sort merging black hole pairs into groups. The fourth catalog of gravitational wave events gives a detailed view of these pairs. How the black holes formed is unclear, and each birth path may leave its own marks. The team take a data led approach, letting mass ranges define the groups.

They find support for at least three groups, split by the heavier hole's mass with sharp borders. The lightest group mixes mass ratios evenly and spins slowly. The middle group strongly favors near equal masses. The heaviest group shows support for fast spins. Each group's traits hint at a distinct birth path. More data will test the split.
arxiv-2509-15946:
Sound in a room bounces off walls and spreads in ways that shape what listeners hear. Sungho Lee and five co-authors present DART, a fast computer method that tracks how sound energy moves between small patches of a room's surfaces. Their work builds on an older method that treats walls as having flexible material traits.

Because DART can be tuned step by step, users can adjust wall materials and see how the sound field changes. Tests show it predicts sound for new speaker and listener spots well, even when few measurements are given. It beats older signal methods and neural nets on those sparse tests, stays easy to read, and comes with open code.
arxiv-2509-16346:
Airborne laser scans map a forest canopy well but miss the tangled growth beneath it, which ground scans catch at high cost. Juan Castorena and three co-authors train a generative model to infer that hidden undergrowth from the canopy view alone. The model learns from paired air and ground scans of the same woods, so its guesses stay true to the real layout.

At tree, plot, and landscape scales, the fake ground scans match real ones in shape and in measures like tree height and crown size. A new quality score helps judge outputs where no ground truth exists. Richer forest maps aid fire and ecology work.
arxiv-2509-16446:
Recommendation models that generate item codes can stumble when two like items receive the very same code. Ruohan Zhang and three co-authors insist the codes stay purely semantic, with no random tag tacked on to split ties. They loosen the usual nearest-center rule and give two methods that assign each item a unique code while keeping its meaning.

Tests span series recommendation, product search, and document retrieval. Both methods lifted overall results and did even better for cold-start items with little history. The lesson is that code uniqueness itself, not extra tokens, drives much of the gain.
arxiv-2509-16646:
Xiyong Yan studies loops in signed graphs in a 2025 solo math paper. Each edge in the graph carries a label from a small set. A loop that visits every vertex once is called Hamiltonian. Its total label, summed around the loop, is its double sign. Yan asks when loops can achieve all four possible signs.

He proves that three distinct signs among small triangles are enough. The proof leans on triangle bases in a binary cycle space. It also uses the structure of tiny subgraphs and builds loops by hand. The result ties a local clue, signs on triangles, to a global trait of the whole graph.
arxiv-2509-16846:
Aryan Dhar, Siddhant Gautam, and Saiprasad Ravishankar speed MRI scans in a 2025 medical paper. MRI can skip some data and still rebuild a good image, if the skipped pattern is chosen well. A pattern tuned to each scan beats a fixed one. Their network predicts such a pattern from low-frequency data at scan time.

Tests used a public knee dataset with many coils. Image quality matched top prior methods at high speed-up rates. The cost of predicting a mask does not grow with the training set size. Faster scans mean less time in the machine for patients and more scans per day for hospitals.
arxiv-2509-17546:
Nathan Grieve, writing alone, works on stability theory for projective varieties in a 2025 arXiv paper. His tools are CM-line bundles, built from the Chow-Mumford line bundle theory of Arezzo and co-authors, with key insights from Paul and Tian. The paper gives an explicit intersection-theoretic account of Donaldson-Futaki invariants, the numbers that test K-stability.

The invariants here arise by deforming to the normal cone along subschemes, for line bundles that are big and nef rather than ample. That step generalizes the slope stability theory of Ross and Thomas to the broader bundle class. A load-bearing fact is that the CM-line bundles vary continuously with the ample cone. The paper is dense, technical work aimed at specialists in K-stability, where explicit formulas for these invariants guide both proofs and examples.
arxiv-2509-17646:
Denis Burgarella and seven co-authors lay out survey plans for a future far-infrared space observatory. Their 2025 arXiv paper describes PRIMA, a cryogenically cooled mission expected to serve astronomers by the early 2030s. Its PRIMAger instrument will image from the mid to the far infrared, with hyperspectral, photometric, and polarimetric modes.

The paper defines the General Observer programmes, above all a wide survey covering a quarter of the sky. That survey would gather data on millions of galaxies out to large redshifts. Medium-resolution spectra can trace dust and gas emission line by line, while the broad bands and polarization add shape and magnetic clues. The authors present the survey as the shared backbone that guest observers will build on, with smaller targeted programmes filling the rest of the mission's open time.
arxiv-2509-17746:
Yuval Kern and nine co-authors photograph single flashes of an intense quantum light source, one shot at a time. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies bright squeezed vacuum, a state with no mean field but wild swings in photon number. It is strong enough to drive extreme nonlinear processes, yet the shape of a single pulse had never been fully pinned down.

The team built a femtosecond source in a single spatial mode and read each shot with spectral interferometry against a known reference pulse. The group delay stayed consistent from shot to shot. The mean pulse length came out far shorter than the pump pulse, with a modest spread across shots. The interferograms also show a nodal pattern that betrays the source's random phase flip of half a cycle. The authors argue this light is a viable femtosecond source for probing ultrafast electron dynamics.
arxiv-2509-17846:
Timmi G Jorgensen and Ross P Church model young star clusters in the galaxy M51. Their 2025 paper asks how hits with giant gas clouds shape the fate of those clusters. They run thousands of cluster sims, each twice: with cloud hits and without.

Most seen mass and age trends in M51 came out of the runs. Old, light clusters near the galaxy core were the most prone to break up. Cloud hits cut the chance to survive for old light clusters by a fair share. In a few cases, cloud hits oddly shielded a cluster and helped it keep more stars.
arxiv-2509-18046:
Yinuo Wang and 4 co-authors train a humanoid robot to walk with a Mamba encoder at its core. Their 2025 frame, HuMam, learns control end to end, from body state to joint targets. Past such policies can train in a shaky way, fuse inputs poorly, or burn too much power.

One Mamba layer blends body state, footstep goals, and a phase clock. A reward with six parts weighs contact, swing, foot place, posture, and body steadiness. On a known humanoid in a sim, HuMam learned faster and ran with more stability than a strong base policy. It also cut power use and peak joint force.
arxiv-2509-18146:
Madi Yerlanov, Qi Wang, and Nancy Rodriguez model crime, targets, and guardians as a three-way moving system. Their 2025 paper builds a flow-and-spread model of a city, with police as an active third part. Past crime models held two parts; adding guardians changes the maths and the tale.

With classic split tools, they set exact terms for when a flat state breaks. Past a policing threshold, hotspots can lock in or pulse in cycles. Guard moves act as the tipping force in that split. Sims show still patterns, pulses, and even chaos. The frame gives new tools for multi-agent social systems.
arxiv-2509-18346:
Fast methods for finding the lowest point of a smooth function often use momentum, a push from past steps. M Parimi and four co-authors revisit why the famous Nesterov method speeds up at all. Their 2025 paper argues that most past accounts work backward from the method to a matching equation. That reverse route, they say, hides the deeper reason for the speed-up.

Instead, the team starts from control theory tools and builds the dynamics first. Their frame explains each term in the Nesterov method and the order of its steps. It covers both strongly curved and plain curved cases. The same frame also yields the triple momentum method's speed-up. It even explains why the older heavy-ball method can fail to reach the best point. The goal is a clear origin story for acceleration.
arxiv-2509-18746:
Difference equations with fractional orders model systems whose present depends on a long past. Janardhan Chevala and Sachin Bhalekar study a linear equation with two fractional difference operators in this 2025 paper. The two orders sit between zero and one. They give a sequence form of the solution that is easier to work with.

A Z-transform approach then traces where the stable region ends, working in the complex plane. When one coefficient turns slightly negative, that boundary folds into multiple points. The folding creates several separate stability regions. The authors chart all possible bifurcations, the qualitative changes, in terms of the parameters. Many worked examples support the claims. The results help predict when such fractional systems stay stable. That matters for control and signal models built on fractional differences.
arxiv-2509-18946:
Kamaljeet Singh and two co-authors study matter made of quarks and gluons at extreme heat and density. Such matter forms for a brief time when heavy atomic nuclei crash into each other. Heat tends to spread through it, but the authors ask a subtler question: can a heat gradient push particles to drift, and can a particle gradient drive heat to flow?

These two linked effects are named the Soret and Dufour effects, and the team studies them in this setting for the first time from first principles. They use a transport equation for fast-moving particles, with terms for both heat and chemical imbalance. They derive formulas for both effect strengths in the free quark phase and in the later phase made of ordinary particles.
arxiv-2509-19146: O. A. Veliev, writing alone, gives a brief explanation of the spectral expansion method for a class of differential operators on the whole real line. The operators are not self-adjoint, which means their behavior is less tidy than in the classic textbook case, and their coefficients repeat periodically along the line while taking complex values. The note's stated aim is narrow: to explain the expansion problem for these operators clearly and briefly, rather than to report a broad new research program.
arxiv-2509-19446:
Magnetars are neutron stars with magnetic fields beyond a hundred trillion gauss, and Rachael E. Stewart and fifteen co-authors use one to test a quantum prediction about empty space. In such fields the vacuum should act like a crystal, bending light differently by polarization, an effect called vacuum birefringence. It has been predicted for decades but never confirmed. The team coordinated X-ray and radio observations of a radio-loud magnetar with three observatories.

In the soft X-ray band the light is strongly polarized, reaching about sixty-five percent at low energies, then dropping sharply. At some rotation phases the polarization nears eighty percent. Radio and X-ray polarization angles both track the star's rotating field geometry. Standard surface models cannot explain the pattern. Propagation through the birefringent vacuum can. The authors call it a significant advance toward confirming the effect.
arxiv-2509-19646:
Sixth-generation mobile networks are still on the drawing board, and Salma Tika and three co-authors survey where the work stands. They start from the strict demands expected of 6G: very high reliability, wide coverage, and support for huge device counts. Enabling tools include terahertz radio, smart reflecting surfaces, massive antenna arrays, and AI-run network control.

The survey maps likely uses, from automated industry to merged physical and digital spaces. It also lists the hard gaps: hardware limits, energy cost, security, and standards that do not yet exist. As 5G still rolls out, such stock-taking guides research money toward the true bottlenecks. The authors write for both industry and academic readers. The paper serves as a status report on a technology a decade from daily use.
arxiv-2509-19846:
Boreal forests hold a huge share of the world's land carbon, much of it locked in permafrost soils that thaw as the climate warms. Kevin Bradley Dsouza and seven co-authors build BoreaRL, a reinforcement learning playground for managing those forests. Its simulator couples energy, carbon, and water flows on physical grounds. Agents learn harvest and care policies under two modes: one tuned to a single site, one trained to stay robust across random conditions.

Trials expose an asymmetry: gaining carbon is far easier to learn than preventing thaw. Policies that guard permafrost struggle where carbon policies thrive. That gap warns managers that the two goals need unlike strategies. A shared testbed lets algorithms compete on the trade-off openly. Climate adaptation needs such tools before thaw locks in losses.
arxiv-2509-19946:
Slurred, hard-to-parse speech from conditions such as cerebral palsy or Parkinson's is called dysarthria, and detecting it automatically could speed referrals. Lovisa Wihlborg and ten co-authors grade seventeen ready-made speech embedding systems on that task. Six datasets of varied origin supply the tests. Small, skewed recordings make naive scores untrustworthy, so repeated cross-validation runs are compared against a crafted null model.

Only scores that beat the null distribution count as real detection. Within one dataset, results swung widely by dataset, whatever the system. Training on one dataset and testing on another exposed still sharper drops. The study is a reality check for a field short on data. Clinics need detectors that travel across recording setups, not just leaderboards.
arxiv-2509-20046:
Fiber optic cables can listen: scattered light reveals sounds along their length. Knut H. Grythe and Jan Erik Håkegård localize an underwater acoustic source with a fiber read from both ends. Their transceiver setup works in forward mode rather than backscatter. A bistatic radar analogy guides the design: two vantage points, one source.

Delay differences between the signals arriving at the two ends fix the source position. Standard distributed acoustic sensing localizes along the fiber; this scheme adds position finding for communication sources. Underwater acoustic links serve vehicles, sensors, and divers where radio fails. Knowing where a caller sits, not just what it said, aids coordination and rescue. The proposal integrates that positioning into the decoding setup.
arxiv-2509-20346:
Sensors built at exceptional points promise extreme sensitivity. Todd Darcie and J. Stewart Aitchison test that promise against noise in a 2025 arXiv paper. At such a point, a sensor's split in tone grows as a root of the push it feels, which hints at endless response. In ideal linear gear, shot noise grows just as fast, so the gain cancels out. Nonlinear gear was predicted to show new blow-ups.

The team studies two linked resonators with gain that can saturate. When the noise math is done with full care, the predicted blow-ups vanish. Patches of instability ring the exceptional point, where phase noise leaks into the size of the wave. Those patches cap both the response and the noise a real sensor can reach. Full stochastic runs of the system back the math, right down to zero detuning.
arxiv-2509-20446:
The faintest galaxy yet confirmed at extreme distance is measured by Marusa Bradac and twenty-two co-authors in a 2025 arXiv letter. A massive cluster, the Bullet Cluster, magnifies the galaxy about fourteenfold, acting as a cosmic lens. Spectroscopy with the James Webb Space Telescope confirmed its redshift near eleven. Its light dates from the universe's first few hundred million years.

Webb imaging and spectra reveal three star-forming clumps, two of them smaller than ten parsecs across. The clumps hold about half of the galaxy's total stellar mass. Most of its stars formed in a burst roughly one hundred fifty million years before the epoch observed. A damping wing in the spectrum signals neutral gas along the line of sight, typical so deep in the reionization era. Despite the magnification, the galaxy's true luminosity is the lowest yet confirmed at such distances.
arxiv-2509-20746:
Designing an optimization algorithm usually means guessing a method and then proving it works. Ibrahim Ozaslan and four co-authors automate that process in a 2025 paper accepted for the IEEE Conference on Decision and Control. They target strongly convex problems with linear equality constraints.

Their approach grows out of robust control theory, which merges design and analysis into one step. The synthesis yields a single-loop, gradient-based algorithm. Its convergence rate does not depend on the condition number of the constraint matrix, an improvement over earlier algorithms. Because the framework exposes performance limits first, the resulting method is built to sit near those limits. The paper shows how control theory can systematize algorithm design.
arxiv-2509-20946:
Laser power meters must measure energy accurately, but scratches and heat damage on their sensor coatings skew readings. Dongqi Zheng, Wenjin Fu, and Guangzong Chen present a real-time inspection system in a 2025 paper. The system runs on the device and learns without labeled defect examples.

Their framework trains only on images of good sensors, learning what a normal coating looks like. Anything that departs from that pattern is flagged as an anomaly, whether or not that defect type was seen before. Preprocessing uses edge detection and clustering to isolate the coating area. The authors target medical and industrial lasers, where bad measurements carry real costs. Unsupervised learning sidesteps the need for large labeled defect libraries.
arxiv-2509-21446:
Forecasting seismic waves before they arrive could help future gravitational wave detectors cancel ground noise. Waleed Esmail and 3 co-authors built a transformer model for that task in a 2025 paper. The setting is the planned Einstein Telescope, a next generation observatory. The model, SeismoGPT, learns from three component seismic waveforms directly.

Trained in an autoregressive way, the model predicts step by step from past motion. It can run on a single station or on an array of stations. Learned time and space patterns give realistic ground motion forecasts. Accuracy is strong in the immediate window and fades further ahead, as expected. The authors frame the work as groundwork for Newtonian noise mitigation and real time control.
arxiv-2509-21646:
Making X-ray photoelectron spectra of strongly linked molecules needs multireference methods that stay fast. Shuhang Li and 2 co-authors formulate such a method in a 2025 paper. Their approach joins core valence splitting with an equation of motion driven similarity renormalization group. Core ionization values come out accurately with favourable scaling in basis set size. A modification of the ground state formalism ensures rigorous core intensivity.

Three variants are developed and compared. Two derive from low order perturbative approximations, at second and third order. One uses a non perturbative scheme truncated to one and two body operators. Benchmarks compute vertical core ionization values for a representative molecular test set. The variants are weighed on hit rate and robustness for strongly linked systems.
arxiv-2509-21746:
Wrong labels are common in real data sets, and most sample-picking methods act as if they were not there. They also force the user to fix in advance how much data to cut. Brian B. Moser and six co-authors built HyperCore to handle both problems. Their 2025 paper offers a coreset method that adapts on its own.

HyperCore fits a simple ball-shaped model, called a hypersphere, for each class in the data. Points of a class should sit near the ball's center, while stray or mislabeled points sit far away. A standard statistic then sets the cut level with no hand tuning. In tests, the method beat its rivals most clearly when labels were noisy or data was scarce, keeping small samples that still teach a model well.
arxiv-2509-21846:
Lu Wei, writing alone, works out exact formulas for a basic quantity in quantum information in this 2025 paper. The quantity is relative entropy, a measure of how different two quantum states are. Wei studies it for random states, drawn from two standard families of random state models. The goal is the average value of the measure when both states are picked at random.

Wei derives exact, explicit formulas for that average, for states of any size. The formulas cover two states from the same family and pairs drawn from two different families. A key step is a splitting pattern the author spots in the averages after doing a hard integral over rotations. For one family, the new exact formula completes earlier work that had only an approximate version for equal-size states, found by a replica method.
arxiv-2509-22246:
Xiaoyang Liu and seven co-authors build a better ruler for judging automatic translation of math statements into formal language. Autoformalization is growing, but scoring its output is hard: string comparisons ignore meaning, while proof-based checks give no graded score when a proof fails. Their 2025 framework, ASSESS, accepted at ICLR 2026, scores a formal statement on both meaning and structure.

On those trees, a new metric measures edit distance while allowing semantic transformations, so equivalent rewrites are not punished as errors. To validate it, the team built a benchmark of over a thousand expert-annotated statement pairs from two known collections. Each pair is labeled both for whether one statement can prove the other and for how alike they are structurally. On that benchmark, the new metric beat existing methods on accuracy and on agreement with the human labels.
arxiv-2509-22546:
Jinfeng Zhou and 6 co-authors teach language models to reason about social life, not just logic puzzles. Logic training gives step-by-step deduction toward checkable answers. Social scenes instead demand reading ambiguous cues with no single right outcome. Their paradigm, Cognitive Reasoning, breaks that reading into linked units like observation and attribution, which combine as needed.

Their framework, CogFlow, first builds data by simulating human-like thought with tree-structured planning. Fine-tuning installs the basic skill. Reinforcement learning then refines it, with rewards for both the thought flow and the final reply. Tests showed clear gains in social decision-making for models, and even for humans who used the approach.
arxiv-2509-22846:
Philippe-André Luneau and Jean Deteix accelerate fixed point iterations with a reduced model built on the fly. Fixed point schemes solve nonlinear equations, optimization problems, and dynamical systems across the sciences. Reduced-order modeling shrinks such problems, but classic versions need offline training and a precomputed basis tied to one geometry. Their on-the-fly version builds a low-dimensional, self-correcting approximation during the iteration itself.

When the iteration map is contractive, inexact fixed point theory keeps the error within a user-set tolerance. Error estimates propagate through block Gauss-Seidel steps for systems of partial differential equations. A multiphysics lid-driven cavity flow in two and three dimensions illustrates the method. The authors also probe when speedups appear and where the method's limits lie.
arxiv-2509-22946:
Matthias Beck, Benjamin Braun, and Alvaro Cornejo study generating functions for q-chromatic polynomials. These polynomials count proper graph colorings, weighted by a chosen linear form. A recent paper showed the count is a polynomial in a q-analog sum. Beck and his co-authors ask what these counts can tell apart.

For one set of weights, the polynomial can tell apart all labeled graphs on a fixed vertex set. Using permutation statistics and polyhedral geometry, they find a formula for the full generating function. For the all-ones weights, they rewrite the polynomial in a q-binomial basis. Some numerator coefficients turn out to be palindromic in q.
arxiv-2509-23346: A short comment paper on Kahler Ricci flow clears up one definition. Xiuxiong Chen and Bing Wang clarify what polarized canonical radius means in a recent study of Laplace comparison on Kahler Ricci flow and convergence. The note is brief and definitional, aimed at readers of that earlier work. The note adds no new theorems or data. It pins down the term so that later work on the flow can use it in one shared sense.
arxiv-2509-23546:
Flood analysts lean on a 1949 formula that links two ways of stating how rare an extreme event is. Francesco Dell'Aira and 2 co-authors extend Langbein's formula to cases its assumptions miss. The formula ties the return period from annual maxima to the average recurrence interval from peak-over-threshold counts. It assumes exceedance counts follow a steady Poisson process, which real rivers can break.

Three breaks are covered: conditions that drift over time, mixed populations of events, and counts that spread more or less than Poisson predicts. For the first two, the classic form survives once terms are redefined. Spread in counts needs a wider form, with the classic result as a limiting case.
arxiv-2509-23746:
Vision-language models point at objects far worse than people do, partly because they must answer in one shot. Wenjie Yang and Zengfeng Huang propose Poivre, a self-refining loop named for its steps: point, visualize, then refine. The model marks its guessed point on the image, looks again, and adjusts if needed, like a person checking a fingertip. Reinforcement learning trains that habit, guided by a process reward with tidy theoretical properties.

Their trained model, Poivre-7B, set a new best score on Point-Bench. It beat closed models such as Gemini-2.5-Pro and large open ones such as Molmo-72B by over three percent. Code, data, and the model are released.
arxiv-2509-24046:
Picking a business partner means weighing many firms on mixed facts: numbers, types, and free text. Lingyao Li and 7 co-authors built PartnerMAS, a team of language-model agents that splits this job into layers. A planner sets the plan, expert agents judge set parts, and a boss agent merges their views.

To test the system, the team built a data set from venture capital deals, where true partner groups are known. Across well over a hundred cases, PartnerMAS matched true groups more often than a lone agent or a debate-style team. Gains reached about a tenth or more. The split of roles, not a bigger model, drove the edge.
arxiv-2509-24346:
Highest weight modules of exceptional Lie algebras carry two key invariants that are hard to compute by hand. Zhanqiang Bai and 3 co-authors develop an explicit algorithm that finds both for any infinitesimal character. The first invariant, the Gelfand-Kirillov dimension, measures the module's growth. The second, its annihilator variety, is the closure of a nilpotent orbit of twice that dimension.

The method reduces the dimension to a known function on a Weyl group, then splits the root system into factors.
