arxiv-2510-23546:
Rui-Hao Li, Semeon Valgushev, and Khadijeh Najafi work on preparing Gibbs states, the quantum states that describe systems in thermal balance. A key step, computing the von Neumann entropy, is costly and hard to store for large systems. The team uses matrix product states, a compact classical format, to judge and tune the preparation circuits without storing the full quantum state.

They test two circuit layouts on small spin chains, including the transverse-field Ising and XXZ models. One layout, based on a thermofield-double design, did better at high temperature, while a hardware-friendly layout did better when cooling. They also find a ceiling on the entropy the second layout can hold, set by its layering. On larger test grids, an interleaved layout usually cut free-energy errors, though it costs far more classical computing as ancilla qubits grow.
arxiv-2510-23646:
R. Scott Johnson introduces Hamming Graph Metrics, a way to compare graphs by their connection patterns at every distance at once. Classic centrality scores rank how important single nodes are, but they miss whether a network's multi-scale wiring is unusual or redundant. That structural fingerprint matters for judging resilience and function, yet tools for it have been thin.

The framework encodes a graph as a stack of tables recording which node pairs sit exactly k steps apart, for every k. The distance between two graphs is then a Hamming-style count of mismatches across that stack. Johnson proves the measure ignores relabeling, behaves as a true metric, and stays stable when edges change, with explicit bounds. Around it he builds per-scale spectral summaries, node and graph-level dissimilarity scores, and extremal results. The package gives network scientists a principled ruler for structural difference.
arxiv-2510-23746:
Laura Mismetti and three co-authors build a system that reads a molecule's structure straight from its tandem mass spectrum. Mass spectrometry is a workhorse for identifying unknown small molecules in metabolomics, natural products, and environmental work. Yet the shattering process is probabilistic, chemical space is vast, and today's tools mostly match against databases of known spectra or chain several costly steps.

Their transformer framework takes the spectrum plus the molecular formula and generates candidate structures end to end, with no hand-built annotations between. Pretraining on simulated spectra supplies transfer learning, and a test-time tuning step adapts the model to fresh experimental data on the spot. On two benchmarks it beat conventional fine-tuning clearly, and even wrong answers stayed chemically close to the truth, scoring high on structural similarity. The authors pitch the tool as guidance for experts facing spectra nobody has seen before.
arxiv-2510-24046:
Tu Anh Hoang Nguyen and five co-authors propose a new way to make fake table data that still respects cause and effect. Real tables are often blocked by privacy rules, so teams make copies instead. Older methods match basic patterns in the data but can break the links between causes and results.

Their method, CA-GAN, first learns a cause graph from the real data and then builds the fake data step by step along that graph. A reward signal also pushes the fake data to keep the same cause links. Tests show strong use for later tasks while keeping privacy and data quality high.
arxiv-2510-24346:
Benjamin D. C. Lowe and seven co-authors present a detailed chemical analysis of sixteen candidate metal poor stars using the X-Shooter spectrograph. The stars were first flagged by an earlier survey, and the team confirms their low metal content with spectral synthesis software. Six stars prove extremely metal poor, with iron below one thousandth of the solar level.

Two of those stars, including the most metal poor in the sample, are kinematically tied to the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger event, raising its known extremely metal poor members to eight. The team measures abundances for sixteen elements, generally matching high resolution studies. This is the first paper in a series on unusual chemistry in halo stars.
arxiv-2510-24446:
Viktoriia Zinkovich leads a team of nine authors on AI vision safety. Reasoning segmentation asks a model to outline things named in words. A user might ask for the object that fits a short text clue. Past safety work mostly warped the image to fool the model. The team instead warps the words while keeping the same meaning.

Their method, SPARTA, rewrites a query so the mask gets worse. The rewrite must stay smooth, grammatical, and true to the first sense. A text autoencoder gives a small space where rewrites are searched. Learning from rewards guides that search without seeing model internals. SPARTA beat prior methods by up to two times on two data sets. Even top models proved weak against careful word swaps.
arxiv-2510-25546: Tommaso Grigoletto, Lorenza Viola, and Francesco Ticozzi shrink models of quantum systems. Their 2025 paper deals with Markov type systems under outside control. The rules of motion change with time in such systems. Their method builds on Krylov spaces and algebra tools made for fixed rules. The small model tracks the key read-outs of the full one in an exact way. It also keeps the Lindblad form that such rules must have.
arxiv-2510-25646:
Elias Fink, Carlo Contaldi, and Giorgio Mentasti cross-correlate gravitational wave observables. Astrometric and timing residuals from distant sources are mixed. Pulsars and galaxies supply those distant observables. Nearby solar system bodies give equivalent observables. A unified spin-weighted formalism derives angular correlations.

They compute expected signal-to-noise and sensitivity for readings. Focus falls on pulsar timing array redshift signals. Pulsar-only surveys currently constrain backgrounds more strongly. The method offers a complementary higher-frequency probe. Future wide-field surveys could reach sub-milliarcsecond precision. That could make the method viable for finding. Varied reading domains share fewer systematic errors. The technique bridges pulsar and LISA frequency bands.
arxiv-2510-25846:
Luis A. Anchordoqui, Dieter Lust, and Severin Lust set out a short note on what they call species quantum mechanics. In gravity theories, the species number counts how many light particle types exist, and a tower mass scale marks where a tower of heavy states begins. Both ideas appear in the swampland distance idea, which limits how far field values can move in a valid theory.

Anchordoqui and his co-authors treat the species number and tower scale as quantum operators with partner variables. They discuss the commutation rules, a possible wave function, and duality swaps between the partners. They argue a known pattern in these theories follows from those basic rules, and they link the setup to Calabi Yau geometry.
arxiv-2510-25946:
Brandon Massett and Walter Shmayda test whether a saturated drying bed can prefer heavy water over light water. Dryer beds with molecular sieves, materials full of tiny pores, are used in fusion plants to trap tritiated water vapor, where tritium is a heavy form of hydrogen. A passive control system could exploit a bed that favors heavier forms of water.

Massett and Shmayda send a humid heavy water stream through a bed first saturated with light water. Clear displacement appears, as heavy water takes over and light water leaves. After capture, the rise in heavy water pressure depends on its humidity, with higher humidity giving faster, steeper transfer that fits a sigmoid curve well.
arxiv-2510-26246:
Alcides Gomes Andrade Junior and Akira Matsubayashi show a limit on using quantum walks to solve the maximum matching problem. A matching pairs up vertices of a graph, and the maximum matching problem asks for the largest possible set of pairs with no vertex reused. Quantum algorithms are judged by query complexity, the number of input lookups, and the best known quantum algorithm beats the trivial bound but may not be optimal.

Quantum walks turn a classical random walk search into a quantum search and have given tight results elsewhere. Andrade Junior and Matsubayashi prove that, when the underlying classical walk does not depend on the input graph. In that case this technique cannot improve the known query bound. Any such design also carries a time cost beyond polynomial limits in their analysis.
arxiv-2510-26346:
Robin Schmöcker, Alexander Dockhorn, and Bodo Rosenhahn study how game-playing search programs can work faster. Their field is Monte Carlo tree search, a method that tests many possible moves and keeps score for each. Grouping states that act alike lets a program share those scores, but in noisy games or games with many moves, such groups are hard to find.

The three authors prove why the groups stay rare, then loosen the grouping rule a little. Their method, called IPA-UCT, gives up a small amount of exactness and finds far more groups. In tests across many domains and time budgets it beat the older OGA-UCT method. The paper also shows how both methods fit inside one wider frame.
arxiv-2510-26846:
Tomasz Matulewicz reports a measurement from the NA61/SHINE experiment at CERN that models of hadron production cannot explain. Isospin symmetry, rooted in the similar masses of up and down quarks, predicts equal numbers of charged and neutral kaons from collisions of isospin-symmetric nuclei. The experiment measured kaon production in argon-scandium collisions at a centre-of-mass energy of eleven point nine giga-electronvolts per nucleon pair.

Matulewicz reports that charged kaon production at mid-rapidity is about eighteen percent higher than neutral kaon production. The stated uncertainty is about six percent. Models of hadron production, including the known effects that break isospin symmetry, fail to account for the gap. The result stands as an open puzzle for hadron physics.
arxiv-2510-26946:
Rebeca Beltran, Chandan Hati, Martin Hirsch, and Ana Martin-Galan study two proposed new particles at the Large Hadron Collider. Heavy neutral leptons are heavy cousins of neutrinos, and axion-like particles are light particles that may link to them. If the second type couples strongly to gluons, the particles that hold quarks together, the collider should make many of them.

The team simulates how future detectors, including the main ATLAS detector and planned far detectors, could spot long-lived heavy neutral leptons made through this route. For very heavy axion-like particles, production acts through a high-order interaction with gluons. The results map where the high-luminosity collider could reach new ground.
arxiv-2510-27246:
Mohammad Tavakoli leads five co-authors in BEAM, a benchmark for long-term memory in language models, plus LIGHT, a memory system that improves it. Existing memory tests often lack narrative coherence, cover narrow domains, and probe only simple recall. The team first builds a framework that auto-generates long, coherent, diverse conversations up to ten million tokens with probing questions across many memory abilities.

BEAM itself holds a hundred conversations and two thousand validated questions. Even models with million-token windows, with or without retrieval help, struggle as dialogues lengthen. LIGHT adds three human-inspired stores: episodic long-term memory, short-term working memory, and a scratchpad for salient facts. It improves every backbone tested, and ablations confirm each component contributes, clarifying what long conversations demand.
arxiv-2510-27446:
Daniel Plummer, Pontus Svensson, and four other co-authors model hot, dense plasma with moving wave packets in this 2025 paper. Dense plasma, gas stripped of electrons at high pressure, sits inside stars and fusion tests. Part of it stays ionized, part binds back into atoms. Tracking both parts at once is hard.

Their method, wavepacket molecular dynamics, follows atoms as fuzzy packets rather than points. A chemical model counts bound states, the allowed orbits of still-attached electrons. Charge shares come from minimizing free energy, the usable energy of the system. Hydrogen serves as the test case. They compare steady traits like structure against path integral Monte Carlo data, a trusted heavy method. The comparison shows where their lighter model's shortcuts hold and where they strain.
arxiv-2511-00146:
Michael Landry and Mingda Li introduce chimeric states of matter, phases where traits of broken and unbroken symmetry coexist in a way enabled by mixed anomalies of higher-form symmetries. Ordinary sorting says solids break translation symmetry and superconductors break gauge symmetry, but anomaly-based generalization widens the options. Their headline example concerns the Meissner effect, the pushing out of magnetic fields taken as the key sign of superconductivity.

Using an effective field theory building, they show that effect can occur in media that are lossy or even insulating under electric probing. Condensed matter readers get a phase concept that scrambles textbook expectations, splitting magnetic pushing out from superconductivity itself.
arxiv-2511-00346:
Kayua Oleques Paim and four co-authors report an attack method against large language models that exploits gaps in their latent space, the internal map where meanings are encoded. Sparse training data leaves discontinuities in that map, and the authors craft inputs that steer models through them. The aim is twofold: universal jailbreaks that bypass safety rules, and extraction of data the model should not reveal.

Unlike many earlier attacks tuned to one system, theirs transferred across seven leading language models and one image generator. Even layered defenses failed to hold consistently in their tests. The authors frame the flaw as architectural, not a surface bug, which would make it a systemic risk that model makers need to address at the design level.
arxiv-2511-00446:
Xin Yao and five co-authors attack CLIP, the model that learns to match images with text from web-scale data. Because CLIP trains on uncurated internet pairs, poisoned data can plant hidden backdoors. Most studied attacks poison images, leaving the text channel oddly unexamined. Their framework, ToxicTextCLIP, crafts adversarial texts that corrupt the model during pre-training itself.

Two hurdles shape the design: poisoned texts must fit the target class's background, and such background-matched texts are scarce. A selector picks texts whose backgrounds align with the target, and an augmenter generates more coherent, varied samples in that style. In classification and retrieval tests the attack reached very high poisoning and backdoor success rates, and it slipped past three published defenses. The study exposes text as a serious entry point for supply-chain attacks on foundation models.
arxiv-2511-00546:
Loukas Kokkinos and Joo-Von Kim survey the behavior of spin-torque vortex oscillators, nanoscale devices where magnetic vortices spin and emit microwave signals. Most studies fix one layer as a polarizer that drives the other. Here both layers are free vortices, and each acts as the moving polarizer for the other, doubling the interplay and the possible dynamics.

Extensive micromagnetic simulations, run with the open-source Mumax3 code and the authors' own coupled equations, map how the relative vortex arrangement and layer asymmetry shape current-driven motion. Regimes include self-modulated gyration, where the orbit rhythmically swells and shrinks, and a distinct C-state pattern. Chaotic transitions between steady gyration and the C-state also appear. The overview helps designers predict which regime a dual-layer device will land in.
arxiv-2511-00746:
Andrew Moore links two computing worlds that rarely meet: Ising machines and neural networks. Ising model computation powers quantum annealers, adiabatic quantum computers, and thermodynamic classical devices, and tradition equates the computed answer with the machine's ground state, its lowest energy configuration. Moore generalizes the picture from ground states to spin averages, letting computation happen at high temperatures instead of only in the cold ground state.

On that basis he builds a systematic correspondence between Ising devices and neural networks, plus a simple method to run trained feed-forward networks on Ising-type hardware. A mathematical proof shows these implementations always succeed. For builders of unconventional hardware, the result means a trained network need not wait for specialized chips: it can be compiled onto the physics of spins.
arxiv-2511-00846:
Zhihao Peng and a large team introduce OmniBrainBench, a benchmark for testing how well multimodal language models read brain images. Existing question answering benchmarks cover few imaging types or only coarse descriptions of disease, so they miss much of the clinical workflow.

The benchmark spans fifteen imaging modalities from thirty verified medical sources, with more than nine thousand validated question pairs and over thirty thousand images. Its fifteen tasks follow clinical stages and were checked by a professional radiologist. Testing twenty four leading models, the team finds the best proprietary model scores far below physicians. All models struggle with complex reasoning before surgery, exposing a gap between seeing an image and clinical judgment.
arxiv-2511-00946:
Fenglong Song, Roland Schwan, Yuwen Chen, and Colin Jones speed up a core computation inside the PIQP optimization solver. Multistage problems, such as model predictive control and racing trajectory planning, repeatedly produce Karush-Kuhn-Tucker systems, the linear equations an interior point method must solve at every step.

Their contribution is a parallel Cholesky factorization and triangular solve designed for the block structured matrices these problems generate, with a banded part plus an arrow shaped border. It is implemented as a new backend for PIQP and released as open source. On chain of masses benchmarks and on a minimum curvature racing line problem, the solver shows substantial speed gains over other state of the art solvers.
arxiv-2511-01046:
Vedant Acharya and colleagues show VayuChat, a conversational tool for air quality analysis in India, where air pollution contributes to about one point six million early deaths each year. The data needed for decisions sit scattered across agencies, and existing tools demand expertise and offer only static dashboards.

VayuChat lets users ask plain language questions about air quality, weather, and policy programs. Answers come back as both executable Python code and interactive charts. The system unifies monitoring data from the Central Pollution Control Board, state level demographic data, and funding records from the National Clean Air Programme, all driven by a large language model. The platform is publicly deployed for policymakers, researchers, and citizens.
arxiv-2511-01446: Eva Horvat studies the symmetries inside a link diagram's cube of smoothings, a knot theory structure where each crossing can be resolved in two ways, generating a cube of related surfaces. A labeled barycentric subdivision adds extra combinatorial structure to that cube. She studies the symmetries preserving this structure, and from them constructs a combinatorial link invariant based on the symmetries of triangulated smoothings.
arxiv-2511-01646:
Bastian Castorene, Francisco Peña, Martin Groves, and Patricio Vargas count, exactly, the states of a classic magnet model at its critical point. The one-dimensional antiferromagnetic Ising chain, spins on a line preferring to oppose their neighbors, has a ground-state level crossing when the magnetic field reaches twice the coupling strength.

At that crossing, the number of ground states follows the Fibonacci sequence for open chains and the Lucas sequence for closed rings. The authors extend the counting to the full excitation spectrum: states are built from topological defects counted through Diophantine equations and repeated Fibonacci convolutions. Open chains step through energies in units of twice the coupling, rings in units of four times, and near full polarization some top energy levels are strictly forbidden. Closed forms and residual entropies follow.
arxiv-2511-01846:
Thang Luong and a large team of collaborators introduce IMO-Bench. It is a benchmark suite pitched at the level of the International Mathematical Olympiad. It measures real mathematical reasoning in foundation models, rather than easy short answers. Every problem was vetted by a panel of top specialists.

IMO-AnswerBench holds 400 diverse Olympiad problems with verifiable short answers. IMO-ProofBench goes further, grading full proof writing at basic and advanced levels with detailed grading guidelines for automatic scoring. The benchmarks were central to the team's gold-level Gemini Deep Think result at IMO 2025. The model scored 80 percent on AnswerBench and about 66 percent on the advanced ProofBench. It beat the best non-Gemini models by wide margins. A companion GradingBench, with a thousand human-graded proofs, supports progress in automatic evaluation.
arxiv-2511-02046:
Soham Joshi, Shwet Kamal Mishra, and Viswanath Gopalakrishnan tackle a data bottleneck for systems that answer questions about text visible in images, such as signs and labels. Building such datasets normally needs skilled human annotators, which is slow and costly. Their alternative is an automated pipeline that manufactures question and answer pairs from scene text in a given image.

The pipeline chains optical character recognition, region detection, caption generation, and question generation, then validates what it produces. The authors report a dataset of about seventy-two thousand question and answer pairs drawn from about forty-four thousand images. They present the method as the first pipeline able to synthesize and check a text-based visual question answering dataset at this scale.
arxiv-2511-02546:
M. H. Naghizadeh Ardabili, Omid Yahyayi Monem, Morteza Nattagh Najafi, and Hosein Mohammadzadeh invent a dial that slides between bosons and fermions, the two great families of quantum particles. Bosons follow Bose-Einstein statistics and fermions Fermi-Dirac statistics. Haldane's exclusion statistics long ago pointed to something in between. Their alpha scheme, built around a changed filling weight, slides between the two. For negative values of its dial setting, it pushes past bosons into a hyperbosonic regime.

Thermodynamic geometry supplies the test: the sign and singularities of its curvature reveal whether the interactions act attractive or repulsive. A crossover temperature marks where the curvature flips sign. Its ratio to the condensation temperature depends only on the dial's setting. In that regime it blows up at certain fugacities, signalling condensation unlike usual Bose condensation.
arxiv-2511-02946:
Srikumar Sastry and six colleagues introduce ProM3E, a model that embeds ecology data of many kinds into one shared space. Field ecology mixes photos, sounds, and text, and a useful model should generate any missing kind from the ones at hand. Their 2025 model learns by masked reconstruction in the embedding space, hiding one modality and inferring it from the rest.

Because the model is probabilistic, it can judge which modality mixes are feasible for a task, in effect learning what is worth fusing. It also supports flipping a query inside the embedding space. Their retrieval method blends cross-modal and same-modal similarity and topped all retrieval tests they ran. Linear probes on the hidden features further showed strong representation learning for ecology tasks.
arxiv-2511-03146:
Kaiyuan Zhang and twenty-one colleagues built MME-CC, a benchmark that probes the visual thinking of multimodal models. Existing tests lean on text reasoning or skip whole kinds of visual cognition. Their 2025 benchmark organizes eleven tasks into three groups: spatial reasoning, geometric reasoning, and knowledge-based reasoning, all grounded in images, with fine-grained scoring per group.

Sixteen leading models took the test. Closed models led overall, with the best near 43 points against about 30 for a strong open rival. Spatial and geometric reasoning stayed weak almost everywhere, at or below thirty percent. The team catalogued common errors: flipped orientations, losing track of objects across views, and ignoring counterfactual instructions. Thinking traces tended to run in three stages: extract, reason, then verify.
arxiv-2511-03446:
Anwesh Ray and Tanushree Shah study the zeros of Alexander polynomials for torus knots and links through an arithmetic lens. The knot-prime analogy has long guided such work. Their family wraps a torus with two winding numbers, and the polynomial is taken against the total linking cover.

As both windings grow, the zeros spread evenly around the unit circle. The authors give an explicit rate at which primitive roots of unity appear among them. A moment sequence for the zero pattern gets a closed-form generating function, capturing finer statistics. Iwasawa invariants for the linked branched covers are also determined, plus growth control from a logarithmic measure. Knot theory and number theory meet cleanly in the shared formulas.
arxiv-2511-03946:
Marcelo P Fiore, Ohad Kammar, Georg Moser, and Sam Staton develop modular abstract syntax trees for programming languages that include second-class sorts. Some calculi, such as call-by-value lambda calculus and call-by-push-value, forbid certain sorts from appearing in variable contexts, which breaks the standard treatment of syntax with binding and substitution.

Banning second-class sorts from variable contexts changes the algebraic picture from monoids in monoidal categories to actions in actegories, the authors argue. Much of the classic development is rebuilt through bicategorical arguments. As an application, substitution lemmas for varieties of call-by-value calculus are proved, giving language designers a firmer formal base.
arxiv-2511-04046:
Guoming Zhang, writing alone, tackles the Kato problem for degenerate elliptic operators of arbitrary even order in weighted spaces. Coefficients are measurable and complex-valued. They satisfy a Garding inequality against a Muckenhoupt weight, extending earlier work by Cruz-Uribe, Martell, and Rios to this broader setting.

As an application, the unweighted Dirichlet, regularity, and Neumann boundary value problems for such operators are solved when the exponent lies close enough to two. Kato-type results link a hard square-root estimate to well-posed boundary problems. Extending them to higher order, degenerate, weighted operators widens the class of equations with a firm boundary theory.
arxiv-2511-04146:
Xiumin Huang, Dong Lai, and Bin Liu calculate the largest eccentricity an inner binary can reach in a restricted hierarchical three-body system. An outer companion perturbs the pair there, and general relativity pushes back. Octupole-order effects can drive extreme eccentricities and orbital flips, while short-range forces can cap that growth.

In highly hierarchical systems, double averaging works well, and flipping orbits share one limiting eccentricity computable from the quadrupole Hamiltonian alone. Adding the Brown Hamiltonian correction for moderate hierarchy does not change that limit. Single-averaging analysis completes the picture. Knowing the cap matters for systems from satellite-planet-star triples to binaries near supermassive black holes.
arxiv-2511-04546:
Goureesankar Sathyanathan and two colleagues improve how sky maps separate signal from foregrounds. Component separation must pull the faint cosmic microwave background out of brighter galactic emission. If the noise model is wrong, the recovered maps and spectral laws pick up bias.

Their extension models linked low-frequency noise as a power law in harmonic space. A modified ridge method sits inside an ensemble-average process for the fit. They derive an analytic correction for the bias that noise creates in foreground leftovers. Tests serve as proof of concept for cleaner microwave background maps from future surveys.
arxiv-2511-04646:
Narjes Nourzad leads four authors with DR. WELL, a framework for embodied multi-agent teamwork. Robot teams must plan together with partial views and limited communication. Planning raw trajectories fails easily, since small timing slips cascade into conflicts.

Symbolic planning raises the level of abstraction and gives agents a shared action vocabulary. DR. WELL runs a two-phase negotiation: agents propose roles with reasons, then commit jointly. Consensus and environment limits shape the final allocation. Each agent then plans and acts on its own symbolic share, which keeps coordination stable while work proceeds.
arxiv-2511-04846:
Jonathan Shaki and two colleagues ask how a principal can persuade agents into a stable matching. Two-sided matching pairs agents by preference, and stability depends on those preferences. In uncertain settings, preferences also reflect what agents believe about the world.

The principal sees the true state and can shape beliefs through Bayesian persuasion. The goal is a stable matching that scores best on the principal's own utility. General cases are intractable on both the matching and persuasion sides. Two special cases get the focus: few agent types, and a second structured setting the authors develop.
arxiv-2511-04946:
Lei Chen and co-authors look at fully homomorphic encryption from the side of storage input and output. This form of encryption lets a machine compute on locked data, which guards user privacy, but its real-world speed has a less studied weak point.

The team tests how storage traffic slows such systems in practice. They report that slow storage can cut the speed of special chips by a very large factor, and can slow graphics chips by a large factor too. Their lessons show where builders must fix data flow, not just math.
arxiv-2511-05146:
Luigi De Masi and co-authors give two variational forms for robust optimal transport, where a network must still partly work when parts of it are damaged. The task weighs build cost against the gain of keeping some flow after harm.

One form models the network as a measure and repair plans as currents, and lets flow switch path after damage, though damage is set as whole closed sets. The other form tracks paths directly. Both frames give math tools to design transport that degrades with grace, a need for roads, grids, and supply lines.
arxiv-2511-05346:
Olaf Adan, Dimitra Dritsa, and Steven Houben introduce semantic interactivity, a way for people at one table to act on a shared display through meaning, not just touch. Most team systems back solo tasks done side by side, not true joint acts.

Their mechanism uses language processing to let a group shape shared content together. It was built into CollEagle, a tabletop system for joint externalization, where a team makes its thoughts visible. The work argues that shared sense-making needs tools built for the group act itself, not a stack of single-user tools.
arxiv-2511-05446:
Zehua Cao and co-authors compute a two-loop correction to superallowed beta decays, the decays that give the sharpest value of the quark mixing term Vud. That reading rests on exact radiative corrections, counted as a series in the charge of the nucleus and the fine structure constant.

They give the first model-free result for the long-distance part at this order, with nuclei treated as heavy point particles. A renormalization group study adds new terms at the next order for double-log parts. Tighter corrections mean a tighter test of whether quark mixing sums as the standard model demands.
arxiv-2511-05746:
Nicola Bariletto, Nhat Ho, and Alessandro Rinaldo make a classic stats method work where its usual summaries break down. Bayesian methods state doubt as a spread of likely values after seeing data. But when the unknown is a grouping of data, or lives in an endless space, a mean or a standard range may not exist at all.

Their method, Conformalized Bayesian Inference, treats the task as a forecast over the space of guesses. From samples alone it gives a best guess, a range with a coverage promise that needs no added premises, and a map of the spread's peaks. A grouping step picks out the main peaks. Tests on fake and real data show the method works at scale.
arxiv-2511-05946:
Ba-Thinh Nguyen and co-authors read pulse signals from face video alone, a technique called remote photoplethysmography. Tiny color changes in the skin betray heart and breathing rates, enabling contactless checks for telemedicine, driver monitoring, and more. The pulse is strongly periodic, yet past methods model that rhythm only weakly.

Their framework, Reperio-rPPG, mixes a relational graph network with a graph transformer to capture the repeating structure of the signal. A tailored mixing augmentation widens the training variety, since data sets in this field are narrow. On three benchmarks the method reached state-of-the-art results. It stayed robust under head motion like talking and walking, and under lighting from dim LED to bright natural light.
arxiv-2511-06146:
Akshar Tumu, Varad Shinde, and Parisa Kordjamshidi use referring expressions, phrases that single out one object in a scene, to probe spatial understanding in vision-language models. Spatial reasoning is core to human cognition, and current models show strain there. Most tests lean on captioning or question answering, which probe the skill only shallowly.

Their platform stresses three hard cases: ambiguous detection, long expressions stacking several spatial relations, and expressions using negation. Both specialized architectures and large models were tested. All struggled, but their strengths split by the kind of spatial meaning involved, such as topological versus directional relations. The authors map which spatial semantics break which models, and point to the research gaps that follow.
arxiv-2511-06446:
Bohan Yu, Wei Huang, and Kang Liu plug live knowledge bases straight into a language model's memory. Retrieval pipelines usually fetch facts with an outside search tool before the model reads them, a chain that can break or lag. SR-KI instead encodes a knowledge base as key-value pairs and loads them into the model's own cache.

Training runs in two stages: first find the model layer best suited to retrieval, then supervise attention at that layer toward the right entries. Retrieval then happens inside the model during a single pass, and updates stay dynamic. The system held forty thousand entries in a seven-billion-parameter model on one graphics card with strong recall.
arxiv-2511-06546:
Nagaraj Vernekar and colleagues introduce LRPayne, a tool that reads stellar chemistry from blurry, low-resolution starlight. Big galactic surveys gather spectra too coarse for classic analysis, yet each spectrum hides a star's temperature, gravity, and elemental mix. A model-driven neural network trained on seventy thousand synthetic spectra does the decoding.

The network predicts what a spectrum should look like for any set of stellar labels, covering two dozen elements. Fitting an observed spectrum then reduces to finding the synthetic match with the smallest error. Tests on benchmark stars and metal-poor stars agreed well with published values for most elements, though a few, like oxygen, stayed stubborn in certain star types.
arxiv-2511-06846:
Federico Vasile, Ri-Zhao Qiu, Lorenzo Natale, and Xiaolong Wang estimate the physical features of objects from video, a task called system identification. Recent methods optimize geometry, appearance, and physics together using differentiable simulation, but they assume flat surfaces for collisions. Real objects collide with curved, complex shapes, where those methods fail.

Their system, AS-DiffMPM, extends the differentiable Material Point Method with a collision mechanism that handles arbitrarily shaped rigid bodies while keeping the whole pipeline differentiable. A falling or rolling object can thus be fitted against the true geometry of what it hits. The system plugs into various novel view synthesis methods, widening the range of scenes where substance features, shape, and appearance can be recovered from plain video observations.
arxiv-2511-07046:
Fabian Kresse and Christoph H Lampert shrink continuous-control reinforcement learning policies until they run on integer-only hardware. Embedded deployments face tight latency and power budgets that small FPGAs can meet, but only if floating-point pipelines are avoided. The authors study quantization-aware training for such policies and build a learning-to-hardware pipeline that automatically selects low-bit policies and synthesizes them onto an Artix-7 FPGA.

Across five MuJoCo control tasks, the selected networks stayed competitive with full-precision policies while using as few as three, or even two, bits per weight and activation. That holds provided input precision was chosen carefully. On the chip they answered in microseconds and consumed microjoules per action, beating a quantized reference design. Unexpectedly, the quantized policies also resisted input noise better than the floating-point baseline.
arxiv-2511-07346:
Sujoy Bhore and co-authors study the Steiner Tree problem on graphs formed where geometric shapes overlap. Given disks, squares, or polygons in the plane, a few marked terminals must be linked through as few extra objects as possible. Planar problems often allow fast methods that grow slowly with solution size.

Here that hope fails. Assuming the Exponential-Time Hypothesis, no algorithm can run in subexponential time in the combined size measures, even for unit disks or unit squares. The hardness result closes a natural line of attack. Algorithm designers learn to seek approximations or different parameters instead of exact subexponential methods.
arxiv-2511-07546:
Edouard Barrier and Nikku Madhusudhan simulate weather on Hycean worlds, a proposed class of ocean planets under hydrogen skies. Such sub-Neptune planets might host liquid oceans and life-friendly conditions. Their three-dimensional climates, though, were largely unexplored before this modeling effort.

A modified global circulation model, built from ExoCAM, treats the temperate planet K2-18 b as a test case. Runs vary surface pressure and reflectivity. The climates behave like slow-rotator locked planets, with either one equatorial jet or twin mid-latitude jets. Knowing likely wind and heat patterns helps observers plan telescope time and interpret spectra from these candidate ocean worlds.
arxiv-2511-07746:
Samuel Yee and Shreyas Vissapragada test why some Neptune-mass planets are puffed to Jupiter size. These popcorn planets hold densities under a third of water, implying internal heat. Too cool for the usual hot Jupiter inflation, they might be swollen by tides flexing on eccentric orbits.

Precise radial velocity tracking with the MAROON-X spectrograph measured the orbits directly. Eccentricities came out too small for tidal heating to inflate the planets now. The title verdict follows: popcorn planets are not actively inflated by eccentricity tides. Another heat source, or a fossil of formation, must explain their fluff.
arxiv-2511-07846:
Xi Chen, Anindya De, and Yizhi Huang recover whole distributions from blurry Fourier clues. Given noisy low-degree Fourier coefficients of an unknown distribution on a high-dimensional torus, can the distribution itself be rebuilt accurately? Earlier answers assumed tidy structure, like separated point sources.

Completely general distributions get an analysis here, with no separation or finite-source assumptions. The recovery question is basic to signal processing, learning theory, and inverse problems. Guarantees without structural crutches mean the method applies where nature has not promised tidiness. Fourier measurements are cheap to collect in many sensors, so broad recovery results multiply their value.
arxiv-2511-08046:
Aya Elgebaly and colleagues present ProSona, a segmentation tool that adapts to individual medical experts through language prompts. Doctors often outline the same lung nodule or prostate scan differently, and averaging their styles into one mask hides real disagreement. Keeping each expert style separate usually needs a branch per annotator.

ProSona instead learns a continuous space of annotation styles on a probabilistic U-Net backbone. Text prompts steer a projection through that space to produce a personalized outline. Contrastive training aligns words and images, and tests on lung and prostate data beat a leading rival on energy distance and Dice score.
arxiv-2511-08246:
Ziyu Ma and colleagues improve many shot multimodal in context learning by choosing carefully where and what task vectors to insert into a model. Showing a model many examples at once runs into context length and cost limits. Task vectors compress those demonstrations into activations, but earlier methods either ignored insertion position or could not pick good values for each spot.

Their sensitivity aware framework finds insertion points from consistent patterns in activation changes across query context pairs. A clustered bank of candidate activations is built for each point, and reinforcement learning selects the best candidate. Tests on several multimodal models and visual question tasks show steady improvements.
arxiv-2511-08346:
Sreeveni Das and colleagues demonstrate reservoir computing in a lithium based magneto ionic device, where computation happens inside the material itself. A voltage controlled crossbar stack with a cobalt iron boron layer and a lithium conducting film produces magnetic domain patterns that change with input voltage. A chaotic Mackey Glass time series is encoded as voltage, and Fourier transforms of the domain patterns form the reservoir output.

Input rate, output smoothing, state size, and training length all shape forecasting skill. Short term prediction favors smoothed, low dimensional states with little training, while prediction near the series delay time prefers raw, high dimensional states and longer training. Faster inputs reduce memory capacity and nonlinear processing strength.
arxiv-2511-08546:
James Ingoldby, Valentin Khoze, and Jessica Turner examine whether metastable cosmic strings could explain the gravitational wave background reported by pulsar timing arrays. They work with a simple dark sector that breaks its symmetry in one step, driven by a single Higgs field.

In their setup the string is stable in classical terms but decays when pairs of monopoles form along it. The authors compute the decay rate using a thin-defect approximation for the string core and the monopole ends. They then map the range of masses and couplings where such a model matches the observed signal. The match holds without extra Higgs fields or multi-stage breaking.
arxiv-2511-08646:
Matheus Pereira and Alexandre Schmidt solve the Schrödinger equation, the basic equation of quantum mechanics, in a coordinate system shaped like a donut. Toroidal coordinates fit ring-shaped systems, but the equation had never been separated and solved exactly in them before.

Using an irregular separation-of-variables method rarely tried in physics, they obtain exact solutions in both the classic Moon and Spencer toroidal system and an electromagnetic toroidal-poloidal variant. A surprise runs through the results: the angular momentum comes out fractional, a direct effect of the hole in the torus. Solutions cover several external potentials, including a magnetic field, and the authors add a plane-wave expansion and a Green function for later work.
arxiv-2511-08746:
Gabriel Wong rebuilds a basic notion in Chern-Simons theory, the physics of a topological quantum field theory, so that it stays truly topological. The usual way to cut the theory into subregions forces a complex structure onto the cut, which breaks topological invariance and makes entanglement entropy diverge.

Wong instead uses a discrete quantizing step, defining a subregion through operator algebras made of functions on a quantum group. A diagram-based method then computes a deformed entanglement entropy carried by anyonic edge modes along the cut. The deformation tames the blow-up and yields a finite entropy tied to a special quantum state. The framework also underpins entanglement work in topological string theory, where a large-N limit of the deformed algebra describes spacetime itself.
arxiv-2511-08946:
Tuhin Subhra De revisits an unfashionable model, the conditional variational autoencoder, and fixes a premise baked into it. Variational autoencoders fell behind diffusion models years ago and are known for blurry, low-diversity images, but they remain simple and steerable when a user wants pictures with chosen traits.

Earlier conditional versions assumed the latent distribution given the labels equals the prior. Real data violates that. De estimates that conditional spread with non-volume-preserving maps, a flexible family of invertible changes, and keeps a trick that treats the decoder's variance as a learnable parameter. The result cuts the FID quality score by about four percent and raises log likelihood by about seven point six percent over previous approaches. The paper is a small, old-school argument that classical generative models still have room to grow.
arxiv-2511-09046:
Jeroen Lamb, Martin Rasmussen, and Kalle Timpe construct planar sets whose thickened boundaries are rough everywhere. Thickening a set by all points within a small distance gives its epsilon-neighbourhood, and one might expect the new boundary to be smooth somewhere, but their examples defeat that hope completely.

In the first example the boundary's singularity set is countably dense, as large as a singular set on such a boundary can be. The second example adds an uncountable subset of non-integer Hausdorff dimension where curvature is not even defined. Both constructions rest on a characterization of star-shaped sets that arise as epsilon-neighbourhoods of their own subsets. The results are pure geometry, marking how wild distance-based thickening can become even in the plane.
arxiv-2511-09246:
Amelia Bielby, Arushi Chauhan, Cassia Pearce, and Yue Ren connect the rigidity of Laman graphs with tropical geometry. A Laman graph is minimally rigid in two dimensions, and its realization number counts its embeddings with fixed edge lengths. That number is believed to grow exponentially, yet the best proven lower bound is only two.

The realization number can be written as a tropical intersection product involving the graph's Bergman fan. The authors define the tropical galaxy of a Laman graph, together with a galactic pairing on it. They study when this pairing is subadditive and link its nonvanishing to arboreal pairs of trees. A software package accompanies the work for computing with tropical galaxies.
arxiv-2511-10146:
Jaime Sebastian Burbano, Arnova Abdullah, Eldiyar Zhantileuov, Mohan Liyanage, and Rolf Schuster choose which edge server a latency-sensitive app should use as network conditions change. Congestion shifts over time, and naive switching causes flapping between servers. Their method, MO-HAN, fuses latency prediction with an adaptive reliability score and hysteresis, so handovers happen only when the expected gain is meaningful.

Inputs are passive readings such as arrival rate, load, and payload size, fed into a rational delay model with decay. No intrusive gear or heavy learning machinery is required, which suits embedded devices. Against static and fair-distribution baselines, MO-HAN lowered both average and tail latency and cut handovers by nearly half compared with purely greedy selection.
arxiv-2511-10346:
Andreas Höfinger and eleven co-authors build a realistic bridge between the antennas that launch spin waves and the magnetism that carries them. All-electrical spin-wave spectroscopy underpins magnonic circuits and quantum proposals, but simplified models assume uniform drive fields that real nanoantennas never produce. Their framework computes the full vector near-field of impedance-matched tapered antennas with finite-element simulations and feeds that field into micromagnetic solvers.

The coupling yields wave-vector weighting functions showing how antenna shape and current return paths filter which spin waves get excited. Tests on a thin yttrium-iron-garnet film matched experiments in dispersion, group velocity, and peak positions, confirming the antenna acts as a tunable wave-vector filter. The authors distill design rules for on-chip magnonic transducers, including low-power and quantum regimes.
arxiv-2511-10446:
Jonghun Lee, YongKyung Oh, Sungil Kim, and Dong-Young Lim bring a classic training trick to neural differential equations. These models describe how a system changes continuously over time. These models handle irregular and noisy time series well, but dropout, the standard guard against overfitting, had no natural continuous-time version. That gap left such models prone to memorizing their training data.

Continuum Dropout treats the on-off switching of dropout as a random process in continuous time, alternating between active evolution and paused states. At test time, repeated random sampling also gives uncertainty estimates for predictions. Across time series and image classification tasks, the method beat existing regularization options for these models. It also produced probability estimates that were better calibrated and more trustworthy.
arxiv-2511-10646:
Aiden J. Mains, Jia-Xin Zhong, Yun Jing, and Bitan Roy turn a nuisance into a tool. Every crystal carries ordinary defects such as vacancies, substitutions, and interstitials, and these flaws are usually seen as geometrically trivial, carrying no topology of their own.

The team shows theoretically that such defects nevertheless probe the topology of the electronic bands around them. A change in the local topological environment shows up as mid-gap bound states near the defect. The states survive weak random impurities. They then observed the effect experimentally in two-dimensional acoustic Chern lattices, using precisely controlled couplings between active meta-atoms and Green's function spectroscopy. The authors suggest the trick could even help trap Majorana modes in topological superconductors.
arxiv-2511-10846:
Rebecca Dorn and six co-authors document a racial bias in automated emotion detection, using anger recognition on African American Vernacular English as the test case. Emotion AI is deployed from wellness apps to hiring, but its training labels reflect dominant cultural norms and dialects like AAVE are scarce in training data.

The team scored 2.7 million Los Angeles tweets for dialect strength and collected community-informed labels on 875 of them from African American, AAVE-fluent annotators. GPT and BERT-based models produced false anger alarms on AAVE text at more than double the rate for general American English. One popular model jumped from 25 percent false positives to 60 percent. Model judgments also tracked profanity-linked dialect features more than the community's own annotations did, and neighborhood demographics correlated with predicted anger.
arxiv-2511-10946:
Yifan Liu, Fangneng Zhan, and their colleagues present SandboxVLM, a way to help picture-and-text models grasp three-dimensional space. Such models learn mostly from flat pictures, so they often fail at depth, pose, and motion tasks that robots need. SandboxVLM gives them simple box sketches that stand for real objects and their layout.

The pipeline builds those boxes from many views, lifts them into a 3D scene, checks them by vote, and then reasons over them. With no added training, it raised scores on spatial tests across several models and backbones. One test showed a gain of more than eight points, which hints at a path to better embodied skills.
arxiv-2511-11246:
Tin Nwe Aye and Linus Carlsson study an endemic disease model that tracks susceptible, exposed, infectious, treated, recovered, and deceased groups over time. Unlike basic models, theirs lets the latent period and the span of temporary immunity vary across cases through distributed delays, stated as integral kernels with bounded support. Real diseases differ widely in both spans, so fixed delays can misstate the dynamics.

Their main result is a smoothing property: under mild conditions on the system functions, solutions gain smoothness over time. They also prove solutions stay bounded and non-negative, as real counts must. Simulations show the continuous model can be approximated well by discrete lag versions.
arxiv-2511-11346:
Andreas Grivas, Lorenzo Loconte, and their colleagues present MTPC, a framework for predicting several future bytes at once to speed up byte-level language models. Byte-level models skip tokenizers but generate slowly, one byte at a time. Predicting blocks of bytes helps only if the joint pattern of those bytes is kept, and doing so serially erases the speed gain.

Probabilistic circuits supply the joint distributions, with architectures that generalize mixture models, hidden Markov models, and tensor networks. Retrofitted onto existing byte-level and byte-converted models and paired with speculative decoding, MTPC sped up generation over independence-based prediction while provably keeping the base model's performance. Trade-offs are studied rigorously.
arxiv-2511-11746:
Sepehr Maleki and Negar Pourmoazemi write a self-contained math introduction to diffusion models. These models power modern image synthesis. All results are derived from first principles. The starting point is basic facts about Gaussian distributions. Densities, expectations, and divergences are covered first.

From there, the forward noising process is built in order. Its closed-form marginals and the exact reverse posterior follow. The variational bound then reduces to the familiar noise-prediction goal. Faster sampling is covered next, including DDIM and adversarial variants. Latent diffusion is explained with Stable Diffusion as the example. A continuous-time view closes the tour. Students get the full chain of derivations in one place.
arxiv-2511-11846:
Afonso Rodrigues estimates how shoppers choose whole baskets, not just single products, across an entire supermarket. Differentiated product markets with tens of thousands of goods defeat standard demand models, so consideration sets, the shortlists shoppers actually weigh, structure the new approach.

Applied to Portuguese supermarkets from 2020 to 2023, anonymized transaction data alone support price elasticity estimates across almost thirty thousand goods and more than five hundred categories. Markups stayed stable through the pandemic period, with only a brief, slight rise afterward among the highest-markup goods, and implied markups match observed figures. Retail competition analysis gains a tool that respects how people really shop, basket by basket.
arxiv-2511-12146:
W. Bock, L. Cristofaro and J. L. da Silva build a stochastic counterpart to a generalized form of Wright analysis. From it they define a new class of random processes, called generalized Fox-H processes, which are neither Gaussian nor Markovian. The class extends known processes such as fractional Brownian motion.

The authors study the joint density and covariance of these processes and show their increments stay stationary in time. The paths are continuous in a strong Hölder sense, and each process can be written as a time-changed fractional Brownian motion. They also characterize the related noise, prove that local times exist, and discuss how the processes spread in an anomalous way.
arxiv-2511-12246:
Fei Wang and five co-authors ask whether familiar phase transition behavior survives when a quantum system is made non-Hermitian, meaning its energy can take complex values. They study a one-dimensional anisotropic XY model under a complex transverse field, a setting tied to open systems that interact with their surroundings.

Within a biorthogonal framework, they compute correlations and entanglement entropy for the ground state. The scaling matches the Hermitian XY model, a match they trace to symmetries that persist, break or emerge. A ferromagnetic phase comes from symmetry breaking, while a Luttinger liquid phase links to a new symmetry and to topology around an exceptional point.
arxiv-2511-12346:
Asmit Bandyopadhyay, Anindita Das Bhattacharjee and Rakesh Das present CLAReSNet, a hybrid network for classifying hyperspectral images, which record many narrow color bands per pixel. Such data are high in dimension, mix spatial and spectral patterns in complex ways, and often come with few labeled samples and uneven classes.

The network starts with multi-scale convolutional blocks and an attention module for spatial features, then adds spectral layers that pair recurrent units with a latent attention step. That attention uses a small set of adaptive tokens, cutting the cost sharply compared with full attention. Cross-attention then fuses the spatial and spectral streams into a final classification.
arxiv-2511-12646:
Hongjin Wu and Ulrik Brandes study when a network of coupled oscillators settles into full synchrony, with every unit moving in step. In the Kuramoto model, the standard test case, guarantees of global synchronization have usually needed very dense graphs or strong expansion properties. The authors focus on threshold graphs, a classic family built step by step by adding vertices that either connect to all earlier ones or to none of them.

They prove that threshold graphs are second-order globally synchronizing: every stable-looking stationary state of the Kuramoto energy on such a graph is in fact the fully synchronized state. That means almost all starting conditions end in step. The proof follows the step-by-step construction, pushing local constraints along the sequence until synchrony is forced. The result shows that dense connections are not the only route to reliable synchronization.
arxiv-2511-12746:
Filippo Caleca, Saverio Bocini, Fabio Mezzacapo, and Tommaso Roscilde study spin chains whose low-energy behavior forms a Luttinger liquid, a standard state of one-dimensional quantum matter. A magnetizing field can polarize such a system, but normally the magnetization vanishes when the field is removed. Building on earlier work, they show odd-sized chains can keep a net magnetization after the field is slowly removed.

The retained magnetization grows more slowly than the system size, at a rate set by the Luttinger exponent. The prepared states also show spin squeezing that gets stronger as the system grows, again at a rate fixed by the same exponent. Squeezing is prized for precision measurement, and it is usually linked to higher-dimensional systems. Finding it in gapless one-dimensional chains ties a useful quantum resource directly to critical behavior.
arxiv-2511-12846:
Zelin Zhu, Yancheng Huang, and Kai Yang present RoS-Guard, an online change detection algorithm built for imperfect knowledge and large systems. Change detection watches a data stream and flags the moment its behavior shifts, a need in power grids, wireless sensing, and finance. Classic methods assume the system model is known exactly, which estimation errors and changing environments make unrealistic, and many are too slow at scale. RoS-Guard is designed for linear systems with stated uncertainty from the start.

The authors relax and reformulate the detection problem so it can be unrolled into a neural form that runs in parallel on GPUs. The algorithm still carries theoretical guarantees on false alarms and detection delay. Experiments confirmed the guarantees and showed large speedups on big systems. The contribution is a detector that is robust, provably bounded, and fast enough for production streams.
arxiv-2511-13046:
Ichiro Matsuda and six co-authors watch students meet themselves, in the form of AI debaters they built. A personalized language model, a Digital Human, sits between self and other: it speaks from your prompts but argues back like someone else. In a research-through-design study, nine junior and senior high school students in teams designed Digital Humans with prompt engineering and retrieval augmentation, then set them debating autonomously and observed. Literacy tests, interviews, and log analysis tracked what the students took away.

Participants deepened their understanding of what AI can do. Something less expected: seeing their own creation act as an other turned them reflective, letting them view their own cognition and values from outside. The authors propose reflecting with AI as a new component of generative AI literacy.
arxiv-2511-13646:
Chunqiu Steven Xia and 4 co-authors introduce Live-SWE-agent, a software agent that rewrites its own scaffold while it works on real coding tasks. Language model agents for software work normally ship with a fixed, hand-designed set of tools and prompts. Searching that design space by hand is slow and costly, and offline self-improvement may not transfer across models.

Live-SWE-agent starts from a minimal bash-only scaffold and evolves its own implementation on the fly, problem by problem. On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark it reached the best solve rate reported among software agents in the study, without test-time scaling. It also led the newer SWE-Bench Pro benchmark in their evaluation.
arxiv-2511-14046:
Li-Cheng Sheng, Yu-Jie Tang, Yu-Xin Wan, and two co-authors probe the inner makeup of exotic pentaquarks by watching how they emit pions. The hidden-charm pentaquarks, including strange partners, might be loose molecules of known hadrons or compact five-quark states, and the question is still open. The team calculates pion emission inside a molecular picture using a chiral quark model with coupled channels.

Their results show the decay widths depend strongly on the internal structure and the spatial shape of the wave functions. That sensitivity is the point: measuring these decays would help settle what the pentaquarks are. The authors hope the work prompts experiments and guides searches for further molecular partner states.
arxiv-2511-14146:
Renjie Chen, Viet Anh Nguyen, and Huifu Xu propose SCOPE, a joint estimator for a random vector's covariance matrix and its inverse, the precision matrix. Estimating both well matters across statistics and machine learning, and sample versions suffer spectral bias. Their formulation is distributionally robust: it minimizes a worst-case blend of two loss functions over an ambiguity set of distributions around the nominal one.

The robust problem reduces to a convex program with nearly closed-form solutions. The resulting estimators shrink eigenvalues nonlinearly toward a positive target, which corrects the bias and improves the condition number. A tuning scheme sets the shrinkage target and strength, balancing the two losses through one weight coefficient.
arxiv-2511-14346:
Siyuan Wang and Qing Xia solve wave bounce problems outside odd shapes with a grid form of the Green's function. The classic route works on the rim of the shape only, which cuts the size of the task and needs no fake outer rim. It uses a base solution that blows up at its source. The grid form has no such blow-up, which makes the sums much simpler to run.

Edge rules are fed in by local fits on cut cells, so the grid need not match the shape's rim. Tests on round, triangle, and twin shapes show the scheme is both exact and tough. The authors keep the rim-only gain of the classic route while using plain grid steps.
arxiv-2511-14646:
Derek Frydel studies search processes in which a wandering particle is repeatedly caught and returned to a starting point. In the standard picture the return is instant, but real returns take time and can leave the next search starting from a slightly wrong place. Frydel looks at returns driven by a shifting harmonic trap, like a spring whose center can move.

The return ends the moment the particle reaches the center, so every outward search starts from exactly the same spot. A feedback signal shortens the return without extra mechanical effort. The analysis shows how to keep the benefits of resetting while removing a common source of error in real search systems.
arxiv-2511-15046:
Panqi Yang and three co-authors present UniHOI, a unified model for understanding human object interactions in images. Finding asks where an interaction occurs, while generation asks to create it. The two dual tasks were long handled separately, limiting shared learning. UniHOI models both in one unified token space.

A symmetric interaction aware attention module links image and interaction semantics in both directions. A semi supervised scheme supports learning with limited labels. Experiments show top performance on both finding and generation. Long tail finding accuracy improves notably. Open vocabulary generation metrics rise sharply as well. Sharing one token space helps the model generalize to rare and unseen interactions.
arxiv-2511-15146:
Eugene Ndiaye extends conformal prediction so it can hand back regions, not just intervals, for multi-output problems. Conformal methods wrap any model's output in a set that is guaranteed to contain the truth at a chosen rate, using only calibration data. Ranking candidates is easy with a single score, but vector scores from several outputs or several models have no natural order.

Optimal transport supplies the missing ranking, through outward-in quantile regions for vectors, but its coverage guarantees are only approximate and a fixed transport map adds error. Ndiaye conformalizes those transport regions so the finite-sample, distribution-free guarantee returns. Multi-output regression and model ensembles both gain honest uncertainty regions.
arxiv-2511-15246:
Tung Giang Le, Xuan Tung Nguyen, and Won-Joo Hwang build a fully quantum graph neural network and test it on wireless power control. Device-to-device links in a wireless network interfere with each other, so setting each transmitter's power is a graph-shaped optimization. Classical graph networks solve it well but grow costly as networks swell.

The quantum version performs message passing with parameterized quantum circuits: features are encoded into quantum states, processed by hardware-friendly operations, and read back out by measurement. On the power control task, aimed at maximizing signal quality against interference and noise, the quantum network matches classical results with fewer parameters. The design is a step toward quantum-accelerated management of large wireless systems.
arxiv-2511-15346:
A. Chakraborty and B. K. Sahoo comprehensively calculate atomic traits of the triply ionized thorium ion for nuclear clock work. Thorium based nuclear clocks promise extreme precision and tests of fundamental physics. Exact atomic data are needed to judge clock systematics. The authors use relativistic coupled cluster theory with single, double, and triple excitations.

Combining theory with lab data yields precise nuclear charge radii differences for thorium isotopes. Magnetic dipole and electric quadrupole moments are found for ground and isomeric states. Polarizabilities and hyperfine induced moments help assess clock uncertainties. One unexpectedly large effect is highlighted for further focus. The data set provides a source for designing and interpreting thorium nuclear clock experiments.
arxiv-2511-15446:
Alexej Brauer and Mario V. Wüthrich work on the Gini score, a rank-based tool used to check whether a model orders risks well. It is widely used for yes-or-no outcomes, where it matches the area under a common accuracy curve. Actuaries, who price insurance risk, have extended it to general outcomes using curves that show how risk is spread.

Those extensions assume every case gets a distinct rank, which real data often break. Brauer and Wüthrich show how the score should handle ties, where several cases share the same predicted rank. They also adapt it for case weights, where some records count more than others, a routine need in insurance work.
arxiv-2511-15546:
Markus Diehl, Oskar Grocholski, Daniel Reitinger, Andreas Schäfer, and Christian Zimmermann study how to extract summary numbers for double parton distributions from lattice calculations. Double parton distributions describe two partons, the quarks or gluons inside a proton, at once. Their Mellin moments are weighted averages that summarize the distribution shape, but getting them from lattice data needs an integral over a variable akin to Ioffe time.

That variable has a partner that acts like a skewness, a measure of imbalance, in the distributions. The authors discuss how the relevant proton correlation functions depend on that skewness. Using several models, they test how strongly that dependence affects moments extracted from existing lattice data.
arxiv-2511-15846:
Charlotte Stix, Annika Hallensleben, Alejandro Ortega, and Matteo Pistillo write a research report on loss of control over advanced AI systems. Despite policy attention, no actionable definition of loss of control exists. Current definitions differ widely in scope and timeline. That gap blocks practical risk checks and response planning, so the authors build a graded scale and a readiness framework from a broad review.

Their scale ranks loss of control by severity and persistence, from deviation through bounded to strict forms. They model how society could drift into a weak spot before any trigger, such as misalignment or malfunction, causes harm. Their framework stresses deployment context, affordances, and permissions as levers that can be acted on today.
arxiv-2511-16246:
Sixuan Zhang and eight co-authors reanalyze the black hole binary Cygnus X-1 using X-ray data taken in May 2022, when the source sat in a low hard state. Polarization data from IXPE had shown a degree about four times higher than simple models predicted, which pushed theorists toward unusual corona shapes.

Combining IXPE, NuSTAR, and NICER spectra, the team finds that two Comptonization components fit better than one, with a cooler disk than first assumed. Simulations show a cooler disk raises the predicted polarization, though not all the way to the observed value. A slab corona sandwiching the disk matches the energy pattern of the polarization, and the authors argue the hard emission comes from such a slab.
arxiv-2511-16346:
Deniz Kasap and five co-authors present VersaPants, a loose fitting textile sensing system that captures lower body motion without cameras or tight inertial suits. Conductive textile patches and a compact acquisition unit are built into ordinary pants. Six capacitive channels per leg track leg movement while preserving comfort. No user specific fitting is required, and privacy is preserved by design.

A lightweight transformer maps capacitance signals to joint angles for edge deployment. Motion data from eleven participants performing sixteen daily and exercise movements train the model. Mean joint position error is reported as the headline accuracy measure. The open hardware platform invites replication. Comfortable, private motion capture could support rehabilitation and home health monitoring.
arxiv-2511-16546:
Xiaoyue Chen and seven co-authors make visual autoregressive image generation cheaper to run. These models predict one scale at a time, which cuts inference steps, but the growing key-value cache across scales eats memory and limits deployment.

The authors notice an asymmetry: early scales are very sensitive to network depth, while later scales tolerate shallow networks. Their VARiant model samples subnets from two to sixteen layers out of a thirty-layer original, giving early scales the full network and later scales a subnet, all sharing one set of weights. A progressive training strategy resolves the conflicts that weight sharing creates. The result nearly matches the original's image quality while cutting memory by forty to sixty-five percent, and the shallowest variant runs several times faster.
arxiv-2511-16846:
Seyed Mohssen Ghafari and seven co-authors present ConCISE, a way to grade how concise a language model's answer is without needing a gold answer to compare with. Long, padded replies are a known flaw of such models: they waste the reader's time and raise the cost of running the model, since many services charge by output length.

ConCISE scores an answer by shrinking it three ways: a short summary in new words. A summary built from its own phrases, and a pass that deletes needless words while keeping the sense. The more that can be cut, the less concise the first answer is rated. Tests reported by the team show the score tracks human judgement, giving builders a cheap check for wordiness.
arxiv-2511-16946:
Mariko Kato, Izumi Hachisu, and Hideyuki Saio model the long-mysterious rising phase of classical nova light curves, the climb toward optical maximum that observations rarely catch and theory had not fully reproduced. Their fully self-consistent explosion models generate light curves from free-free emission, the radiation of hot ionized gas, rather than from the photosphere alone.

A white dwarf model of one and a quarter solar masses matches the observed rises of KT Eridani, V339 Delphini, and V597 Puppis excellently. A heavier model fits SMC Nova 2016-10a. The agreements say the climb to maximum is dominated by free-free emission in these novae. They also validate the white dwarf masses and distances previously derived for the four systems, and show the post-maximum decline follows steady-state envelope sequences well.
arxiv-2511-17246:
Zeyu Huang and seven co-authors give scenic live streams a layer of interactivity. Such streams, fixed cameras broadcasting famous landscapes with no host, draw large synchronous audiences but offer viewers little to do. The team overlays mixed reality content matched to a site's geography and local culture, calling the result MRSLS, and prototypes it at a UNESCO-listed heritage site in China.

Design work began with interviews to identify the site's scenery and cultural highlights, followed by two iterative studies. A mixed-methods comparison then showed the mixed reality version gave more immersive appreciation of the scenery, stronger cultural impressions, and a more vivid sense of shared experience than the plain stream. The authors argue this underexplored format balances authenticity, participation, and cultural value, and deserves more attention from interaction designers.
arxiv-2511-17546:
S Rathi, K von Schoeler, P Indelicato, and B Ohayon propose a new way to pin down the electric quadrupole moments of light transition elements. A measure of how their nuclei deviate from a sphere. Their route uses muonic atoms, where a heavy cousin of the electron orbits close to the nucleus and its X-ray lines shift in ways that encode the nuclear shape. Those lines are too weak and too crowded for standard tools to read well.

The team pairs cryogenic microcalorimeters, detectors with fine energy resolution and high efficiency, with state-of-the-art theory. Calculations and realistic simulations support the plan. They argue the base moment for a whole chain of isotopes could be fixed far more sharply, perhaps ten times better, within about a day of measurement time.
arxiv-2511-18046:
V. Garcia-Rojas and J. F. Perez-Torres quantify how strongly spin and orbital motion are entangled in materials where a transition metal ion holds a single electron in its outer shell. In that setting, measured magnetic moments often look anomalous. Their framework rests on relativistic crystal field theory.

They study several double perovskite materials and a molecular system, all in their paramagnetic phases, deriving entanglement entropies from measured optical transitions and effective magnetic moments. One excited state family shows no such entropy, while for others a larger magnetic moment goes with greater spin orbital entanglement. Still, it does not track a larger spin orbit coupling constant.
arxiv-2511-18246:
Jun Seok Oh, Sávio Ribas, Kevin Zhao, and Qinghai Zhong close the last open case in a counting problem for a family of groups. The groups mix a ring group with a flip of size two. The question asks how long a list of group items must be to force a special sub list. In that sub list the items, in some order, multiply to the neutral item, with length equal to the group size.

That threshold is called the Gao constant, and both its value and the shape of tight lists were known save for one sub case. The team settle that case in full. With it, the constant and its tight list form are now known for the whole family. The result ends a long case by case hunt in zero sum theory.
arxiv-2511-18346:
Wenshuo Gao, Junyi Fan, Jiangyue Zeng, and Shuai Yang relight video and swap its backdrop with no new training. Film and media work needs such edits, but past tools trade off smooth time flow, true shape, and natural light. A fix that holds all three has stayed out of reach.

FlowPortal starts from a flow based video model and adds a fix term to its flow. When input matches, the output is exact by design; when light shifts, the edit stays true to the source shape. Split controls steer light apart from the rest, and a fine detail pass keeps texture crisp. A mask keeps the subject relight apart from the new backdrop build. Tests show gains in smooth flow and shape hold.
arxiv-2511-18446:
Mustapha Ouchen and Alex Prygarin test how particle counts spread in proton proton collisions. A scaling rule due to Koba, Nielsen, and Olesen says the shape of that spread stays fixed as energy grows, once counts are scaled by their mean. Data from the ATLAS detector give the test bed.

Three models are checked against the data curves: an AGK model, a Kharzeev-Levin model, and a plain exponential form. All three near coincide with the data across a broad energy range. Terms that break the scaling shrink near a special scaled count of two, where the rule is restored. The authors link that point to saturation of a basic bound and to a memory free spread at high energy.
arxiv-2511-18546:
Siyue Liu and Victor Reis round a fractional work plan into a whole one with a tight error bound. The chairman assignment problem, from a 1973 result by Tijdeman, asks for such a rounding where each prefix of the plan stays near fair. Their form adds weights to the jobs, which the old result lacked.

They prove a whole assignment exists where each weighted prefix gap stays below the largest single weight. The proof also settles a case of a flow conjecture by Morell and Skutella. As a use, they give a scheduling method with a factor three guarantee. Jobs have release times and machines have closing times there, and the goal is to cut the worst flow time.
arxiv-2511-19046:
Anglin Liu and six co-authors build MedSAM3, a text prompted segmentation model for medical images and video. Segmentation maps anatomy for research and care, yet past tools port poorly and each new use demands long hand annotation. Their model fine tunes the Segment Anything Model 3 on medical images paired with semantic concept labels.

Text prompts can then name the target structure in open vocabulary, in place of boxes or points alone. That mode, promptable concept segmentation, aims at precise targeting by description. A MedSAM3 Agent wraps a multimodal model around it to reason and refine in a loop. Broad tests span many imaging modes. Concept words as the scalpel is the shift.
arxiv-2511-19346:
