Nahid Sultana, M. M. Rizvi, and I. B. Wadhawan build a model for sharing irrigation water wisely. Water managers must balance farm output against groundwater sustainability and the flow rivers need to stay alive. Rainfall varies and the climate is uncertain, which makes the balance harder. The authors present a multiobjective optimization model for this allocation problem.

The model jointly decides which crops to plant, how much groundwater to pump, and how much flow to release for the environment. It keeps the plan economically and hydrologically feasible. A case study grounds the model in a real setting. Tools like this help regions farm productively without draining their aquifers. The approach suits water-stressed areas worldwide.
arxiv-2601-19846:
Qian Huang, Christian Rohde, and Ruixi Zhang prove that a simpler system can stand in for the equations of incompressible flow. The incompressible Navier-Stokes equations govern slow, dense fluids. The authors study a two-parameter hyperbolic relaxation system that approximates them. It blends first-order relaxation with the artificial compressibility method.

Starting from tiny perturbations of the initial velocity, they prove convergence. Both velocity and pressure approach the Navier-Stokes limit as the parameters vanish. The proof builds an intermediate affine system to control the error. The result is stated for the three-dimensional case, the hardest and most relevant. Rigorous limits justify using relaxed systems in computation, where they are often easier to solve.
arxiv-2601-19946:
Nikhil Raghav, Avisek Gupta, Swagatam Das, and Md Sahidullah work on speaker diarization, the task of marking who spoke when in a recording. Unsupervised diarization gets no labelled examples and no pretraining to lean on. That makes it hard, but the payoff is a system that works on any new recording collection.

Their method builds a sparse graph from speaker embeddings. Multiple kernels measure similarity between voices in complementary ways. The graph then feeds spectral clustering to carve the recording into speaker regions. A key observation concerns how those kernel similarities should be combined. Accurate diarization underpins meeting transcripts and media archives. The work pushes the label-free end of the field.
arxiv-2601-20146:
Claudio Hernández-Vera and a large team map where complex organic molecules sit. They work in the Horsehead nebula, a cloud of gas and dust shaped like its name. Such molecules are seen as steps toward the chemistry that precedes life. How they form is still unclear, above all where ultraviolet light is strong.

Ultraviolet light was once expected to destroy these molecules quickly. Yet they are found in regions bathed in that light, called photodissociation regions. The team reads the spatial pattern of the organics as signposts of chemistry driven by atomic carbon. The map helps test how hardy carbon chemistry can be near bright stars.
arxiv-2601-20446:
Yusei Fujimaru and nine colleagues simulate the remnants of Type Ia supernovae in three dimensions and predict their X-ray spectra. These explosions of white dwarfs serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic distances. Yet recent work shows a diversity of progenitor systems and explosion mechanisms behind them.

The authors run hydrodynamic simulations of the expanding remnants and synthesize the X-ray light they should emit. Comparing those spectra with telescope data can reveal which explosion path a given remnant took. That in turn tests whether all Type Ia events are alike enough to trust as distance markers.
arxiv-2601-20546:
Kumiko Nakajima, Jan Zuiderveld, and Sandro Pezzelle evaluate creativity in large language models using human-based methods grounded in creativity theory. Models are increasingly used for verbal creative tasks. Yet earlier assessments rest weakly on human creativity research and are hard to interpret.

The widely used Divergent Association Task measures only novelty. It ignores appropriateness, a core part of what makes an idea creative rather than merely odd. The authors move beyond divergent creativity alone. Better grounded measures would help buyers and researchers judge what models can truly contribute to creative work.
arxiv-2601-20646:
Zhejian Yang, Songwei Zhao, Zilin Zhao, and Hechang Chen present TGSBM, a transformer-guided stochastic block model for link prediction. Link prediction powers recommendation, search, knowledge graph completion, and collaboration forecasting. Large networks are hard: they hold hundreds of thousands of nodes and edges, with overlapping communities that change over time.

Stochastic block models capture community structure; transformers capture rich patterns in data. Guiding one with the other aims at both structure and flexibility. Better link prediction improves friend and content suggestions, and helps forecast which scientific teams will form. It is built for the web as it is, not as we might wish it to be.
arxiv-2601-20746:
Eduardo Souza, Rafael Leite, and Andre Souza study the food web of Chesapeake Bay. Their 2026 paper treats the bay as a complex network. Chesapeake Bay is one of the largest estuaries in the United States. Its web of who eats whom has thirty-six trophic components. All of them are linked to each other in some way.

The team analyzes these links with network methods. Their focus is robustness: how the web holds up when energy flow is cut past a set level. Such a cut mimics stress, like the loss of a food source. The study maps which parts of the web bear the most strain. It gives ecologists a view of where the bay's food web is strong and where it is thin.
arxiv-2601-20846:
Jamie Hathaway, Alireza Rastegarpanah, and Rustam Stolkin teach a robot skill in simulation and move it to the real world. Their 2026 paper concerns sim-to-real transfer for reinforcement learning policies. The test task is robotic cutting. Learning in simulation is cheap and safe. But the gap between simulated and physical systems blocks deployment. Real-world samples are also scarce.

Their approach is end-to-end and example-based. It uses neural stylisation to make simulated experience look more real. The policy then transfers with less shock. Cutting is a hard test: contact forces shift fast and materials vary. Success here suggests the method can handle other contact-rich tasks. The work speaks to factories that want trained robots without costly real-world trials.
arxiv-2601-21146:
Francesco Paladino, Shulu Li, and Edward Lee present a simple rule that unifies many classic timing methods. Their 2026 paper introduces maxwait, a coordination rule for distributed time-sensitive systems. Such systems must balance timing needs against consistency. Delays and sync errors make that balance hard. Maxwait makes the trade-offs explicit. Each node waits a set time before it acts on stamped events.

The authors show the rule subsumes classic methods. It covers PTIDES and Chandy-and-Misra protocols, with or without null messages. It also covers Jefferson's Time-Warp and Lamport's fault detection by time. One rule that covers so many is a real economy. The rule enables real-time behavior in cyber-physical systems. It gives builders a single knob for safety and speed.
arxiv-2601-21846:
Konstantinos Varsos, Adamantia Stamou, George Stamoulis, and Vasillios Siris look for ways to save energy across information and communication networks. Energy demand from these systems keeps surging. Providers need users to accept greener choices, such as adaptive bitrate streaming, without feeling that quality has dropped.

Their 2026 preprint introduces an approach built on gamified incentives, rewards and game-like prompts that nudge users toward energy-efficient behavior. It also models how users decide whether to accept such incentives. Managing services with energy in mind could cut a real share of global electricity use. Since networks and data centers run around the clock whether anyone is watching or not.
arxiv-2601-22246:
Ya Jiang, Massieh Kordi Boroujeny, Surender Suresh Kumar, and Kai Zeng tackle proof of who wrote a text in the age of chatbots. Their 2026 preprint, MirrorMark, hides a mark in model output that can carry more than a yes-or-no sign. Past marks could warp the text or prove too weak to find.

Their mark leaves the word choice odds just as they were, so the text reads the same. Yet the mark can still hold a short code with more than one bit. Strong, clean marks help firms trace text back to a model. They also help fight false claims of authorship.
arxiv-2601-22346:
Chris Mascioli, Satyam Goyal, and Mithun Chakraborty built a transformer that splits goods that cannot be cut. Their 2026 preprint, FairFormer, tackles fair division: who gets what when each person values the items in their own way. No money changes hands, so the split itself must feel fair.

FairFormer reads items and people as loose sets, not fixed lists. It then gives each item a set of odds for who should get it, all in one pass. The design trades pure gain against envy, the sense that a peer got more. It offers a fast, learned path to fair splits.
arxiv-2601-22746:
Pingping Liu and a large team built UrbanMoE, a sparse mixture-of-experts frame that profiles city zones across many tasks at once. Region profiling guides planning and resource use. Their 2026 preprint notes that most tools do one task at a time, missing how a zone's traits interlock.

Their frame mixes data of many kinds and routes each zone to expert sub-models. Joint profiling should catch links a single-task tool would miss. Cities could then plan housing, transit, and services as one problem. The work fits the multi-faceted truth of urban life. It is built for breadth.
arxiv-2601-22846:
Guy Shtotland extends a famous bridge between algebra and geometry to a new symmetric setting. The Kazhdan–Lusztig picture links the Hecke algebra of a p-adic group with the geometry of its dual group. That link was a key step in proving the Deligne–Langlands conjectures on smooth representations.

Here the setting is a quotient involving general linear and symplectic groups, a classic symmetric pair. A relative version of the isomorphism would organize representations in this paired world. Such results deepen the Langlands program, which unifies large parts of modern mathematics.
arxiv-2601-23046:
Keitarou Matsumoto and eight co-authors explain the X-ray sources seen in a giant solar flare. The flare, classed X7.1, erupted on October 1, 2024, in active region 13842. Two space telescopes viewed its hard X-rays from different angles, giving a stereoscopic picture.

They match those views with a data-constrained simulation of the Sun's magnetic field in three dimensions. The aim is to find the structures that accelerate particles during the flare. Understanding big flares helps forecast space weather that can harm satellites and power grids. Stereoscopic views from two observatories give depth, letting the team place X-ray sources in the flare's three-dimensional structure.
arxiv-2601-23146:
Ahmed Farag Ali counts quantum states in de Sitter space from an observer's point of view. De Sitter space models a universe with steady accelerated expansion. Following Maldacena's observer-centered approach, the count depends on where the observer sits.

The observer is modeled as a heavy worldline at the equator carrying an SU(3) clock, an internal quantum marker. State counting here is relational: it depends on the clock and path chosen. Such frameworks probe how gravity and quantum theory fit together in an expanding universe. An observer-dependent count reframes entropy in de Sitter space as something measured relative to a worldline, not absolutely.
arxiv-2602-02546:
Xianglong Yan and 7 co-authors squeeze large language model weights below four bits without the usual accuracy collapse, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Weight-only post-training quantization shrinks memory and speeds deployment without specialized hardware. Their analysis blames two causes for the damage at very low precision.

Down-projection matrices are a known bottleneck whose fidelity usually demands extra bits. Quantization also shifts activation distributions, and fix strategies were underexplored. The system attacks both sides. A dual-scale quantizer tailored to down-projection matrices uses an absorbable scaling factor to gain accuracy within the same bit budget. A deviation-aware fix adds a mean shift inside normalization layers to realign activations. Across several model families and metrics, the method delivered the best sub-four-bit weight-only results reported.
arxiv-2602-02746:
Jonathan D. Kroth and 1 co-author compute a new source of photons in the quark-gluon plasma that could solve the missing direct photons puzzle, in a 2026 paper. Heavy-ion collisions emit fewer direct photons than theory predicts in some channels and more in others; the mismatch is long-standing. Their mechanism involves parity-violating plasma parameters: a chiral chemical potential and a chiral gradient coupled to fermions.

Exact fermion wavefunctions in these backgrounds plus a constant magnetic field are derived first. Synchrotron radiation from those fermions grows when the violating parameters are present. At the same time the radiation's elliptic flow coefficient, traditionally large, decreases. Applied to the quark-gluon plasma, the contribution points toward the missing photons. The same wavefunctions yield a fresh derivation of the chiral magnetic effect, a benchmark phenomenon of anomalous transport.
arxiv-2602-02946:
Hitomi Endo and 1 co-author test a basic assumption of thermodynamics in a 2026 paper. Local balance says each small region of a system behaves as if it were in balance, even during change. The authors study a one-part model with fractional spatial derivatives, tuned to mimic a two-part phase shift.

Steady heat flows through the model from boundary heat baths. Ordered and disordered phases coexist, separated by a stationary interface. The interface temperature systematically differs from the balance shift temperature. That gap shows local balance failing. The measured temperature matches predictions from global thermodynamics for steady states. The authors argue such breakdowns are intrinsic to nonequilibrium first-order shifts, regardless of dimension.
arxiv-2602-03146:
Santiago Cifuentes, in solo research dated 2026, proves that general agents must contain world models even when randomness and partial observability enter the picture. Earlier results showed almost optimal deterministic agents in fully observable settings carry enough knowledge to reconstruct their environment by black-box queries. Real agents, though, randomize and see only part of their surroundings at any moment during operation.

Cifuentes removes both earlier assumptions. The theorem now covers stochastic agents in partially observable environments. Fundamentally, randomization cannot let an agent avoid learning its environment. The result is also strengthened by weakening what counts as a general agent. Less powerful agents, the proof shows, already contain a model of the world they operate in.
arxiv-2602-03546:
Digital machine learning burns enormous energy, and analog resistor networks might one day do the same work cheaply. Jonathan Lin and 3 co-authors tackle the training problem for such hardware in a 2026 paper. Physical systems demand local learning rules, but the known ones, like equilibrium propagation, come with awkward requirements such as full readouts.

The authors derive exact gradients analytically from Kirchhoff's laws using a graph-theoretic framework. They also introduce Generalized Equilibrium Propagation, which unifies a broad family of Hebbian learning rules, including coupled learning. Simulations show resistor networks can train while reading only the output layer, with no replica network. Updating only a subset of resistances degrades performance surprisingly little.
arxiv-2602-03746:
Bastiàn Espinoza and 2 co-authors study how evenly the blocks inside an infinite word must appear, a property called factor-balancedness. Their 2026 paper works in combinatorics on words, where balancedness measures how evenly letters and longer factors occur. The notions connect to wider math and computer science.

The first result gives general sufficient conditions for an infinite word to be factor-balanced, uniformly or not, phrased in S-adic terms. The tests cover every linearly recurrent word and extend Adamczewski's results on substitutive words. Using them, the authors pin down exactly which Sturmian and ternary Arnoux-Rauzy words are uniformly factor-balanced. A second part relates balancedness to factor complexity, including a factor-balanced word with exponential complexity.
arxiv-2602-04246:
Latent reasoning is fast but usually demands surgery on the model. Fangwei Zhu and 1 co-author reframe it as tool use in a 2026 paper. Their CoLT framework lets a large model reason in compressed seed tokens that stand for whole reasoning steps.

When a latent tool call fires, a smaller external model reads the seed token's hidden states and unpacks the full step. The main model keeps reasoning in ordinary tokens, preserving its abilities, while the helper absorbs the verbose parts. On four math datasets, CoLT improved accuracy while shortening reasoning chains, without restructuring or exhaustively retraining the main model.
arxiv-2602-04446:
Light shaped into swirling, particle-like patterns called skyrmions is the subject of a 2026 paper by Cade Peters and 5 co-authors. The team asked whether these patterns could carry information through open air without losing their basic structure.

The researchers sent optical skyrmions across a real outdoor free-space link and tested them under many weather and turbulence conditions. Moving air badly distorted the light's brightness, phase, and polarization. Yet the topological number, a count that defines the pattern, stayed unchanged in every case. Information passed through with very high fidelity in most tests. The result suggests topology could make future optical communication more reliable.
arxiv-2602-04846:
Clark Barrett and 7 co-authors introduce CSLib in a 2026 paper, an open-source library for proving computer science theorems in the Lean proof assistant. They aim to do for computer science what Mathlib did for mathematics, where a vast shared library made Lean popular with researchers.

Computer science knowledge in Lean is currently quite limited. CSLib will expand that base substantially and provide infrastructure for real-world verification projects. The authors expect two effects. First, broader use of Lean in computer science education and research. Second, easier engineering of large-scale formally verified systems, both manually and with AI assistance. The paper presents the library's goals and design as a community resource.
arxiv-2602-05046:
Keeping a machine inside safe limits while steering it optimally is a classic control problem. Abhijeet and Suman Chakravorty address it in this 2026 control theory paper, working with the iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator, a workhorse algorithm for nonlinear control. Their version must respect box constraints, upper and lower bounds on both states and inputs.

The trick is to add logarithmic barrier terms to the cost, which punish the controller smoothly as it nears a bound. Because the barrier's curvature is positive, the algorithm's quadratic approximations stay well behaved, and numerical stability and convergence improve. The authors also show a neat effect at convergence: when a control channel saturates, its feedback terms fade to zero, leaving pure feedforward action. Tests on constrained nonlinear problems confirm the bounds hold and convergence stays favorable.
arxiv-2602-05246:
Tuning a car-following model should capture how drivers vary, not just how the average driver behaves. Menglin Kong and 2 co-authors build a Bayesian calibration toolkit that scales in this 2026 applied statistics paper. The classical Bayesian route, Markov chain sampling per trajectory, is far too slow for today's massive naturalistic driving datasets.

Their toolkit is simulation-based and active. A residual-augmented simulator generates synthetic leader-follower trips, with two choices for the residual process. A neural density estimator learns to map any seen trip straight to a single-driver posterior distribution over settings, in one forward pass at test time. An active design plan spends the simulation budget where the fit model is most unsure, while keeping contexts real. On the HighD highway dataset, predictions improved and mock trip spreads matched seen ones more closely than Bayesian baselines allowed.
arxiv-2602-05346:
Distributed ledgers increasingly rely on trusted execution spaces, hardware enclaves meant to keep code honest, but enclaves sometimes fall to attacks. Shubham Mishra and 6 co-authors present a consensus protocol, developed under the project name Pirateship, in this 2026 distributed systems paper. The design goal is a ledger that keeps its integrity promises even when the hardware layer breaks.

The build nests a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol inside a crash fault-tolerant one, with no extra messages exchanged. That feat required reworking both protocols until their shapes aligned, so the Byzantine machinery rides along inside the crash-tolerant flow. Speed stays in line with plain enclave-based consensus, so the extra safety costs no speed premium. The authors frame the work as cautious trust: use enclaves for speed, but never let the ledger's integrity rest on them alone.
arxiv-2602-05546:
Correlators describe how fields in the early universe relate to each other, and computing them for de Sitter space is a demanding task. Shibam Das, Debanjan Karan, Babli Khatun, and Nilay Kundu ask how these quantities can be rebuilt from simpler pieces. Their tool is the momentum-space dispersion formula, applied to the discontinuities of the correlators, viewed through de Sitter Witten diagrams.

Working at tree level with conformally coupled and massless scalar fields, the authors use single-cut rules that link correlators to their discontinuities. For diagrams with several interaction points, they cut internal lines one by one and rebuild the full correlator from lower-point contact pieces. Along the way, they recover known dressing rules that turn flat-space Feynman diagrams into de Sitter correlators. The paper should interest cosmologists who compute primordial signals from inflation-era physics.
arxiv-2602-05646:
Time series models that learn from a single data type miss context that other forms of data could supply, such as charts and news. Peng Chen and 9 co-authors take an early step toward multimodal foundation models for time series. Their pretraining design uses modalities derived from the series itself, namely images and text, plus outside knowledge from real-world news, giving several views of the same signal.

An automated pipeline builds MM-TS, a large multimodal time series data set spanning six domains with up to a billion points. On top of it they train HORAI, a model with a frequency-enhanced encoder that fuses the modalities and a time-frequency decoder. After pretraining, HORAI reached state-of-the-art zero-shot results on forecasting and anomaly detection. The authors argue the gains show the value of cross-modal fusion for generalization.
arxiv-2602-05746:
Prompt injection, where hostile text hijacks an AI agent instructions, is usually crafted by human red teamers by hand. Xin Chen, Jie Zhang, and Florian Tramèr present AutoInject, a black box reinforcement learning framework that learns attack suffixes automatically. The hard part is the reward: success is binary, and random suffixes almost never trigger the needed tool call, so standard optimizers get no signal to climb.

Instead of pass or fail, each try is ranked against the best one found yet. That ranking guides the learner where a yes or no signal leaves it stuck. The same setup works in two modes. Attacks can be tuned live through queries, or suffixes trained offline can move to new targets unaided. On AgentDojo, it beat plain templates and reshaped jailbreak tools across production models. It even cracked a model built to resist prompt injection, where templates got nowhere.
arxiv-2602-05846:
Why do neural networks learn features in stages, with plateaus between sudden improvements? Leonardo Defilippis, Florent Krzakala, Bruno Loureiro, and Antoine Maillard give a sharp theory for two layer networks trained on hierarchical multi index targets. These targets depend on nested sets of directions, so some features must be found before others become visible.

The authors derive exact information theoretic scaling laws for subspace recovery and prediction error. Hierarchical features are learned in sequence through a cascade of phase transitions, which explains the plateaus. A simple spectral estimator, indifferent to the target, achieves the optimal rates, matching the small learning rate limit of gradient descent. Once the representation is found, the readout can be learned optimally with an efficient procedure. The paper unifies scaling laws, plateau phenomena, and spectral structure for shallow networks. It is a theory contribution aimed at researchers who study how representation learning unfolds.
arxiv-2602-05946:
Alignment methods for language models can be read as divergence estimators between preferred and unpreferred behavior, a view that yields recipes for new losses. Rajdeep Haldar, Lantao Mei, and 3 co-authors extend that view beyond preference data to general alignment, including reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, where feedback arrives only as scalar scores.

They introduce a family of on policy objectives built on f divergences, plus a hybrid loss that mixes on policy reward optimization with off policy preference supervision. The objectives provably estimate divergences between reward aligned and unaligned response distributions, and expected reward improves after alignment. On math reasoning tasks, their method improved over GRPO. In safety alignment with learned reward models, the hybrid loss reduced reward hacking, the classic failure where a model games the scorer. The paper offers a unifying design principle for alignment algorithms. It should interest researchers who build post training methods.
arxiv-2602-06046:
Keeping stored information safe from heat and noise takes constant upkeep, and Amadeus Brandes asks what that upkeep must cost. He frames the problem in thermodynamics, the physics of heat and energy. A new measure, called preservation stiffness, tracks how strongly a system resists loss.

Brandes proves a simple rule for the best setup: at the ideal point, stiffness equals the share between stored content and upkeep capacity. For systems where extra effort buys less and less, he shows the best share stays below one half. He checks the idea against proofreading inside bacteria and overhead in internet traffic rules.
arxiv-2602-06146:
Q-learning is a workhorse method for teaching agents by trial and reward, often paired with linear models that estimate action values. Prashant Mehta and Sean Meyn study when this training settles down instead of wandering off. Recent work showed the estimates stay bounded under a softened, slightly random action rule.

Boundedness alone, though, leaves open whether a target equation has one answer or many. The pair show that with a fixed, non-adaptive training rule, that equation may have no answer or several, and training can go unstable. Even with an ideal feature set, two answers can exist under a greedy rule. Far more structure is needed to promise convergence.
arxiv-2602-06246:
Learning a sparse polynomial over yes-or-no variables, exactly and with few questions, is the problem tackled by Yigit Efe Erginbas and 3 co-authors. Writing such a function in the AND basis is called a Möbius transform. The parity basis version is well understood, but AND basis vectors overlap too much for standard compressed sensing tricks.

The team turns adaptive group testing, a method for finding rare items with pooled tests, into a working transform. Their fully adaptive version asks close to the fewest possible questions. A partly adaptive variant trades some extra questions for far fewer rounds of adaptivity. The methods also speed up rebuilding hypergraphs from edge-count questions.
arxiv-2602-06346:
Flow models make pictures by following a learned path from noise to image, and fast versions try to jump the path in one or few steps. Tianyi Zhang and 7 co-authors find two flaws in how those fast models are trained. Random pairings of noise and data bend the target path, and small errors pile up over long jumps.

Their framework, FlowConsist, trains the model on velocities from its own marginal path instead, keeping it on a consistent trajectory. A rectification step lines up the distributions of made and real samples at every point along the path. On a standard image benchmark, the method set a new quality record for one-step generation.
arxiv-2602-06546:
Judging translation quality for English to Hebrew has had no public benchmark, despite the language pair's practical importance. Andy Rosenbaum and 2 co-authors release MTQE.en-he, the first such benchmark they know of. It pairs hundreds of English segments from a standard translation set with Hebrew machine translations and expert quality scores.

Three human experts rated each translation. The team tested prompting a commercial chatbot, plus two established quality estimation models, and found that combining all three beat the best single model. Full fine-tuning of the models proved unstable, but lightweight tuning methods trained steadily and improved scores. The benchmark and results support future work on this under-resourced pair.
arxiv-2602-06646:
How far a random path can stray is the question behind transport inequalities named after Michel Talagrand, and Peter K. Friz and four co-authors study them in a curved setting. Their setting is Brownian motion on Carnot groups, spaces that model motion with restricted directions. A leading example is the rough path lift, a tool for handling very jagged signals.

They give a direct proof of the inequality on the enhanced path space and show equality holds for a natural class of couplings. A second route proves the result for the heat kernel measure and lifts it to Brownian paths. The paper also shows where a standard shortcut from flat geometry fails in this curved setting, though a rounded-off version of the Heisenberg group partly repairs it.
arxiv-2602-07046:
Murad Farzulla asks if crypto markets treat infrastructure shocks and regulatory shocks differently. He studies returns and conditional variance for 50 events and six assets, from January 2019 through August 2025. His models are GJR-GARCH-X. He traces the variance gap across inclusion screens.

Hand-picked events yield a multiplier near three and a half times. A mechanical filter on a broad candidate pool yields only about half to one and a half times. That pattern is descriptive and tied to the screen used, not an inferential contrast between screens. The hand-picked gap is not significant against a sharp per-asset-equality null under a Student-t-copula bootstrap, with a p-value near four tenths. Other inference choices give one-sided p-values from two hundredths to twelve hundredths, so the verdict hangs on method. The paper's main gift is an inference ladder and a calibration study.
arxiv-2602-08046:
Making and completing 3D objects is hard when inputs are incomplete or data distributions are complex and varied. Yahia Hamdi and three co-authors combine deep 3D convolutional GANs with a mixture-of-experts method, letting the network dynamically select the most relevant expert sub-networks for each input.

The hybrid architecture produces high-quality 3D models and reconstructs damaged or partial objects more effectively than a single monolithic generator. By routing other shapes and damage patterns to other experts, it handles heterogeneous, structurally intricate data that strains ordinary GANs. Computer-vision teams and 3D-content creators gain a more flexible generator for completion and synthesis tasks where one model rarely fits all.
arxiv-2602-08146:
Automated test generation usually chases coverage or readability, but rarely robustness: do the tests actually catch bugs in corner cases? Pengyu Chang and five co-authors propose AdverTest, an adversarial framework in which two language-model agents spar over test quality.

A test-generation agent writes tests while a mutant-generation agent creates code mutants that exploit the current suite's blind spots, forcing the test agent to refine its cases iteratively. The loop targets vulnerable execution paths that coverage alone would miss. Software engineers gain a testing approach that treats bug detection as an adversarial game, producing suites hardened against the very mutants designed to slip past them.
arxiv-2602-08446:
Tiny internet-of-things devices want to learn together without sharing raw data, but their small models falter on diverse, skewed data and hostile updates. Pouria Arefijamal and three co-authors introduce RIFLE, a federated learning framework that swaps gradient sharing for logit-based knowledge transfer. Their arXiv paper aims to make deep models practical on constrained hardware.

A divergence-based check scores the trustworthiness of each client's update without exposing private data. Tests on three image benchmarks under skewed conditions show false positives down by up to 87.5 percent, poisoning mitigation up by 62.5 percent, and accuracy up by 28.3 percent over standard baselines within ten rounds. Training time for a large vision model collapses from centuries to under two hours on typical devices. Readers get a robust recipe for edge learning.
arxiv-2602-08546:
Data analysts hunting for highlights issue groups of related queries and stitch the results together by hand. Marios Iakovidis and Panos Vassiliadis introduce the ANALYZE operator, a cube-querying tool that gives a 360-degree view of data in one call. Their arXiv paper defines its semantics as five internal facilitator queries.

Those queries report on the chosen subset, contrast it with peer subspaces, and drill down to finer granularity. The authors prove the facilitator queries can be merged without changing results, yielding a multi-query optimization strategy with three variants. Experiments show the intermediate merging strategy performs consistently strongly, with the others winning in specific overlap regimes. Readers get a formal tool for intentional exploration.
arxiv-2602-08646:
Reward-guided generation with one-step models can be unlocked by optimizing noise at test time, but that trick invites reward hacking and runs slowly. Jisung Hwang and Minhyuk Sung propose gradient preconditioning to make it efficient and reliable. Their arXiv paper projects reward gradients onto a compact spectral set that captures white Gaussian noise statistics.

Each update is reshaped into a noise-aligned direction, driving faster reward ascent while blocking hacking. The projection is closed-form with fast-Fourier-transform complexity, adding negligible overhead. On FLUX with four reward models, the method matches the leading regularized method's aesthetic score using only thirty percent of its wall-clock time. Readers get a cheap guardrail for test-time reward optimization.
arxiv-2602-08846:
Sam Speight and one co-author build a mathematical model for a type theory that mixes linear and ordinary reasoning. Linear types track resources that must be used exactly once, while ordinary types allow reuse. Their model grows out of a linear combinatory algebra, a spare algebraic setting for computation.

To make the model work, they add a universe with two decoding rules, one for each kind of type, closed under large products of both kinds. They also add a rule for turning linear terms into ordinary ones. Lists over a linear type serve as a case study, and the whole construction is checked in the Rocq proof assistant.
arxiv-2602-08946:
Andrei Poblaguev shows that two kinds of Coulomb correction in proton-nucleus scattering are secretly the same. Within the eikonal approximation, the corrections to non-flip and spin-flip scattering strengths coincide whenever both share the same exponential form factors. That match turns a hard problem into a tractable one.

Both electric and hadronic elastic scattering strengths can then be worked out with high precision in the massless-photon limit, including soft magnetic photon exchange. The recipe uses analytic formulas plus integrals over a finite impact range with well-behaved integrands, giving researchers a controlled tool for phenomenology.
arxiv-2602-09146:
Finding a video by how things move, not how they look, is surprisingly hard: most video models lean on appearance and scene, while optical flow lacks semantic meaning. Saar Huberman and four co-authors expose that bias with SimMotion, a benchmark pairing controlled synthetic clips with a new human-annotated real-world set. On it, existing models often fail to separate motion from looks.

Their answer, SemanticMoments, is training-free: it works out time stats, mainly higher-order moments, over traits from pretrained semantic models. Across the benchmarks it consistently beats RGB, flow, and text-supervised rivals. The result suggests that simple statistics in semantic feature space offer a scalable, perceptually grounded basis for motion-centered video search.
arxiv-2602-09346:
Spanish varies sharply by region, and Yoshifumi Kawasaki's single-author 2026 study tests whether large language models capture that variation or flatten it. Treating models as virtual informants, the study probes their dialect knowledge with yes-no and multiple-choice questions drawn from a large expert-curated database of Spanish words. The survey covers more than nine hundred items across twenty-one Spanish-speaking countries, scored at country and dialect-area levels.

Results show systematic unevenness rather than uniform knowledge. Varieties tied to Spain, Equatorial Guinea, Mexico and Central America, and the La Plata region are recognized most accurately, while Chilean Spanish proves hardest for models to pin down. Strikingly, the sheer volume of digital text per country does not explain the pattern. The study offers fine-grained evidence for debates about digital linguistic bias in Spanish, suggesting forces beyond data quantity shape dialect representation.
arxiv-2602-09446:
Urban visual pollution, from tangled wires to cluttered signage, harms city life, yet research on automatic detection remains scattered. Mohammad Masudur Rahman and four co-authors map the field in a 2026 scoping review following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, searching seven academic databases and finding twenty-six relevant articles. Most work targets narrow pollutant groupings with detector variants from the YOLO, Faster R-CNN, and EfficientDet families.

Datasets cover single areas and lack shared groupings, while few studies reach real-time systems, and those skew by place. The authors propose a watch system that folds detection into a visual clutter index scoring severity for a given area. They call for a unified management system joining a pollutant grouping, a cross-city benchmark dataset, a general model, and a scoring index to serve lasting urban beauty and resident well-being.
arxiv-2602-09646:
Fernando de Ávila Silva and three co-authors study global solving for a class of diff chains on the product of a torus with flat space. The chains link to systems of flow ops. Their 2026 paper works within time-repeating Gelfand-Shilov spaces, where coeffs are real-valued Gevrey functions on the torus and the spatial op is fully round and normal. A natural diff chain made by these ops is set up and studied.

Solving is studied in both function and ultra settings. A full account comes in terms of a Diophantine rule using the constant part of the linked one-form and the spectrum of the spatial op. Global smoothness of the chain is also studied. The results extend prior work on scalar ops and constant-coeff systems to diff chains with time-changing real coeffs.
arxiv-2602-10046:
Reproducing a paper's numeric tables is essential for building on its results, yet agents that attempt it rarely leave executable proof. A 2026 paper by Doehyun Baek and Michael Pradel presents Artisan, an agent that reproduces tables of numeric results from a paper and its artifact. The task is framed as code generation, so users can audit and rerun the reproduction script themselves.

Automated judges steer the agent toward correct results without revealing them and block shortcuts such as copying precomputed numbers. The team also built Artisan-Bench, sixty tasks drawn from twenty-three software engineering papers. Experiments show Artisan works effectively and efficiently, and its runs surfaced twenty new errors in papers or artifacts.
arxiv-2602-10446:
Federico Fraternale and four co-authors explain a puzzling Voyager 1 observation from beyond the heliopause in a 2026 paper. In 2020, the spacecraft recorded a jump in magnetic field strength in the very local interstellar medium. A distinct hump and a persistently strong field followed. The origin of those traits had been debated.

The team interprets the data with a self-consistent magnetohydrodynamic model of the solar wind meeting interstellar space. The model is driven by solar views and turbulence analysis of Voyager data. Their simulations show that compressions driven by the solar cycle, striking the heliopause, can reproduce the observed jump and hump. The traits appear tied to solar cycle 24, linking distant interstellar readings to the Sun's own rhythm.
arxiv-2602-10646:
Matthew H. Y. Xie and two co-authors compute equivariant Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomials for a special matroid in a 2026 paper. The thagomizer matroid, shown as the graphic matroid of the complete tripartite graph, has the hyperoctahedral group as its full automorphism group. Its equivariant polynomials encode model-theory data that plain polynomials collapse.

Exploiting the palindromicity of the equivariant Z-polynomial, the authors reduce the work to known symmetric-group theory for cycle-graph matroids. A flip rule then yields the inverse polynomial. Each number proves to be an honest model whose parts all differ. Passing to sizes brings back the known number results, showing the equivariant detail carries strictly more information.
arxiv-2602-10846:
G. Quintana-Lacaci and six co-authors portray the chemistry of a rare old star in a 2026 paper. High spread-speed carbon stars combine carbon-rich chemistry with spread speeds typical of oxygen-rich big stars. AFGL 2233, new as a high-mass old object that used up hot-bottom burning, tests knowledge of these objects.

A complete line survey at millimeter wavelengths uses far-infrared views and wave-mix maps of key molecules. It shows the star-ring shell's makeup and isotope ratios. The study finds nitrogen- and oxygen-bearing species inside a carbon-rich setting, a chemical oddity. Spin diagrams and light transfer modeling under a large-velocity-slope guess turn spectra into amounts, showing how such stars evolve and feed their surroundings.
arxiv-2602-11146:
Tuning image generators needs reward models that are cheap and true to the generator's own space. Gongye Liu and ten co-authors propose DiNa-LRM, a diffusion-native latent reward model that learns preferences straight on noisy diffusion states. A noise-tuned likelihood lets doubt grow with diffusion noise.

Built on a pretrained latent diffusion backbone with a timestep-aware reward head, the model also supports noise ensembling at test time. Across image matching tests it beats prior diffusion-based rewards and rivals leading vision-language rewards at a fraction of the cost. In preference tuning it speeds matching and uses fewer resources, making it a practical reward for diffusion models.
arxiv-2602-11246:
How many traits can a layer store if decoding must stay straight? Nikhil Garg and two co-authors build a math frame for the straight form idea, splitting it into straight code and straight decoding. Classic compressed sensing answers the question when decoding may be curved.

Requiring straight decoding changes the problem fundamentally. The authors prove nearly matching upper and lower bounds for straight compressed sensing, showing a measured gap from the classic case. The upper bound confirms that neurons can store an exponential number of traits under the idea, supporting overlap. The lower bound uses rank arguments for near-identity matrices and a graph theorem, and extensions cover decoders with signal and bias.
arxiv-2602-11446:
Portable ultra-low-field MRI could widen neuroimaging access, but diffusion imaging suffers most. Mark D. Olchanyi and nine co-authors offer a nine-direction, single-shell ultra-low-field diffusion sequence plus two companions: a Bayesian bias-field correction with angular dependence, and a super-detail network that generalizes across data sets without retraining.

Built downsampling and matched low- and high-field scans show the pipeline recovers white-matter microstructure and volume at ultra-low field. The super-detail method also applies straight to Alzheimer's classification on degraded scans, improving agreement with undegraded metrics. Recipes and code are freely released to advance low-field reconstruction and sequence harmonization.
arxiv-2602-11746:
Most open-source projects never reach sustainability, yet forecasting models rarely tell maintainers what concrete steps to take. Nafiz Imtiaz Khan and one co-author close that gap by using language models as evidence miners over the software engineering literature. A retrieval pipeline plus two-layer prompting extracts researched actionables: concise, evidence-linked recommendations tied to specific project practices, drawn from 829 conference papers.

Follow-up prompting filters hallucinations, extracts impact and evidence, and judges soundness and precision. The pipeline yields 1922 actionables, of which 1312 pass strict quality criteria, organized into practice-oriented categories linkable to project signals from tools like APEX. The result is a reproducible, scalable route from scattered research findings to structured, evidence-based actions that guide open-source projects toward sustainability.
arxiv-2602-12146:
Lossless compression must shrink files without losing a single byte, yet older tricks often miss patterns in complex data. Mahdi Khodabandeh led this work with three co-authors, building a system on a T5 language model that is trained with reinforcement learning. Instead of squeezing data into dense vectors, it keeps data as token strings.

That choice matters because tokens stay close to the shape of the source file. An off-policy training method rewards shorter token strings, cutting needless repeat while keeping meaning intact. The team reports much better shrink rates than old methods, without leaning on outside grammar or world facts. The result is a flexible tool for storage and transfer where exact recovery counts.
arxiv-2602-12346:
Robots that gather information face a costly maths problem: mutual information is a principled guide for sensor placement and path planning, but it demands repeated large determinant calculations. Kalvik Jakkala led this work with two co-authors, presenting Schur-MI, a Gaussian process formulation that reuses work across planning steps and factors determinants through Schur complements. Per-evaluation cost drops from cubic in candidate sites to cubic in selected sites.

Tests on real bathymetry data show up to 12.7 times speedup over the standard formulation. Field trials with an autonomous surface vehicle doing adaptive path planning confirm the method in practice. By making mutual information cheap enough for online use, Schur-MI bridges information-theoretic planning and real-time robotic exploration.
arxiv-2602-12446:
Temporal graphs change over time, with vertices and edges appearing and vanishing, yet most graph theory assumes a fixed graph. Binh-Minh Bui-Xuan led this work with three co-authors, adapting Courcelle's theorem to temporal graphs. For static graphs, that theorem says any problem expressible in monadic second-order logic runs in linear time on graphs of bounded tree-width.

The new adaptation avoids relying on a parameter tied to lifetime, or on maximum time-edges per vertex, which can exceed lifetime in the worst case. The team also defines a derivative over a sliding time window, with tree-width and twin-width for that derivative. Meta-theorems for a temporal variant of first-order logic follow, covering a wide range of temporal graph problems, including temporal cliques useful for finding communities in time series databases.
arxiv-2602-12546:
Automatic speech recognition usually pairs a speech encoder with a text decoder, but a single stack could do both jobs. Jaeyoung Lee led this work with one co-author, Masato Mimura. They present a decoder-only Conformer for speech recognition that processes speech and text in one stack. No outside encoders or pretrained models are used.

The model uses modality-aware sparse mixtures of experts, with separate expert pools for speech and text, hard routing, and top-1 selection. Those experts sit in hybrid-causality Conformer blocks, bidirectional for speech and causal for text. Training joins CTC on speech positions with label-smoothed cross-entropy for text generation. The 113-million-parameter model beats a 139-million AED baseline on LibriSpeech, with lower word error rates on test-clean and test-other. On Common Voice, a single multilingual model across five languages cuts average word error rate from above 12 percent to below 11 percent.
arxiv-2602-12746:
Speech models trained on their own can learn one language well, then lose earlier languages when taught new ones. Jing Xu and four co-authors propose Lamer-SSL, a lean method for adding languages without that forgetting. Its core is a layer-aware mix of small adapter experts: deeper layers, where meaning is richer, get more experts, so shared and language-specific knowledge can be balanced.

A replay trick also keeps old knowledge alive with only a little past data. Tests on speech recognition and language identification show the method extends models to new languages while holding performance on languages learned before. Only 2.14% of parameters need training, which keeps the update cheap. The design suits continual expansion of speech models to more tongues.
arxiv-2602-12846:
Training language models with verifiable rewards tends to amplify common reasoning paths while starving rare but valid ones, a flaw the authors call a normalisation squeeze. Zesheng Hong and two co-authors characterise the effect theoretically: mode-seeking gradients plus finite sampling act as a high-pass filter that can drive rare correct traces to extinction. Their remedy, amortised reasoning tree search, separates generation from verification instead of forcing the model to internalise search.

A flow-matching objective lets the verifier track conservation of probability flow, steering search through sparse, high-entropy spaces where standard discriminative objectives fail. On MATH-500 the method reaches 74.6% with best-of-16 sampling, matching fully fine-tuned policies at 74.7% without touching the generative backbone. On long-tail problems where coupled optimisation collapses to zero, it recovers substantial performance.
arxiv-2602-12946:
A birational selfmap is a transformation of a variety that is defined almost everywhere and has an almost-everywhere inverse, and the collection of all such maps forms a group. Enrica Floris studies that group for varieties that resemble a conic bundle, a family of conic curves varying over a base. The question is how large and how structured the group can be.

The answer is striking in its size: the group maps onto a direct sum of uncountably many copies of the two-element group. Such a surjection forces the group itself to be uncountable, far larger than any finite or countable symmetry group. The result gives a clean, algebraic witness to the richness of birational symmetries for conic fibrations, where geometry and group theory meet.
arxiv-2602-13146:
Strong-coupling thermodynamics starts from the Hamiltonian of mean force, yet explicit operator forms exist only in narrow settings. Gerard McCaul presents a quenched density system that rewrites the reduced equilibrium state as an average of local propagators in imaginary time, using the Hubbard-Stratonovich change. The approach cleanly separates the setting's number-based definition from the system's algebra response structure.

For a harmonic setting whose coupling commutes with the system Hamiltonian, the correction to the Hamiltonian of mean force takes an exact closed form. The result is checked with finite-bath trace-out sums and random sampling in imaginary time for a five-level projector-coupled model. For theorists, the system offers a rigorous route to mean-force operators beyond the usual restricted cases.
arxiv-2602-13346:
Naming cell types in single-cell RNA data is a bottleneck: markers shift with tissue and state, and new states have no reference to match. CellMaster imitates expert practice as an AI agent, using language-model knowledge to annotate cells on the fly with readable reasons, without pretraining or fixed marker tables. That zero-shot design aims at exactly the rare and novel states where standard tools fail.

Across nine data sets spanning eight tissues, automatic mode beat the best baselines by 7.1 percent, and human-in-the-loop refinement widened the lead to 18.6 percent, with a 22.1 percent gain on subtypes. Code and a web app are available for reuse. Zhen Wang leads the work with twelve co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13446:
Wireless systems that serve many users at once on shared spectrum must untangle overlapping signals, and non-orthogonal multiple access does this by design. This paper builds an end-to-end autoencoder for downlink NOMA over Rayleigh fading channels, learning signal constellations that are aware of interference and adapt to channel conditions. Unlike prior work that assumes simple noise channels or treats fading without full end-to-end learning, the framework embeds the wireless channel into both training and inference.

Practical channel knowledge is handled through limited feedback, with uniform and Lloyd-Max quantization of channel gains compared on training and bit error rate. With perfect channel knowledge, the autoencoder beat existing analytical NOMA schemes, and Lloyd-Max quantization beat uniform quantization on error rate. Selma Benouadah leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13546:
Radar targets that fall between Doppler grid points can defeat classic matched-filter detectors, which saturate even at high signal-to-noise ratios under strict false-alarm limits. The principled fix, a continuous-parameter generalized likelihood ratio test, scans densely at high cost and stays sensitive to covariance mismatch through whitening. DopplerGLRTNet amortizes that test with a lightweight regressor.

Its regressor guesses the true Doppler inside one cell from whitened data, while its detector scores that guess with matched filter energy in a single GLRT style test. Monte Carlo tests in Gaussian and compound-Gaussian clutter show off-grid saturation eased, dense-scan performance nearly matched at a fraction of cost, and robustness to covariance estimation improved. Yadang Alexis Rouzoumka leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13746:
Thermal power systems couple performance variables in a hierarchy of importance, making joint tuning hard or infeasible and limiting integrated, scalable operation. This paper presents a fully machine-learning-powered bi-level tuning framework. Upper- and lower-level goal functions use artificial neural network models, and the lower-level problem is embedded analytically through Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality conditions. The reworked single-level framework, ANN-KKT, was tested on benchmark problems and on real runs of a 660 megawatt coal plant and a 395 megawatt gas turbine system.

Results matched bi-level benchmark solutions, with best solutions computed in 0.22 to 0.88 seconds, yielding 583 megawatts for coal and 402 megawatts for gas at best turbine heat rates of 7337 and 7542 kilojoules per kilowatt-hour. The method also maps a workable, robust operating envelope accounting for uncertainty while raising thermal efficiency across settings. Talha Ansar leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13846:
Adson Duarte and eleven co-authors report a 2026 arXiv paper on gauging heart output from ultrasound video. Cardiac output guides care for heart disease, yet its gold-standard measure needs an invasive catheter test. The team sought a safer read from routine heart scans.

They pre-trained a model on the same small set of four-chamber echo videos used for the main task, using a self-taught method called SimCLR. That step cut overfitting and lifted the test correlation to 0.41 on average. The result beat PanEcho, a model trained on over one million exams, showing that smart pre-training can help when labeled scans are few.
arxiv-2602-14146:
Yu Wang and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv model of a quantum battery fed by a charger. The setup is a two-qubit system: one qubit stores charge, while the other charges it under the influence of a reservoir. A time-local master equation in Lindblad form governs the process, with a dephasing rate that can turn negative early on.

That negative rate signals a memory effect in the early charging stage. The authors find it can raise the battery's maximal ergotropy above the Markovian case with the same long-run dephasing rate. Non-Markovian quantum jumps explain the boost. A discrete-time, measurement-enhanced version is also sketched as a quantum circuit with global and random local operations.
arxiv-2602-14346:
Huyuan Chen and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv fractional elliptic equation from a closed MEMS model. The equation sets a fractional Laplacian of u equal to lambda over (a minus u) squared, in a bounded domain with zero Dirichlet boundary conditions. The function a vanishes at the boundary, modeling an elastic membrane that contacts the ground plate there.

The paper establishes both existence and nonexistence results, showing how boundary decay of the membrane shapes solutions and pull-in voltage. When the membrane profile decays in certain ways, solutions exist; in other regimes, none do. The analysis links the geometry of contact at the boundary to the device's pull-in behavior, a central concern for micro-electromechanical systems.
arxiv-2602-14446:
Zhe Yang and five co-authors study a 2026 arXiv holographic superconductor-insulator transition. The model is an Einstein-Maxwell-Dilaton-Axion p-wave cold wire, tracked through its cold gap. Nearing the quantum key point closes the gap and brings early blocker traits, hinting that raised quantum wiggles curb cold order and spark the shift.

That act shows only when condensate aim lines up with the path of shift-symmetry breaking, the authors hint. Two holo gauges probe the shift: link entropy and link wedge cross-section, a mixed-state link gauge. Unlike entropy, which big setups swamp with heat entropy, the wedge cross-section shows sharp key scaling, giving a tough gauge of the quantum phase shift.
arxiv-2602-15146:
Theißinger and colleagues move quantum circuit synthesis beyond reinforcement learning. It translates abstract quantum algorithms into gate lists for hardware. Exact solutions are infeasible since the search space grows exponentially. Existing methods suffer misaligned objectives, heavy training costs, and weak transfer across qubit counts.

The team uses supervised learning to approximate the minimum description length of residual unitaries, then combines that estimate with stochastic beam search to find near-optimal gate lists. Their lightweight model works zero-shot across qubit counts, sharply cutting training overhead against prior baselines. Across benchmarks, the method builds circuits faster in wall-clock time while beating state-of-the-art success rates for complex circuits.
arxiv-2602-15446:
Abou El Kheir and Bernasconi probe trapped states in the band gap of glassy blends like Ge2Sb2Te5, which control current flow via Poole-Frenkel. Grasping the source of in-gap states and change during aging is key for taming drag drift in storage chips.

They use an ML teaching inter-atom force field to build copies of Ge2Sb2Te5 whose charge layout is studied in thickness working model with mixed working. A number study of frame patterns on which the in-gap states are trapped shows that most in-gap states use bad bonds, same-atom or Ge-Sb bonds. They are joined by Ge in pyramid shapes or over-linked bits. Meta-motion runs aping aging back the view that frame settling drains in-gap states and raises drag. The runs thus give ideas for easing drag drift in storage chips.
arxiv-2602-15546:
Garriga and colleagues build a tool for what-if questions about time series, where the aim is to judge how an event or a treatment shaped outcomes over time. Such questions matter in finance, health care, and marketing, but older counterfactual methods were not built for time series data. The team adapts variational and adversarial autoencoder methods to that setting, then goes further with a new design.

Their Conditional Entropy-Penalized Autoencoder, or CEPAE, adds an entropy penalty over the latent space to push learned features apart into cleaner parts. The method follows the abduction-action-prediction steps inside a structural causal model frame. Tests on synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real data show CEPAE beating the adapted methods on the measures used, with theory to back the design.
arxiv-2602-15746:
Salgueiro and colleagues develop a slow focus sensor for the Keck I laser guide star adaptive optics system. Laser guide stars have served ground telescopes for decades, widening sky coverage. But slow drifts in sodium layer altitude corrupt focus measurements, creating slow focus error that normally needs a natural guide star. The team builds focal plane wavefront sensing for slow focus tracking at Keck I, aiming to raise sky coverage and cut lag error.

They test three focal plane algorithms: Gerchberg-Saxton, linearised focal plane technique, and Gaussian fit. Tests use near-infrared H and K bands plus 2025 Keck bench and on-sky data. On linearity, compute cost, and resistance to low signal and residuals, Gerchberg-Saxton emerges as the main on-sky candidate. On-sky tests show it fixing deliberate focus errors even under high turbulence. Lessons transfer to other 8 to 10 metre telescopes and future 30 to 40 metre giants.
arxiv-2602-15946:
Das and colleagues move particle tracking intelligence onto the detector chip itself. At the Large Hadron Collider, pixel sensors record rich patterns of ionization, yet most of that detail is thrown away because data rates, delay limits, and power budgets are so tight. Deciding what to keep, right at the sensor edge, sets how much science an experiment can collect.

The team shows that neural networks built into front end electronics can infer a charged particle path from a single silicon layer. Their networks estimate hit positions and incoming angles together with calibrated uncertainty, while meeting strict limits on numerical precision, delay, and silicon area. The work points toward smart sensing at the edge, where high rate instruments judge their own data before it ever leaves the detector.
arxiv-2602-16046:
Marta Kladz-Duda leads a team of three math researchers. They work on spaces and on how sets can cover a space, a theme in set theory and topology. Their paper studies productively Scheepers spaces and their kin. It asks when a space keeps its cover trait after taking products with other spaces. The main claim needs two size measures for sets to match. Under that match, in the class of hereditarily Lindelof spaces, each productively Scheepers space is productively Hurewicz.

The same claim holds for all plain spaces under a distinct size rule. The proofs use tools from combinatorics and the Menger cover trait as tied to ultrafilters. The authors also show that, under near coherence of filters, the Scheepers trait matches a Menger trait tied to any ultrafilter. In short, the work ties these cover traits to each other in a tight, exact way.
arxiv-2602-16246:
Yun-Shiuan Chuang and coauthors propose a scalable way to evaluate multi-turn tool-calling language model agents. Such agents are increasingly used in production, and benchmarks must compare models reliably and yield on-policy training data. Prior benchmarks rely on fully deterministic backends, which are costly to build. Their Proxy State-Based Evaluation framework preserves final state-based checks without a deterministic database. A scenario specifies user goals, facts, expected final state, and expected agent behavior.

A language model state tracker infers a structured proxy state from the full trace. Language model judges then verify goal completion and detect hallucinations against case constraints. Empirically, the benchmark produces stable, model-differentiating rankings, and its rollouts provide supervision that transfers to unseen scenarios. Careful case specification yields near-zero simulator hallucination rates. Human-judge agreement exceeds ninety percent, indicating reliable automated evaluation.
arxiv-2602-16346:
Nivya Talokar leads four coauthors measuring how LLM-based agents can be drawn into illicit assistance over many turns. Such agents run real workflows through tools and memory, which also lets ill-intended users steer them toward complex misuse. Existing misuse benchmarks mostly test single prompts, leaving a gap around multi-turn help with harmful tasks.

The team introduces STING, a red-teaming framework that builds a stepwise illicit plan around a benign persona, probes the target with adaptive follow-ups, and tracks phases with judge agents. An analysis treats multi-turn red-teaming as a time-to-first-jailbreak variable, yielding discovery curves, hazard-ratio attribution by language, and a metric, Restricted Mean Jailbreak Discovery. Across AgentHarm scenarios, STING reaches higher illicit-task completion than single-turn prompting or adapted chat baselines. In six non-English settings, success did not consistently rise in lower-resource languages, unlike chatbot findings.
arxiv-2602-16546:
Mostafa Rahmani Ghourtani and co-authors present Failure-Aware Access Point Selection. It aims to keep cell-free massive MIMO networks working when access points fail. The method weighs each point's failure chance alongside its channel strength. A tunable factor models how stressed the network is. Performance is judged by the worst-served user's rate. It is also judged by the share of users left with no active point.

Simulations show the failure-aware choice holds up far better than failure-blind clustering. At high failure levels, outage falls by more than four fifths. Worst-case user rates improve too. Network designers get a practical, low-cost way to buy resilience. Dense wireless systems face hardware faults as a fact of life.
arxiv-2602-16646:
Felipe Rojas and a large team report two warm sub-Saturn planets found in TESS full-frame images. Warm giants are key to pinning down how giant planets form and evolve. Mass plus radius, joined with modest irradiation, lets researchers gauge bulk makeup, a core clue to formation and structure. Both worlds orbit sun-like stars and were checked with ground-based spectra and photometry.

Joint fits of light curves and radial velocities confirm TOI-883 b and TOI-899 b. Their masses, radii, periods, and equilibrium heats are all measured. Though alike in mass, period, and host type, the two seem to hold varied inner makeups, hinting at distinct birth paths. Both are apt targets for air studies that could further test formation stories for Neptune-class giants.
arxiv-2602-16746:
Yongzhong Xu gives a geometric account of grokking, the delayed shift from rote memory to broad skill in small algorithmic tasks. A principal component study of attention weight paths in transformers trained on modular arithmetic shows training moves mainly within a low-dimensional execution subspace. One component captures most of the path variance.

Commutator defects, which gauge non-commutativity of successive gradient steps, are projected onto that subspace. Curvature grows sharply in directions at right angles to the subspace while the path stays largely confined to it. Curvature growth always precedes broad skill across learning rates and settings, with lead time obeying a power law in grokking timescale. Tests show motion along the subspace is needed for grokking, while raising curvature alone is not enough.
arxiv-2602-17146:
Giovanni Palermo led a three-author team arguing that social network structure alone can warp what people think everyone else believes. Bias is usually blamed on mental shortcuts or thin information, but the authors show that when news travels through connections, the network itself distorts perception. A simple model with a binary trait, such as atheist or believer, produces systematic misreadings of peers.

Those misreadings survive aggregation, undercutting naive faith in the wisdom of the crowd. The team derives an estimator that predicts the size and direction of the bias from network features, and they validate it against three large opinion surveys. The message is practical: network structure drives collective misperception, with real stakes for segregation, polarization, and the marginalization of minorities.
arxiv-2602-17346:
David Stein led a three-author paper on partial optimality in the preordering problem, a generalization of clustering and partial ordering with uses in bioinformatics and social network analysis. Given a finite set and a value for every ordered pair, the problem asks for a preorder maximizing the sum of values for pairs the preorder includes. The problem is NP-hard, and prior work could solve it only partially.

Building on that state of the art, the authors contribute new partial optimality conditions plus efficient algorithms for deciding them. Experiments on real and synthetic data show the new conditions increase, in particular, the fraction of pairs decided efficiently to belong in an optimal preorder. The work thus extends how much of an optimal preorder can be pinned down without full search.
arxiv-2602-17546:
Jyotin Goel led a three-author team behind a 2026 arXiv paper on keeping language models safe while they are fine-tuned. Safety behavior can slip under harmless fine-tuning and worsen under hostile updates. Existing defenses often protect little, or trade safety against usefulness. The paper introduces a training framework that adapts regularization in response to safety risk, so models stay aligned through fine-tuning.

Risk is estimated two ways. A judge-based Safety Critic scores harm in training batches, while an activation-based predictor reads harmful intent from intermediate model activations. Each signal holds higher-risk updates close to a safe reference policy, while lower-risk updates train normally. Tests show harmful intent is predictable from pre-generation activations, and judge scores give high-recall safety guidance. Across model families and attack scenarios, adaptive regularization lowers attack success, preserves downstream performance, and adds no inference-time cost.
arxiv-2602-17646:
Sima Noorani and team build a principled frame for multi-round human-AI teamwork on high-stakes choices. As people lean more on chat-based AI, joint work must truly lift decision quality rather than erode it. Two rules govern their view: counterfactual harm, or not harming human strengths, and added value where humans tend to err.

Users state what harm and added value mean for their task through plain rules. An online algorithm with finite-sample backing then upholds those rules as the teamwork unfolds. Tests span a mock medical task and a crowd-run picture task. The method holds set breach rates even as exchanges shift, and easing or firming the rules shifts human scores in foreseen ways.
arxiv-2602-17846:
Nick Dodson and team give a geometric picture of memorization in diffusion models. Diffusion models generate high-quality samples but can memorize training data, raising privacy concerns. It remains unclear where along the noise schedule memorization arises. It is also unclear how data geometry shapes it, and how effects at varied noise scales interact.

The authors partition the noise schedule into three regimes. The split rests on coverage of training data by Gaussian shells and concentration of the posterior, two objects argued to govern memorization and generalization. Memorization risk proves highly non-uniform across noise levels, with a danger zone at medium noise where memorization peaks. Small and large noise regimes resist memorization through distinct mechanisms: small noise through limited training coverage, large noise through low posterior concentration and provably near-linear Gaussian denoising. For medium noise, geometric conditions support a targeted, geometry-informed intervention that mitigates memorization.
arxiv-2602-18146:
Lionel Salesses and four co-authors build a learning system that predicts heat patterns on meshes far into the future. Their 2026 paper targets jobs like powder-bed 3D printing, where the heat history of each spot decides flaws and strength. Full physics simulations get the physics right but cost too much to run again and again.

The system pairs two models that run at different time scales, both built on graph networks that work straight on mesh shapes. A compact latent code keeps memory low and training steady over thousands of steps. On simulated printing data the forecasts stay true across varied shapes and beat older baselines. Though tested in two dimensions, the design is meant to extend to three dimensions and other physics with many time scales.
arxiv-2602-18246:
Rhyd Lewis offers a visual tour of graph coloring, a puzzle with real jobs to do. His 2026 paper treats the problem of coloring nodes, edges, and faces under rules that keep neighbors apart, a task behind sports schedules, maps, street navigation, and timetables. The subject is also a staple of university courses on graphs, algorithms, and combinatorics.

Lewis reviews the key theory for all three coloring types and pairs each idea with its algorithm. The review comes alive through detailed, visually engaging figures built to sharpen understanding and hold interest. Readers get both the results and a feel for why they work, making the tour useful for students meeting the subject and for practitioners hunting a clear reference.
arxiv-2602-18346:
Pavithra PM Nair and one co-author built Vichara, a framework that predicts and explains Indian appellate judgments. Their 2026 paper targets a heavy backlog, where higher courts review lower court rulings. Vichara reads English appellate proceeding documents and splits them into decision points, each capturing the issue, outcome, reasoning, deciding authority, and timing.

Explanations follow a structured format adapted from the IRAC frame for Indian legal reasoning, letting lawyers judge prediction soundness quickly. On the PredEx dataset and an expert-annotated slice of the Indian Legal Documents Corpus, Vichara beats existing benchmarks across four large language models. GPT-4o mini leads, near eighty-two percent on PredEx and near eighty percent on the expert set, and human judges rate its explanations clearest, best linked, and most useful.
arxiv-2602-18546:
Lin Chen and five co-authors link city movement to social resilience, the capacity of venues to maintain visits and diversity. Their 2026 paper notes cities thrive on social life, yet shocks such as pandemics, hurricanes, and wildfires disrupt them, with venues responding differently.

The study analyzes movement data from fifteen cities with over one hundred three million residents across three shocks. Despite declining visits, thirty-six to fifty-three percent of venues show reduced segregation, and twenty-one to thirty-nine percent show more visits. A mobility network linking venue types reveals eigenvector centrality predicts social resilience, raising explanatory power by over eighty percent over intuitive features. Core venues show shorter visits, broader visitation, and steadier appeal than peripheral ones. The pattern implies a dual mechanism: core venues sustain ties through frequent interaction, peripheral ones through deeper engagement. The team proposes a well-and-pool analogy for mobility budgets.
arxiv-2602-18646:
Yingkai Sha and eight co-authors downscale weather with AI. Their 2026 paper develops an AI-based Limited-Area Model for downscaling over the Southern Great Plains and southeast United States, with strong generalization. Trained using zero point two five-degree, three-hourly ERA5 forcings and CONUS404 targets from 1980 to 2019, the model produces four-kilometer, hourly outputs, plus post-processing.

Evaluated across multiple forcing datasets, periods, and climates, the model produces stable multi-year simulations for present-day downscaling in 2021 to 2024 water years. Its deterministic verification scores match other forecasting models. It generalizes robustly to a one-degree, six-hourly non-ERA5 dataset with minor changes. Frontal cyclone and hurricane cases show realistic, interpretable weather-scale structure from coarse boundary information. Downscaling thirty-year global climate runs from 1980 to 2010 and 2070 to 2100, plus ensembles from 2025 to 2027, the model remains stable hourly and captures future climate-change signals.
arxiv-2602-18846:
Vision-language models are powerful, but their dense visual tokens make them expensive. Aditya Kumar Singh, with four co-authors, presents DUET-VLM in 2026. It is a dual-stage, plug-and-play token reduction framework for training and inference.

Stage one compresses the vision encoder's output into information-preserving tokens, removing redundancy. Stage two drops visual tokens layer by layer inside the language backbone, guided by salient text. That coordinated management keeps accuracy high while cutting tokens sharply. On one benchmark model, accuracy stays above ninety-nine percent of baseline with two-thirds fewer tokens. With training under compression, results stay strong even at extreme reductions, and video results can even surpass the baseline.
arxiv-2602-18946:
Fast training need not mean training on the edge of a breakdown. Sacchit Kale, with four co-authors, shows in 2026 that acceleration in separable logistic regression does not need instability at all. The paper keeps every step inside a stable range, yet still reaches its target at an exponential pace.

For plain gradient descent, a simple step-size plan that grows over time but never adapts to the run does the job under a margin condition. It works at any stopping point, with no need to know the total run length or the target accuracy in advance.
