They also reshape soldier cells inside tumors, curb cells that damp the response, and stir both fast and lasting defenses. Pairings with checkpoint drugs, light-based therapy, and cell therapy show added force in early work. Safety over time, large-scale making, and clear rules still stand between lab promise and clinic use.
pmc-13286446:
Qingqiu Cheng and colleagues untangle the genetics of a 26-year-old woman whose ovaries failed early, alongside short stature and mild intellectual disability. The 2026 case report shows the limits of standard testing: chromosome study, copy-number scanning, and exome sequencing all failed to explain her condition. Her chromosomes looked balanced at first glance.

Long-read sequencing, which reads much longer DNA stretches, mapped a rearrangement spanning five chromosomes and pinpointed where three genes were broken. A separate test showed her normal X chromosome was switched off in almost every cell, an extreme skew the authors blame for most of her symptoms. The case argues for long-read methods when ordinary tests leave complex rearrangements unsolved.
pmc-13286546:
Claudia Consentino and colleagues describe a posture study of orchestral musicians in a 2026 protocol article. Years of holding asymmetric instruments in fixed poses saddle players with pain that can end careers, yet hard numbers on orchestra posture remain scarce. The OPErA project will photograph 250 Italian professionals, pianists aside, with skin markers placed to measure tilt, rotation, and asymmetry with and without the instrument in hand.

Pain and disability questionnaires accompany the calibrated photos, covering arm, back, and neck function. Recruitment ran from 2023, and 240 of the target players had enrolled by February 2026. Analysis now under way will link posture faults to pain that limits performance, hunting instrument-specific patterns. The team expects the map to guide ergonomic fixes and prevention programs tuned to each section of the orchestra.
pmc-13286746:
Shuran Zhang and colleagues report a new mutation behind severe inherited high cholesterol and test whether it can be repaired in cells. The 2026 study centers on a woman with the homozygous form of the disorder, which standard treatment handles poorly. She carried one damaged cholesterol-receptor gene from her mother and a second, brand-new damaging change found in neither parent.

The team recreated the new mutation in human liver cells using gene editing. The change clearly blocked normal production of the receptor protein. A high-precision editing method, prime editing, then corrected the faulty letter with about 98 percent efficiency in the laboratory system. The authors see a path toward personalized gene therapy for this rare, hard-to-treat condition.
pmc-13286946:
Xiaofeng Li and co-authors review mitochondria as a key front in cancer immune therapy. The 2026 review notes that checkpoint drugs and lab-grown T cells changed cancer care. Yet these tools often stall in the suppressive zone around a tumor. Mitochondria steer how both cancer cells and immune cells burn fuel in that zone.

When mitochondria falter, immune killer cells lose strength. Tumor cells gain room to hide and grow. The review sets out ways to fix cell power plants and so lift immune attack. Fresh ideas span vaccines aimed at mitochondria, edits to their small genome, and grafts of healthy units into weak cells. Safe delivery and clear proof are still the hard parts.
pmc-13287046:
Phillip A. Martin offers a 2026 philosophical treatise on reality and the mind. He proposes that what we live through is a model built by the brain from delayed signals. Writing as an independent researcher outside academia, he draws on physics, neuroscience, and information theory. One layered framework holds the parts together.

Under his scheme, the base layer of information forms a wide field of states that tend to expand. Formal pieces follow from that base. One scheme uses reaction and diffusion rules, with the golden ratio as an attractor. Another links field motion to perception through a staged filter. Four testable predictions close the case, and claims marked as guesses stay flagged as such.
pmc-13287146:
Antonia Kleeberg and co-authors tested a simple blood-based score in 2026 as a predictor of death after a stroke caused by a blocked brain artery. The score, called EASIX, combines creatinine and lactate dehydrogenase values with platelet count and is meant to reflect stressed blood vessel linings.

Registry data came from Heidelberg, with 4,188 patients, and Vienna, with 2,273 patients for checking the result. Higher values tracked with higher mortality over short and long follow-up, even after other risk factors were considered. A threshold of 1.211 separated risk groups in the second cohort. The authors propose the score as an aid to early risk sorting.
pmc-13287546:
Meifang Wang, Ansheng Tan, and Fenglin Zhuo ran a split-face trial in 2026 for rosacea, a long-term facial flushing condition. Thirty-six patients had light pulse treatment on the whole face each month for three sessions. One random half of each face also got a salicylic acid peel at each visit.

Thirty-three patients finished. After three months the peel side showed larger drops in redness scores on two device measures than the light-only side. Doctor and patient ratings improved on both sides without a clear gap. Skin water rose and water loss fell on both sides. Side effects were mild and similar. The authors favour the pairing for stubborn redness.
pmc-13288546:
Ulluwis Hewawansa and colleagues test a sugarcane drink rich in polyphenols against gut damage from hard exercise in heat, in a 2026 double-blind placebo-controlled trial. Fourteen volunteers each ran for two hours at a set effort in 34.4 degree heat twice, drinking either the extract beverage or a matched placebo daily for fourteen days beforehand and taking gels during each run.

Core temperature and strain ran slightly higher on the extract trial, which complicates any simple benefit story. Still, a gut leak marker started lower after the extract fortnight, the rise in the inflammatory signal IL-8 was blunted, and gut symptoms, though common in both trials, averaged milder. The authors read the pattern as modest protection for the gut lining and immune response.
pmc-13289346:
Xuedi Ma and colleagues present a 2026 multilevel study on drug burden, adherence, and quality of life in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in China. This long-term lung disease needs care at many levels of the health system. Taking many drugs can wear people down, yet how burden, adherence, and daily well-being connect was unclear.

Clinics in a national pharmaceutical care network enrolled 2125 patients from September 2023 to September 2024. Burden was counted by drug number and a complexity index, while adherence and quality of life used standard scales. More drugs tied to worse quality of life both directly and through lower adherence in the models. The chain suggests simpler regimens could help people stick with care and feel better.
pmc-13290646:
Kelly N DuBois and colleagues classify dementia causes from blood proteins plus machine learning in a 2026 study. Telling apart Alzheimer's disease, frontotemporal degeneration, Lewy body disease, and vascular disease during life is hard. Mixed and atypical cases blur clinical judgment further. The team ran a multiplex plasma panel, NULISA, measuring over one hundred nervous system proteins. Blood came from 194 participants with known or suspected diagnoses.

Each disease left a distinct protein pattern in plasma. Supervised XGBoost classifiers learned those patterns and separated the causes with high specificity. The trained models were then turned loose on participants with mild cognitive impairment. Their predictions sorted those uncertain cases into likely causes in a stable, data-driven way. The authors present blood proteomics as a feasible, low-burden route to differential diagnosis. Such sorting could sharpen trial enrollment as cause-specific therapies arrive.
pmc-13290746:
Automated insulin pumps give preschoolers with type 1 diabetes better blood sugar control in real-world use, Risa Wolf and colleagues report in a 2026 multicenter analysis. Data on the youngest children have lagged behind older groups, so the team drew on the T1D Exchange collaborative across 37 pediatric sites.

The cohort held 3,521 children aged six and under. Just under half, 48%, used automated insulin delivery, and their average HbA1c was 7.9%, against 8.8% for children on multiple daily injections, a significant gap. Only a quarter of all children met the target below 7%, but automated users had nearly double the odds of getting there after adjustment. Wolf and colleagues say the findings support offering these systems to the youngest patients, not only to older children.
pmc-13290846:
Adjuvant capecitabine delays bile duct cancer's return without clearly extending life, Fabian Bartsch and colleagues report in a cohort study from 2026. Since the BILCAP trial, the drug became standard after surgery for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, though that trial mixed several biliary cancers and left this one's benefit uncertain.

A German center compared resected patients from before and after the practice change, 2008 to 2017 versus 2018 to 2023, then matched 75 patients per era. Median survival was 29.1 months in the later group against 20.5 earlier, a gap that was not statistically significant. Recurrence, though, came significantly later after BILCAP-era care, and recurrence-free survival improved too. Bartsch and colleagues say longer follow-up may yet reveal whether delayed recurrence converts into longer lives.
pmc-13291046:
Alip Ghosh and colleagues profile a new intravenous drug called MP-04 in a 2026 preclinical study aimed at failing energy balance inside cells. MP-04 is a form of dihydronicotinamide riboside meant to restore NAD+, a molecule that drops in severe liver disease, sepsis, and acute kidney injury, where current care mostly supports rather than repairs.

Cell work in liver, T-cell, and kidney lines plus human blood cells showed fast, dose-linked rises in NAD+ after MP-04 exposure. Energy output, immune behavior, and drug handling were tracked in cells, rats, and a mouse model of drug-induced kidney injury, with formal safety studies in rats and dogs. Kidney protection in the injury model anchors the claim that restoring NAD+ could defend organs during severe illness.
pmc-13291146:
Yan Huang leads a 2026 study on judging liver scarring in autoimmune hepatitis. A stiffness scan often helps grade scarring. But active inflammation can stiffen the liver too. That mix-up can mislead doctors who rely on one scan value.

Records came from 86 patients who had both a biopsy and a stiffness scan. Biopsy set the true scarring stage. Patients were split by how strong their inflammation was. The scan worked far better in the mild group than in the severe group. A correction model built from these data improved accuracy. Sorting patients by inflammation first should make scan results safer to trust.
pmc-13291246:
Newborn screening in the Emirates is counted by Khadija Shafique and colleagues in a 2026 review of records. Screening spots hidden gene, hormone, and body chemistry faults early. Early care can cut harm and death in babies. The team asked how common each fault is.

Data came from a national reference lab for 2021 to 2023. Samples spanned 20 hospitals and labs in four emirates. Of 29,290 babies screened, about one in fourteen tested positive. A lack of one enzyme, G6PD, was by far most common. Cystic fibrosis came next in rate. Carriers of blood gene faults formed a large group too.
pmc-13292046:
Yangyang Zhang and co-authors map a 2026 study of an immune checkpoint called TIM3 inside the prostate cancer environment. Prostate tumors answer immunotherapy poorly, so the team mined single-cell data from primary, metastatic hormone-sensitive, and castration-resistant disease. They combined gene expression, regulon analysis, and cell-communication modeling, then tested leads in lab-grown macrophages.

TIM3 sat mainly on monocytes and macrophages, marking a tumor-associated state rich in SPP1, chemokines, and matrix remodeling. A regulator named PRDM1 emerged as the switch driving that program, confirmed by binding assays and reporter tests. Galectin-9 signaling through TIM3 pushed macrophages toward a suppressive M2-like state, and blocking TIM3 weakened that push. The authors propose myeloid TIM3 as a drug target for reprogramming prostate tumors.
pmc-13292346:
Patrik Ulvdal and colleagues test a 2026 upgrade for forest planning software: adding stochastic programming so long-term plans can reckon with bad or uncertain data. Decision support systems for forestry seldom handle uncertainty head-on. The team plugged a stochastic model into a classic long-term planning problem, compared it with plain deterministic optimization, and workshopped the result with potential users.

The stochastic version lifted total expected net present value by at least 2 percent over the deterministic plan in their comparison. Workshop users liked the decision gains but worried about harder setup and murkier outputs. The authors recommend friendly presentation, with intuitive charts and simple summary statistics, to win adoption. They judge integration feasible on both the numbers and the user side, despite longer computing times.
pmc-13292446:
Zihao Liu and co-authors chase a 2026 target in multiple myeloma, starting from the toad-venom compound bufalin as a molecular fishing hook. Proteomics pulled out MAGEC2 as a direct binding partner. Checking patient cohorts, the team found high MAGEC2 matched poor overall survival in this incurable plasma cell cancer.

In cells and a mouse transfer model, MAGEC2 pushed malignant growth and blunted two standard drugs, adriamycin and bortezomib. Beyond its known habit of boosting E3 ligases, it grabbed the deubiquitinase USP16 and cranked up its activity, which stabilized the growth driver c-Myc by trimming its ubiquitin tags. Extra MAGEC2 also worsened bone lesions in animals. The authors nominate MAGEC2 as both a warning marker and a drug target.
pmc-13292846:
Chen Sun and Hongye Zhang review 160 young children with flat brown marks on the face in a 2026 hospital study from Nanjing. Most marks appeared in the first year of life, often on the forehead or temples, and parents worried when color deepened as a child cried.

Clinic notes and skin-scope images showed two patterns, one with tiny blood vessels visible and one without. Among 110 children followed over time, nearly all marks faded fully by about age three, based on the share the authors report. The authors class the condition as harmless and short-lived, needing no set treatment, which can reassure families.
pmc-13293346:
Saurabh Dudhe and colleagues describe a jaw diagnosis puzzle in a case report from 2026. A twenty-five-year-old man arrived with pain and swelling at the front of his lower jaw, and scans showed a clear hollow area in the bone near a dead premolar tooth. Several cyst types can look alike on images, so the team needed more than radiographs to settle the question.

Needle sampling drew no fluid, and surgery revealed an almost empty cavity with no lining, a hallmark of a traumatic bone cyst. Tissue examination showed fibrous tissue with mild inflammation and no surface lining, confirming the diagnosis. Treatment was surgical cleaning of the cavity with stimulation of bleeding to prompt healing. The case shows why direct inspection and tissue study remain essential when jaw lesions overlap in appearance.
pmc-13293746:
Amanda Blanque Becceneri and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, a light-activated ruthenium drug for breast cancer across three-dimensional tumor models of rising realism. Light therapy can kill tumors precisely, yet flat dish tests overstate how well drugs will work in bodies.

The drug killed cells and cut tumor aggression after light dosing in loose cell balls, printed cell balls in gel, and printed patient-derived organoids. Needed doses rose with model realism, from the lowest in loose balls to the highest in organoids, which resisted most. Printed models thus give a sterner, truer test before patient trials, the authors argue.
pmc-13294046:
Radha Korupolu leads a 2026 pilot trial pairing vagus nerve stimulation with arm rehabilitation after cervical spinal cord injury. The pairing boosted brain plasticity and movement after stroke, but spinal injury evidence was thin. Six adults with chronic incomplete cervical injury got implanted devices and were randomized to active or sham stimulation alongside therapy.

Care involved 18 clinic sessions over 6–8 weeks plus a 90-day home program. No serious adverse events or unresolved surgery problems appeared, and clinic attendance stayed high. Everyone on active stimulation showed mild to moderate arm gains right after treatment. As a pilot, the goal was safety and workability, not proof of benefit.
pmc-13294246:
Yuhan Yao and colleagues test whether the allergy drug desloratadine can ease schizophrenia-like traits in mice for a 2026 study. The serotonin 5-HT2A receptor is a proven drug target in schizophrenia, yet reused drugs against it are underexplored. Male mice given MK-801 to mimic the illness received the antihistamine, with brain cell sequencing and pathway tests to trace the mechanism.

Treated mice improved across a full set of behavior deficits. The receptor sat mainly in prefrontal cortex neurons and rose with illness, then fell after treatment. Forcing receptor excess recreated the traits, and boosting the downstream AKT pathway erased drug benefit. A feed-forward loop through PI3K, AKT, and mTOR is the proposed target.
pmc-13294346:
C K Revathi and H Santhi fuse three image networks into a hybrid coronary disease classifier in a 2026 study. Each parent model has flaws: heavy compute, weak long-range links, or hunger for huge datasets. Their IUM blend merges InceptionV3, U-NetR, and MobileNetV2 with dynamic weighting, fine-tuned on angiographic images, plus heatmap views that show why the model votes as it does.

Reported scores reached 0.97 accuracy, 0.99 F1-score, 0.98 specificity, and 0.97 sensitivity in the authors' metrics. Clear heatmaps aid trust and cut manual reading slips. Fast, explainable sorting could speed heart care where expert readers are scarce.
pmc-13294446:
Olivia F Krol and coauthors forge a consensus syllabus for consumer health informatics in a 2026 eDelphi study. Digital tools now mediate much patient care, yet no standard entry course existed for the field. Literature themes became draft goals, an advisory board polished them, and experts voted through three online Delphi rounds to settle core competencies.

Eleven competencies survived as essential for a first graduate course. Coverage spans patient-facing technology, data handling, and person-centered design skills that graduates need on day one. The set is built to last while flexing with new tools, giving schools a shared starting point instead of each inventing its own list.
pmc-13294946:
Matheus Londero da Costa and co-authors issue a correction in 2026 to their study of dye cleanup using a lithium niobate catalyst made from Brazilian minerals. The original work tested photocatalytic ozonation, a light-and-ozone treatment, against rhodamine B dye and used machine learning to weigh which process settings mattered most. The notice fixes two things: a missing space in one author's surname, now printed as Yolice Patricia Moreno Ruiz, and a figure whose discussion needed rewriting.

The replaced graph shows the model's feature rankings for the treatment process. In the corrected reading, reaction time and ozone flow rate push dye removal upward, while a higher starting dye concentration pulls it down. Catalyst amount helps positively when kept low, a nuance the earlier text had graded differently. Readers comparing versions should use the new figure and wording for the study's conclusions about its most influential variables.
pmc-13295846:
Merna G. Aboismaiel, Mohamed N. Amin and Laila A. Eissa report a 2026 rat study of silymarin, a plant compound, against kidney damage from diabetes. They test whether it calms a chain involving miRNA-223 and the NLRP3 inflammasome, which drives a fiery form of cell death.

Diabetic rats given silymarin by mouth, early for twelve weeks or later for four, showed better kidney function, blood sugar and blood fats than untreated rats. Kidney levels of miRNA-223 rose while NLRP3 and related harm markers fell, with early dosing working best. The authors say more work is needed to prove the chain is causal.
pmc-13295946:
Mirja Baumgart and co-authors present a 2026 protocol on health workers living with lasting symptoms after COVID-19 in Germany. Staff were hit both as carers and patients, and many still report draining symptoms years later.

The study extends an existing cohort of 2,436 affected workers with two further survey rounds, plus interviews with sixty workers about care routes and treatment experiences. Thirty workers will also log symptoms and coping day by day, and insurance records add another view. Findings aim to show where care for these workers succeeds or leaves gaps.
pmc-13296546:
Sharon Nofech-Mozes and colleagues audit HER2 testing in womb cancer at a large academic centre, in a 2026 study. Some of these tumours make large amounts of the HER2 protein and might respond to drugs aimed at it. Testing practice, however, varies between hospitals because no standard scoring method exists for this cancer.

The audit covered 494 tumour samples from 458 patients tested over roughly four years. Results shifted depending on whether gynaecologic or gastric scoring rules were applied to the same tissue. That dependence means the scoring choice can change who qualifies for targeted treatment. The authors argue for scoring guidelines written specifically for endometrial cancer.
pmc-13296646:
Errikos Petsas and colleagues use computer models to design one molecule that acts on several heart and metabolism targets at once, in a 2026 study. Heart disease, blood sugar trouble, and long-term swelling in the body feed each other, so a drug aimed at one point may leave much of the harm untouched. Starting from a known base shape, the team screened kin compounds against six targets tied to cholesterol, gut hormones, and swelling.

One candidate, called D4Z, fit the whole set best in the models. It docked well into each target, stayed stable in long motion runs, and looked drug-like, with high uptake from the gut predicted. Nothing was tested in a lab yet. The value lies in a ranked lead for making and checking in real tests.
pmc-13297146:
Vanessa Ndiangang and Pengcheng Liu benchmark three insect-inspired motion detectors for collision warning in a 2026 evaluation. Insects spot looming objects fast with tiny brains, a trick robots would love to copy. Synthetic test scenes with known answers were used to compare two classic models and a hybrid spiking network.

The hybrid system scored best overall, with perfect precision and faster running than the classic looming detector. The looming model showed the rate sensitivity expected from biology. The directional model correctly stayed quiet for looming stimuli, confirming it answers a different question. The authors flag the jump from synthetic scenes to the real world as the main hurdle ahead.
pmc-13297346:
Lucía Cascobelo-Águeda and colleagues review how a gluten-free diet shapes daily life for children and teens with celiac disease, in a 2026 survey. Celiac disease is a lasting immune reaction to gluten, and strict avoidance of gluten is its only working treatment. Thirteen studies from recent years met the entry rules.

Young patients generally reported lower quality of life, above all in feelings, friendships, and school life. Sticking to the diet eased symptoms, yet it also brought social limits, uneven nutrition, and extra cost. Families reported stress and changed routines as well. Care should reach past diet alone, the authors argue, with mind support, social help, and public steps that cut the cost of gluten-free food.
pmc-13297446:
Car dampers that adjust themselves could ride better if their controls borrowed tricks from chameleons, proposes a 2026 engineering study led by Niancheng Guo. The authors model intelligent dampers for semi-active suspensions and ask which model forms, force ranges, and response delays give the best comfort per cost.

A function-prediction damper model performed well, paired with a force range spanning below 0.2 and above 1.4 times the passive curve and a delay of 10 ms. Particle swarm optimization tuned the controller settings for different road grades and speeds. Borrowing the chameleon's graded adaptation, the team weighted comfort more heavily on smooth Grade A and B roads and stability on rougher Grade C and D surfaces.
pmc-13297746:
Hengjie Zhang, Xiaoying Lu, and Fang Wang add group consensus building to a graph method for analysing conflicts, in a 2026 paper. Real disputes often pit groups whose members judge options differently, and the classic graph model forces simple rankings that flatten those differences. Their upgrade lets members rate statement weight by paired comparisons and state support on a sliding scale.

A consensus process then nudges views together with the smallest total change, while a fairness term counts how members feel about uneven adjustments. Two models of that process feed agreed preferences into the graph method's stability checks, which hunt for stand-off points no side wants to leave. A supply chain carbon-cutting case walks through the method.
pmc-13297946:
Nasrin Dabirian and others present a 2026 study asking how cupping therapy changes blood signals in tissue over time, not just on average. Eighteen healthy volunteers got cupping at two pressures and two durations in a factorial design. Near-infrared spectroscopy tracked oxygenated and deoxygenated hemoglobin before and after treatment.

Wavelet, entropy, and fractal analyses measured oscillation, complexity, and scaling in the signals. Pressure and duration mainly worked jointly rather than alone, with clear interactions across several deoxyhemoglobin and oxyhemoglobin measures. Pressure alone shaped one neurogenic signal, while duration alone altered fractal scaling. The authors argue dose choices should consider that joint pattern when planning cupping research.
pmc-13298446:
A vibrating, cooling bee-shaped device may take some sting out of dental injections for children, test Prabhadevi C Maganur and colleagues in a 2026 crossover study. Thirty-eight children aged 6 to 10 needing numbing injections on both sides of the lower jaw received the Buzzy BEE device on one visit and standard care on the other.

Pulse rates after injection dropped significantly with the device at both visits. At the second visit, children's own pain ratings and observer scores for eye and movement reactions also fell. However, effects carried over between visits, muddying the subjective results. The authors recommend bigger studies with longer washout periods before firm conclusions.
pmc-13298546:
The Canadian Nosocomial Infection Surveillance Program reports hospital-acquired illness and drug resistance trends from 2020 through 2024, in a 2026 surveillance summary. Data came from more than one hundred sentinel acute care hospitals plus provincial and territorial labs. Tracked problems ranged from gut illness to bloodstream cases involving drug-resistant organisms and a concerning yeast.

Rates for C. difficile and MRSA bloodstream cases stayed broadly stable across the period. Bloodstream cases from resistant gut bacteria rose clearly, and carbapenemase-producing cases climbed from a low base. Counts for the resistant yeast also grew. The program argues standard reporting guides safety work in hospital care.
pmc-13299146:
Jie-Hong Huang and others map the medical and genetic range of ANO3-related dystonia in a Chinese cohort, in a 2026 study. Gene variants cause an inherited movement disorder usually centred on the head and neck, yet presentations vary widely and Asian data were scarce. Exome sequencing covered hundreds of patients with dystonia plus a comparison group with other movement disorders.

Rare variants were enriched among dystonia patients, including several never seen before. Neck involvement and trembling features were frequent, and some cases stretched beyond classic isolated dystonia. Medicines and botulinum toxin helped unevenly, while deep brain stimulation markedly helped selected patients who had failed drug treatment.
pmc-13299846:
Fit older folks who take the right mind drugs walk as fast as those who take none. Wrong-picked mind drugs, though, walk with them more slow. María Ángeles Caballero-Mora and her team show that split in a 2026 study. They checked 119 free, sound old folks past the age of 70. Each mind drug plan was graded by set rules for old-age care.

Wrong-picked use tied to a gait pace cut of 0.109 m/s once all else was weighed, a gap that counts for fall risk. Right-picked use showed no such tie, at a cut of just 0.018 m/s. The team say staff should mend how drugs are picked, not just drop mind drugs that old folks need.
pmc-13300046:
A K Kahle leads a multicentre registry study of hospitalisations after rhythm control for atrial tachycardia, published in 2026. More than a thousand patients got ablation or electrical cardioversion, then were tracked for cardiovascular admissions over roughly two years. Two thirds needed such a stay, most often because the rhythm problem returned.

Older age, higher body mass, weaker heart pumping, accompanying fibrillation, and certain rhythm features predicted admission in single-factor checks. In the combined model, weak pumping and ablation of reentrant rhythms stayed significant. The authors argue structured risk factor treatment must accompany rhythm control to cut the long-term healthcare burden.
pmc-13300846:
Liton Devnath and co-authors combine deep learning image features with clinical data to predict who will not respond to pembrolizumab alone in advanced lung cancer, in a 2026 study. Over half of patients with high PD-L1 expression still fail this first-line immunotherapy, so early warning would speed a switch to other treatment. The retrospective cohort held ninety-seven patients for training and seventeen for a preliminary test, with responses judged from follow-up scans.

From 128 image features, the team ranked the ten most discriminative and paired them with five clinical descriptors in a support vector machine. That blend reached the best balance on the small test set, catching most non-responders while keeping false alarms moderate. Performance looked stronger inside the training data, a gap the authors openly note. They present the fused model as a promising decision aid that needs bigger validation cohorts.
pmc-13302346:
Kidney dosing goes wrong in primary care for structural reasons, Anna Maria Dworakowska and colleagues argue in a 2026 Perspective on European practice. Labs report kidney function indexed to body size, while drug labels demand absolute clearance figures, often computed with the aging Cockcroft–Gault formula. Frailty, age, and body shape muddy the conversion further at the prescribing desk.

The authors propose a stepwise, context-aware framework that blends regulatory text, several estimation methods, and patient-specific modifiers into one decision path. Short clinical vignettes show how rival estimates push the same patient toward different doses. Their plea is for aligned rules and practical tools, reframing dosing as clinical judgment rather than arithmetic.
pmc-13302846:
Anxiety and depression, more than the drug on the label, drag down life quality in metastatic prostate cancer, Selahattin Çelik and colleagues find in a 2026 real-world study. One hundred thirty men on androgen receptor targeted therapies, abiraterone or enzalutamide among them, completed quality-of-life and mood questionnaires at one center. Groups were compared and poor quality of life modeled directly.

Unadjusted scores favored some drugs over others, with the abiraterone group lowest overall. Once mood entered the model, treatment type lost its grip: anxiety multiplied the odds of poor quality of life by 6.62 and depression by 3.40. Routine psychological screening belongs in these clinics, the authors argue.
pmc-13304646:
João Barros, Nicolas Dreyfus, and co-authors make, in a 2026 chemistry study, sugar-like molecules designed to interfere with Alzheimer's disease chemistry. Toxic amyloid oligomers bind the prion protein on neurons, switching on a kinase that damages the tau protein. The team built a library of selenium-bearing galactose mimics hoping to block that contact.

Several candidates bound the oligomers in magnetic resonance tests, mostly through their aromatic and ring-edge atoms. One phenylureido compound performed best overall, raising its binding signal by over half in head-to-head tests and slightly weakening the oligomer–prion contact. Selenium at the key position beat sulfur and oxygen cousins. The leading compound dissolved well in water, resisted breakdown in liver samples, and showed no toxicity to kidney cells, earning further development work.
pmc-13304746:
Jinhua Yu leads a 2026 study of a gene switch that helps the yeast Candida albicans resist a common antifungal drug. Upc2 controls sterol building in the cell membrane, but its wider role in drug tolerance was unclear.

Deleting the gene left cells unable to splice a key stress message correctly, so misfolded proteins piled up inside. Gene scans showed weaker stress-response and calcium-linked pathways in the mutant. The altered yeast grew, formed filaments, and built biofilms less well under fluconazole. Blocking this stress route may restore drug power against resistant infections.
pmc-13305846:
Raiker Witter presented a compact nuclear magnetic resonance setup in a 2026 methods report aimed at hard-to-study magnetic materials. The benchtop system spins samples at 50 kHz inside a 1.4 T permanent magnet with a narrow 18 mm bore.

Tiny rotors about 1.8 mm wide ran stably at high speed, helped by a probe layout that eases angle alignment in tight space. As a tough test, lithium signals from a layered cathode oxide showed huge shifts spanning thousands of parts per million, yet stayed measurable. The authors present the design as a route to cheaper, portable high-speed instruments.
pmc-13306446:
Zoran Vlaović tested whether lab measures on foam stacks can predict sitting and lying comfort in a 2026 study. Six three-layer cushions near 60 mm thick mixed standard, resilient and slow-recovery polyurethane foams with latex in different orders.

Press-in testing followed an international standard method across two cushion groups. One group barely changed with layer order, holding support factors near 2.6 to 2.7 in reported values, while the other varied widely and recovered less. The authors argue that layer sequence matters only for some builds, so single-material tests miss real cushion behaviour.
pmc-13306746:
Aung Min Naing built a low-cost indoor watcher joining air, vibration and network checks in a 2026 study. Small sensor nodes based on ESP32 boards feed a Raspberry Pi gateway that interprets conditions without using cameras.

Carbon dioxide readings separated ventilation states clearly, rising from 395.47 ppm in an open empty baseline to 1083.16 ppm in a closed occupied room in reported trials. Vibration patterns split calm, footstep, play and jump states by signal strength features. Message tests confirmed the linked system can flag both stale air and local disturbance. The set up is low cost and guards privacy since it uses no camera at all.
pmc-13308646:
Forrest Bohler and co-authors describe in 2026 a robotic repair of a trapped liver hernia at a small rural hospital in Montana, a first for this rare state. A woman aged 73 years came in with three days of growing pain, a stuck bulge, and a swollen belly from a known upper hernia.

Scans showed the left liver lobe pushed through a small wall gap, and blood tests flagged liver strain from poor flow. Robot aided surgery freed the starved liver part, which bore a small surface tear, and no cut out was needed at all. She healed with no snags. Small rural teams can thus tackle rare, urgent hernia cases with robot help.
pmc-13308946:
Omar A Bamalan and co-authors report in 2026 a small bowel hole torn by a plant stem in a man aged 50 years. He has no teeth and drinks herb tea each night. He came in with one day of low belly pain and no tale of fish, chicken, bones, or toothpicks in his food.

Blood work showed a mild white cell rise, and plain films showed nothing of note for the care team. Contrast scans found a dense line like body that pierced the end of the small bowel wall. Surgeons cut out the hurt span and joined the ends, and he healed with no snags. Herbs join the list of odd causes to weigh.
pmc-13309346:
Waseem Jerjes and Azeem Majeed argue in 2026 that patient centred care, for all its worth, leaves the real power with the clinic. They press for patient shaped care in its place. Patients are still asked to pick from menus set by staff and systems, with rules fixed long before they walk in the door.

Fixed slot lengths, split duties, and stiff access routes can crush care for people with many long term states, no matter how kind the doctor is. Shared calls mean little when the paths on offer bend to stock and risk caps, not to patient aims. The pair urge joint rule over access, follow up, and what counts as success.
pmc-13309746:
Nabilah Anzoom and co-authors screen gene changes in the RET gene for harm and drug effects in a 2026 computer study. RET drives several cancers and developmental disorders when altered. Single-letter changes that swap one protein building block for another may break the protein or shift drug response.

From 28,335 catalogued changes, ten prediction tools flagged 33 high-risk variants, most predicted to destabilize the protein. Eleven variants looked most likely to cause disease, clustered in the protein active region. Docking tests with eight RET drugs showed binding shifts by variant, with one drug holding strong binding across all. Motion simulations backed the split. The authors offer the ranked list for lab follow-up.
pmc-13309946:
Wei Zhang writes a 2026 letter on sequencing cell therapy after antibody therapy fails in lymphoma. The topic is diffuse large B-cell lymphoma that returns after bispecific antibodies, drugs that link T cells to tumor cells. A study by Li and colleagues reported full response in all patients given CAR-T cells afterward, a striking result.

The letter welcomes the finding but probes what response rates hide. Prior antibody exposure may tire T cells, which could weaken the CAR-T product grown from them. Whether longer prior therapy tracked with slower cell growth in the lab went unreported in the study under discussion. The author asks for T-cell fitness data before the sequence becomes standard practice.
pmc-13310646:
Daniela Correia and co-authors model how alcohol policies could cut cancer across the European Union in a 2026 study. Alcohol causes seven cancer types, yet the preventive payoff of population-level controls had never been quantified for the bloc. Four real-world policy options anchor the scenarios.

Tax rises, a Sunday sales ban, a marketing ban, and Lithuania integrated package were each applied to drinking data for 27 countries, with a ten-year lag to cancer outcomes. An estimated 146,194 cancer cases in 2022, or 16.1 percent across the seven linked sites in the model, were tied to alcohol. Each scenario cut cases by a modeled share. The authors present the numbers for policy debate.
pmc-13310746:
Takuto Nosaka reports a 2026 case of acute fatty liver of pregnancy that a common scan tool failed to show. A woman aged 29 years, pregnant for the first time, grew jaundiced at 33 weeks with liver, blood, and kidney problems. The rare disease can turn fatal fast, so an urgent cesarean birth was done.

Weeks later a stiffness scan tool read the liver fat level as normal. A liver sample told a different story, with tiny fat drops seen under both standard and electron scopes. Stains backed the finding. The case warns that the scan tool can miss this fat pattern and that tissue checks still matter.
pmc-13311146:
Jiacheng Xie and co-authors study an RNA binding protein that shields colon cancer from chemo in a 2026 paper. Colon cancer kills many people yearly, and oxaliplatin based care often fails as resistance grows. Iron driven cell death offers a bypass, yet tumor guards can block that death route.

The protein PUM2 binds and mutes a helper gene message, which lets a guard protein pile up and block iron death. Tumors with high PUM2 thus shrug off oxaliplatin. In mouse models, pairing oxaliplatin with a guard blocker restored strong tumor control. The chain gives clinics a target pair for resistant disease.
pmc-13311246:
Linjia Guo and co-authors share their 2026 case of pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1B with normal blood calcium but low potassium. The disorder makes the body resist parathyroid hormone and stems from faults near the GNAS gene.

The patient, a 32-year-old Han Chinese man, had bouts of numbness and clear low potassium. Hormone levels were high, yet calcium stayed normal and brain scans showed no calcium deposits. A methylation test found the gene imprint pattern typical of type 1B, with no family history. The case warns that odd mineral shifts can appear even when calcium looks fine.
pmc-13311946:
Kathleen Markey and Benash Nazmeen comment in a 2026 article on a qualitative study of self-management barriers among immigrants living with several long-term conditions. Culture and language shape how people handle daily illness work.

The discussed study by Monari and colleagues interviewed culturally and linguistically diverse immigrants about what helps or blocks self-care. The commentators argue that staff must build culturally responsive habits into routine care, not treat them as extras. Health teaching should mirror patients' values, beliefs, and communication likes in both content and delivery. They call for studies on how such approaches play out over time.
pmc-13312546:
Jie Fan and colleagues report, in a 2026 food science study, that freezing waxy corn puree inside a magnetic field protects its quality. Fresh waxy corn spoils within about a week even refrigerated, and ordinary freezing damages texture and nutrients. The team tested magnetic field-assisted immersion freezing at three field strengths against slow, air blast, and plain immersion freezing.

The 5 millitesla treatment froze fastest, cutting the phase transition time by 40.32 percent against plain immersion freezing in the reported comparison, and it best preserved phenolics, flavonoids, color, and texture. Starch analysis showed the treatment kept granules intact and raised relative crystallinity and short-range order, which limited water movement and rearrangement on thawing. The authors identify the mild field treatment as an effective option for high-moisture starchy foods.
pmc-13312846:
Jae Hyeok Choi and colleagues report a 2026 case of a 69-year-old woman whose dream-acting sleep disorder proved to be the front edge of two overlapping brain diseases. REM sleep behavior disorder, in which the normal paralysis of dreaming sleep fails, is one of the strongest known warnings of Lewy body and related synuclein diseases. Most patients convert over time.

The woman arrived with confusion and behavior changes after starting antiseizure and antipsychotic drugs, showing slowness and rigidity when doctors checked her. Dopamine transporter imaging showed reduced uptake, a sleep study showed lost muscle atonia in REM sleep, and dream enactment seen in the lab completed the picture of dementia with Lewy bodies. Brain scans also showed multiple cortical microbleeds pointing to amyloid in vessel walls, and amyloid imaging showed widespread cortical deposits. The authors stress sorting true signals from drug and seizure confounders in such mixed cases.
pmc-13313146:
Luis M Canal de Velasco and colleagues propose, in a 2026 review, a combined framework for rebuilding body composition in men with low testosterone. Deficiency of the hormone brings more fat, less muscle, weaker performance, and worse metabolic health. It feeds muscle loss and heart and metabolic disease. Replacement therapy restores hormone levels. On the evidence reviewed, it raises muscle protein synthesis, activates satellite cells, and improves cell energy function, laying the biological groundwork for change.

The authors argue testosterone works best as a foundation rather than a solo treatment. Resistance training layered on top amplifies muscle growth and functional gains. Adequate protein supplies the raw material for remodeling and protects lean mass. Judging success by body weight alone misses these shifts, so the review urges composition-based targets. Open work includes sharper patient selection, better protocols, and proof of long-term outcomes.
pmc-13313246:
Yujing Tan and fellow authors compare a breast cancer drug class across high and low land in China in their 2026 study. CDK4/6 blockers are the standard care for advanced breast cancer that feeds on hormones and lacks HER2, but whether altitude changes their effect was unknown.

The team gathered records on 350 patients from four cancer centers, with 268 patients in the low-altitude group and 82 patients in the high-altitude group. In first-line use, low-altitude patients did better on each measure the authors report: response rate, benefit rate, and time with no growth, stated as 42.1 months versus 15.2 months for that span. Gaps also showed in later lines of care. The study warns that place and height may shape drug results, so care plans may need to adjust by region.
pmc-13314146:
Monyer Abdulameir Abd Alfatlawi and Mohammed Qasim Hadi characterize, in a 2026 molecular study, the tick-borne parasite Theileria ovis infecting sheep in Central Iraq. The disease drains sheep health and farm productivity wherever ticks thrive, yet local genetic data were missing. The researchers extracted DNA from sheep blood and copied a fragment of the parasite's marker gene with nested PCR. They sequenced ten sample isolates and compared them with global records in a family-tree analysis.

All ten sequences landed in GenBank and matched known isolates at between 98.81 and 100 percent identity. Egyptian and Turkish strains were the closest relatives. The tree placed the Iraqi isolates firmly inside the parasite's grouping alongside worldwide reference strains, confirming the species while showing little genetic diversity. The authors read the conservation as good news for tests built on this gene. They call for a broader molecular watch to follow the parasite's movement.
pmc-13314746:
Munkhsuvd Chimed and colleagues report a 2026 case of scarring around blood vessels that spread far beyond its usual range. Perivascular fibrosis wraps the aorta and its branches in thick soft tissue, and it can mimic big-vessel inflammation or lymph tumors on scans.

Their patient was a 55-year-old man with long-standing scarring behind the belly and a blocked lower aorta. The disease also gripped his chest aorta, a coronary artery, and the branches above the aorta, a spread seldom seen. Over 20 years of follow-up, as the report states, a narrowed coronary artery caused a full heart attack that needed a stent and bypass surgery. Tests for the usual IgG4 marker came back negative. The case shows why layered imaging matters to tell this scarring from its many doubles.
pmc-13314946:
Tarek Sallam and Ahmed M. Attiya use a physics-guided neural network to shape antenna beams, in their 2026 paper. Radar and broadcast arrays often need a cosecant-squared beam shape, which lights a zone evenly while keeping stray side lobes low.

Their method tunes only the phase of each array element, which keeps the hardware simple. A deep network trained with a loss that enforces match to the wanted pattern learns the phase set for big flat arrays. Two aims rule the training: crush side lobes and smooth ripples inside the shaped beam. The team set their method against genetic algorithms and particle swarm optimization, the standard search tools named in the report. Number tests gave their approach the edge on pattern quality, by the results reported.
pmc-13315646:
Nadine Berndt, Serge Schneider, and Stefania Oliverio evaluate, in a 2026 study, what changed in Luxembourg during the first year after the country legalized cannabis in 2023. It allowed home cultivation and private use. Data streams miss part of a drug market. The team triangulated seizure laboratory results, wastewater metabolite data, toxicology from driving cases, and a survey of adults who had used cannabis recently. They compared streams before and after the reform.

Most indicators moved little. Potency in seized cannabis and resin stayed stable, wastewater loads were flat, and surveyed users reported habits, prices, and buying channels, mostly illegal ones. Only a minority grew their own or planned to. The exception stood out: cannabis-related driving cases rose significantly, with blood concentrations but patterns hinting at chronic use among some drivers. The authors conclude legalization's market footprint was modest, new initiation limited, and impaired driving the outcome demanding surveillance.
pmc-13316646:
Adilson J M de Oliveira reports a 2026 national cohort of the first 100 brachial plexus operations in Angola. It covers babies hurt at birth and adults with arm nerve injuries, treated from January 2021 to December 2025. One nerve surgeon assessed and operated on every patient.

Sixteen babies were included, most with upper trunk injuries treated by a nerve transfer, and seven reached useful strength grades at follow-up. Among 86 adults, most had complete injuries and nearly all suffered nerve pain, which eased in nine of ten after surgery. Recovery rates stayed low, blamed on long waits averaging 14 months for adults. Lessons stress full care teams, child specialists, and partnerships beyond the surgeon alone.
pmc-13317546:
Xiang Qi and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, how colorectal cancer spreads to bone, a rarer landing site that brings fractures, cord pressure, and calcium crises when it comes. The cancer ranks third worldwide in frequency, and bone spread usually travels with liver or lung disease.

The review walks through the TGF-beta pathway, shape-shifting of tumor cells, the Wnt pathway, chemical beacons, and immune dealings inside the bone niche. It carefully separates proof gathered in this cancer from findings borrowed from others, and grades evidence in a table for clinical use. By naming where knowledge is solid and where it is guesswork, the authors aim to steer drug development toward targets that truly fit this disease.
pmc-13318546:
Elisabetta Cozzi and colleagues present a 2026 screening study hunting for long non-coding RNAs that help drive acute myeloid leukaemia or shape response to the drug venetoclax. Protein-coding genes in this blood cancer are well mapped, but these RNA molecules are not.

Using CRISPR interference in the MOLM-13 cell line, the team dampened 7,996 candidate RNAs and watched growth, maturation, and drug sensitivity. Altogether 58 RNAs affected growth, 4 affected maturation, and 23 changed venetoclax response in the screens reported. Four were followed up in depth, including CATG00000106133.1, tied to immune signalling, and AC009299.3, tied to drug response and poorer patient outcomes, giving new leads for prognosis and treatment.
pmc-13318646:
Günhal Şatırtav leads an international expert group whose 2026 review gives guidance on when injections for wet age-related macular degeneration can safely stop. The Vision Academy panel read the literature and agreed on recommendations plus a step-by-step algorithm.

Stopping can be considered when the eye shows no fluid, no sight loss, and no new bleeding across at least three visits at the longest treatment interval a clinic uses. People whose disease stays active, or who rely on one good eye and have relapsed before, may do better continuing. After stopping, scan and vision checks should continue at an agreed pace set with the patient, since the disease can wake again.
pmc-13318746:
Chengjian Cao and co-authors review, in 2026, natural anti-inflammatory compounds for chronic rhinosinusitis. Current treatments calm downstream inflammation but miss the immune faults driving recurrence. The review centres on a regulatory axis of three players. They are FOXP3, the complement receptor C5aR1, and the factor LIF.

Literature from 2000 to 2026 across three databases was searched. In sinus disease with polyps, protective regulatory T cells are heavily depleted. Complement signalling through C5aR1 blocks new regulatory cells forming. LIF pushes the other way, raising FOXP3 and calming harmful responses. Compounds such as curcumin and rosmarinic acid act on these pathways. Bromelain and cineole already have clinical support in acute sinusitis.
pmc-13318846:
Brittney P Kokinos and co-authors examine, in 2026, early bone lesions in young pigs that model a joint disease of growing animals and children. Osteochondrosis begins as a focal failure of bone formation in growth regions. Early stages are rarely imaged before symptoms force treatment, so timing and location patterns are poorly known.

The team imaged thigh bones from pigs at several ages, using both computed tomography and magnetic resonance scans, with tissue checks in subsets. Abnormal growth plate widths appeared first, then defined growth plate lesions by twelve weeks. Lesions in the joint surface region appeared later and grew larger. A previously uncharacterised irregular lesion type was common at the oldest age. Both scan methods supported the same conclusions about developmental timing.
pmc-13319046:
Fengjiao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of ozone injections into arthritic knees, focused on how long benefits last. Sixteen randomised trials with 1,172 patients were included. Searches ran across five databases to December 3, 2025. Pain, stiffness, and function scores were tracked by follow-up time.

Benefits were clear early on. At one month, total arthritis scores improved with a standardised effect of −0.63 in the pooled result. At two months, pain, function, and pain-scale scores all improved significantly. By three months, no outcome differed significantly from control. The authors conclude the effect is time-limited rather than sustained. They offer the timeline as a guide for phased treatment planning in knee osteoarthritis care.
pmc-13319946:
Lingyun Xiang and co-authors study how reward and punishment reshape learning from surprise in a 2026 brain wave study. People update beliefs when outcomes clash with what they expect, and wins and losses may not weigh those clashes in the same way. A sorting task with shifting odds was paired with scalp brain wave records and a layered math model of belief change.

People did better when learning for reward than when learning to dodge punishment. Yet punishment drove faster belief updates in the model, without turning into better scores. Brain wave marks of surprise grew stronger under punishment at key points. The split shows that fast updating alone does not mean good learning, and motive colors how the brain weighs surprise.
pmc-13320046:
Lindsey West and co-authors dig into why floating wind farms at sea stall in tangled rule systems in a 2026 study of the Celtic Sea in Britain. Floating wind could speed the shift to clean power and lift coastal areas, yet growth unfolds inside split marine rule systems that serve many aims at once. Past work named the blocks but rarely traced their deep roots.

Using ideas from the study of institutions, the team traced blocks to root traits that set who does what, who links to whom, and who holds power. Blocks fed each other as a system rather than acting as lone faults, through habits such as clinging to old paths and piling new rules on old ones. Fixes must reshape the rule system itself, with more room to learn and adapt.
pmc-13320346:
Jeong-Uk Eom and co-authors study how storage before cooking shapes harmful compounds in grilled chicken in a 2026 food safety study. Harsh heat on meat makes compounds tied to cancer risk, yet past work stared at the cooking step and skipped what storage does first. Cold and frozen holds were compared for how they prime the meat chemistry that feeds those compounds.

Two weeks in the fridge drove fat and protein decay and reshaped the pool of free building blocks and sharp carbonyl compounds in the breast meat. That primed pool then fed most of the harmful compounds when the meat was cooked. Frozen storage held decay back and cut total harmful load, bar one compound. Storage checks could flag risky meat before it hits the heat.
pmc-13320446:
Zheyu Fan and co-authors study how a withdrawn gut drug harms nerves by draining a vitamin form in a 2026 study. The drug was pulled after it was tied to a nerve illness wave in Japan in the last century. A link to lack of thiamine, a B vitamin, was long suspected but unproven. Chemical scans of cells flagged the active form of that vitamin as the chief casualty.

The drug was shown to wreck that vitamin form through stress driven chemical change, which starved cell power houses and forced a shift to sugar burning. In a mouse model of Alzheimer disease the same drain and nerve harm showed in the brain. Topping up the vitamin form or a shield compound eased the harm and even boosted plaque clearing by the drug.
pmc-13320546:
Daiji Nagayama and co-authors look back at records in a 2026 Japanese study of the weight and diabetes drug tirzepatide. The drug aids weight loss and blood sugar control, but its effect on stiff arteries was less clear. The team tracked vessel stiffness with a heart to ankle index in adults with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

Weekly treatment in 24 people, over a median of about a year, lowered the stiffness index from 8.5 to 7.8 at the median. Weight, muscle and fat measures, and blood sugar marks also fell, with the sugar mark HbA1c dropping from 6.6 to 5.6 percent at the median. Higher doses gave larger weight loss in this small group.
pmc-13321046:
Fatai Lu and colleagues test a human defence peptide against bone cancer in a 2026 study. Osteosarcoma is an aggressive bone tumour with poor outlook once it spreads or returns. The peptide LL-37, part of innate defence, can fight tumours in some settings, but its role in this cancer was undefined.

In cell tests, LL-37 curbed cancer cell survival while barely harming normal bone marrow stem cells. It cut colony growth, movement, and invasion, stalled the cell cycle, and triggered two forms of cell death. Gene scans showed cholesterol making was turned down, with the key enzyme SQLE sharply reduced. Mouse tumour graft work was used to check the effect in living tissue.
pmc-13321546:
Pooja Yashwant Pawar and colleagues assemble first genomes for four threatened Asian hornbills in a 2026 study. Hornbills are flagship birds of wet tropical forests, hit by hunting and habitat loss, yet whole genomes existed for only two of 32 Asian species. Long and short read sequencing were combined for the new assemblies.

Genomes for Great, Rufous-necked, Malabar Pied, and Wreathed Hornbills ran from 1.1 to 1.3 billion letters, with completeness above 95.9 percent in the report. Over 10,000 gene groups were shared, and keratin related families had expanded. Past population tracking showed falling numbers during the late Pleistocene, which sharpens the case for protection.
pmc-13321746:
Mohsen Kamali and Amirmohammad Atashinsadaf survey nurse leadership and staff satisfaction in Iranian hospitals in a 2026 study. Head nurses shape how ward teams feel and perform, yet styles may work differently in specialist and general wards. The census study covered 1354 nurses in 71 wards across six teaching hospitals tied to Zanjan University of Medical Sciences.

Satisfaction with head nurses averaged 68.94 in specialised wards and 66.11 in general wards on the study scale, fairly high in both. Balanced leadership, mixing task and relationship focus, was most common in specialised wards, while relationship led style led in general wards. Task only leadership was rarest in both settings and scored lower on satisfaction.
pmc-13322946:
Atthaphong Phongphithakchai and colleagues test an international kidney risk tool in Thai patients, in a 2026 validation study. Their cohort held 133 adults with biopsy-proven IgA nephropathy at a tertiary centre, followed for a median of 3.4 years of care.

The tool predicts a halving of filtration rate or progression to end-stage kidney disease, and 45 patients reached that endpoint during follow-up. Both versions of the model, with and without a race term, sorted patients well and split kidney survival clearly across risk groups. Fit to observed outcomes looked broadly sound, though ranges around the estimates were wide. The authors support using the tool for risk talks in Thai practice.
pmc-13323146:
Adwoa Asante-Poku leads a community survey in Ghana on knowledge of tuberculosis and diabetes, published in 2026 after outreach on World Tuberculosis Day in 2022 and 2023. Sessions ran in a hospital outpatient area, schools, a nursing college and a market, with screening offered.

Replies came from 285 adults, mostly women with basic schooling in the reported profile. Among 179 people who knew of tuberculosis, just under half correctly named bacteria or germs as the cause, while a small share held myths such as spiritual causes. People found with either disease were referred to Korle-Bu Teaching Hospital. The authors stress that gaps in knowledge and attitudes can slow care-seeking and weaken control work.
pmc-13323446:
Elif Tunc-Ozcan reviews neurons that release more than one chemical messenger, in a 2026 article on co-transmission. The classic picture of one neuron and one transmitter has given way to evidence that many neurons juggle several, with distinct release arrangements.

Transmitters may share one vesicle, sit in separate vesicle pools at one terminal, or split across different branches of the same cell. Each layout sets its own rules for release timing, target reach and short-term change, letting signals span several timescales and shift with firing pattern. No single method proves the release route, so the field joins molecular profiling, electrical recording, fine anatomy, light-based control and live sensors.
pmc-13324446:
Wei Wang and co-authors survey genetic variants in neuroblastoma, a childhood solid tumor, in a 2026 study. The cancer varies widely between patients, and its mutation patterns in Chinese patients were little known.

Whole-exome sequencing covered tumor, nearby tissue, and blood from nine Chinese patients with confirmed disease. The team found 77 missense variants, with C to T changes the most common type. Variants in MAP1A and RBM33 had not been reported in this cancer before, though each was rare. No MYCN growth or ALK, ATRX, or DAXX changes appeared. High-risk cases showed distinct patterns tied to the tissue matrix, a lead for further study in larger groups.
pmc-13325146:
Tugba Celik Caglar and Birol Kayranli test raw date seeds as a reusable sponge for the dye Rhodamine B in a 2026 water study. Dye waste from industry harms water life, and cheap plant sorbents could cut cleanup costs.

Best removal came at pH 3 with 1.0 g of seeds at 303 K and 30 minutes of contact. Modeling pointed to a varied surface holding several dye layers, with surface binding as the slow step. Charge tests backed charge attraction as a main grip. Among four regeneration routes, alkali washing plus drying at 120 °C kept the surface most intact. That route still removed 88.1 percent of dye in the fourth cycle, down from 96.3 percent at first.
pmc-13325446:
Spoorthy Sandras and co-authors track metabolism inside living neuron-like cells with a fast NMR method in a 2026 study. As neurons mature, their fuel use shifts, but the change unfolds in under a minute at each step.

Cells were grown in alginate beads and matured inside the gel while nuclear magnetic resonance watched labeled pulses pass through. Maturation slowed sugar breakdown through glycolysis and raised TCA cycle activity and glutamate output. Fructose 1,6 bisphosphate marked the young state, while glutathione marked the mature one. The method can now probe how stress or drugs reroute neuron metabolism in near real time.
pmc-13326946:
Roberto Bonanni and co-authors review how exercise may calm epilepsy through neurosteroids in a 2026 narrative review. Brain-made steroids tune GABA signaling, the main braking system whose failure lets seizures fire.

Steroids such as allopregnanolone and pregnenolone rise with moderate to hard exercise in the evidence surveyed. Those same steroids steady inhibitory transmission and may raise the seizure threshold. Clinical views of exercise in epilepsy have flipped from danger to asset, with gains in thinking and life quality reported. Many patients stay drug-resistant, which keeps non-drug routes valuable. The authors call for trials that pin dose and mechanism down.
pmc-13327446:
Viktor Olsson and colleagues tackle a hidden source of MRI error in a 2026 methods study. Extra magnetic fields, called concomitant gradients, distort diffusion scans, and the harm grows at low field strength and with very strong gradients. The team derived a compact formula for these fields and tested fixes in simulation.

They modeled fields from 0.03 to 7 tesla and gradients from 20 to 600 mT/m, splitting the error into lost signal and extra diffusion weighting. Signal loss came mostly from resampling steps that broke the built-in compensation, reaching 100 percent error in bad cases, while a design-stage waveform fix cut bias below 1 percent for most systems. Using the true waveform during analysis handled the weighting error.
pmc-13329746:
Joanne Daggy and team asked if country living shapes return trips and death among older veterans sent home from VA hospitals. Their 2026 watch group study took in veterans aged 65 or older sent home from VA hospitals in fiscal year 2023. It modelled return trips, death, and death after return trips with a semi-competing risk model, cutting off at 30, 90, or 365 days.

Among 99,557 patients, 28.4% lived in country areas, and only 18% of country dwellers lived within thirty minutes of a VA site against 80.3% of city dwellers. At thirty days, country patients showed 5% lower return risk but 20% higher death risk, with higher death after return trips. The team holds that country veterans face fewer returns but more deaths, and calls for work on changeable drivers such as social forces and timely services to shrink gaps.
pmc-13330446:
Xiaolong Li and co-authors review how neutrophil traps help cancers resist immune therapy in a 2026 article. Traps are webs of DNA and proteins cast out by neutrophils. Inside tumours they can wall off immune cells and wear T cells down, blunting checkpoint drugs that help many patients.

Trap parts in blood, such as DNA complexes and altered histones, may serve as signs of disease course and therapy response. Tumour signals and tiny vesicles steer trap formation. The review sorts resistance into physical blocking and biological dampening, then gathers counter-moves: stop trap making, dissolve formed webs, or block their downstream effects. Such moves could restore anti-tumour immunity, the authors propose.
pmc-13333146:
Disha C Shetty and colleagues report a 2026 case of BRASH syndrome managed with transvenous pacing and continuous renal replacement therapy. BRASH stands for bradycardia, renal failure, atrioventricular nodal blockade, shock, and hyperkalemia, a life-threatening cycle in which high potassium and nodal-blocking drugs together drive profound slow heart rate and unstable circulation. The patient was a 71-year-old man with stage IIIB chronic kidney disease, heart failure, and coronary artery disease after bypass surgery.

He took carvedilol, losartan, and torsemide, and was brought from a rehabilitation facility after fainting and unresponsiveness. He had lately been in hospital with multifocal pneumonia and a respiratory syncytial virus infection, plus suspected volume loss and ongoing nodal blockade feeding the syndrome. He arrived in respiratory distress, profound shock, and bradycardia at thirty beats per minute. The case shows how pacing plus continuous renal support can break the BRASH cycle.
pmc-13336446:
Seo Yun Jang and colleagues study 2026 salt mix design for at once surface steadying in silicon-nickel-rich full cells. The pairing of silicon anode and nickel-rich cathode offers high energy density but suffers from severe surface wobbles during cycling. Silicon goes through repeat volume changes that shake its SEI, while NCM811 faces surface breakdown and metal leaking, both worsened by salt mix side reactions.

A dual-add salt mix design with FEC, a store-standard SEI-forming add-in, and DMDMS is put forward to steady both pole surfaces at once. FEC promotes making of a LiF-rich SEI on the silicon anode, whereas DMDMS curbs acid-driven breakdown by mopping up HF and steadying PF5. This design well curbs gas buildup, surface resistance growth, and pole swelling.
pmc-13336746:
Yu Fu wrote a 2026 comment on a machine learning study of wound infection after ankle fracture surgery. The original work followed 509 patients and built models to predict infection within 30 days of open reduction and internal fixation, with a 10 percent infection rate. Its best model, a gradient boosting machine, scored 0.919 on discrimination.

Fu notes that low albumin, open injury, diabetes, high blood pressure, and longer operations drove risk, all clinically plausible factors. He praises the pairing of discrimination with calibration and explainable outputs, but warns that the high infection rate may not travel to other hospitals. External validation must come before fixed risk cutoffs guide stronger preventive care.
pmc-13336846:
Simon W J Dietzmann and co-authors question whether some reported carbon pores are real in a 2026 analysis. Pore charts from gas uptake often show narrow micropores in activated carbons and metal-nitrogen-carbon catalysts. The authors argue many are artifacts of the math models used, not true holes.

By building carbons with known surface sites, they showed the phantom pores match gas molecules preferring certain sites. Zinc-nitrogen sites in a framework-derived carbon become nitrogen sites after zinc removal, each with its own gas pull. Comparing nitrogen, carbon dioxide, and argon uptake plus energy calculations pinned the effect down. Reading these artifacts correctly could speed work on batteries, capacitors, and catalysts.
pmc-13337046:
Zhenguang Li and colleagues built a magnetic stimulation platform in 2026 to guide stem cells in the joint toward cartilage repair. Their bone marrow stem cell targeted magnetic nanomotors spin and bounce inside lysosomes under a rotating magnetic field.

pmc-13350046:

pmc-13350546:

pmc-13351446:

pmc-13351946:

pmc-13352946:

pmc-13356046:

pmc-13358846:

pmc-13395446:
