Each subgenus held a clear, year-after-year nutritional lane, reached either by loyalty to certain plants or by flexible foraging. Species inside one subgenus, Pyrobombus, shared a niche, which could set them competing for the same pollen mix.
pmc-13396346:
Yu and co-authors study, in 2026, how tree grapes of the genus Cyphostemma repeatedly evolved succulence, the water-storing body plan of desert plants, as they spread from rainforest into dry lands. Combining genome assemblies with ecology and morphology, they found the genomes were reshaped from within by long terminal repeat retrotransposons. These mobile DNA sequences copy themselves into new positions, and they thrived during the genus's radiation.

These insertions expanded introns, the non-coding stretches inside genes, a pattern rarely documented in flowering plants of this group. In two species examined closely, retrotransposons accounted for 58.23 percent and 54.65 percent of total intronic repeat length respectively. Rebuilding the family tree showed 72.8 percent of succulent species shifted toward larger genome sizes over time. The authors argue the restless retrotransposons made the genomes more tolerant of change, easing the evolution of succulence under aridity.
pmc-13396446:
Yuh-Shan Ho mapped three decades of world research linking oral health and nutrition, in a 2026 bibliometric study. Teeth and diet shape each other: sore mouths change what people eat, and food choices drive decay and gum disease, yet the combined field had never been charted as a whole.

Records came from the Science Citation Index Expanded for the years 1991 to 2024, gathered with a two-tier search vocabulary. The analysis traces publication counts, citation leaders, author and country patterns, and how themes shifted over time. Such a map shows newcomers where the crowded ground lies and which questions at the mouth-diet junction remain open.
pmc-13396746:
Brandon Tan and co-authors report that ivermectin, a familiar anti-parasite drug, coincided with better wound healing and less itching in one patient. The patient has junctional epidermolysis bullosa, a blistering skin disease caused by faulty skin glue proteins. Their 2026 report sits in a field where over 21 genes and a thousand mutations have been tied to the wider condition.

Splicing faults, which garble how gene messages are cut and joined, often produce partly working proteins and mid-level disease. Because no cure exists, clinics repurpose safe, cheap drugs where they can. A single case cannot prove cause, but documented gains in healing and itch give other teams a reason to test the drug formally.
pmc-13397646:
Lusine Yaghjyan and colleagues test oral contraceptive links to stem cell markers in benign breast tissue in a 2026 study. Whether contraceptives alter stem-like cell populations in healthy breast tissue could illuminate breast cancer risk pathways.

Among 731 cancer-free women with benign breast disease in Nurses' Health Study II, contraceptive histories updated biennially since 1989 were linked to CD44, CD24, and ALDH1A1 staining in normal tissue cores. Current contraceptive use tracked with stromal CD44 expression. The paper offers a tissue-level clue to hormonal effects on breast stem biology in healthy tissue.
pmc-13398246:
Diego de Oliveira Corrêa and co-authors chain three living systems into one treatment line for pig farm wastewater. Their 2026 study joins a vertical-flow constructed wetland, a microbial fuel cell and an algae photobioreactor. Pig waste runs extremely rich in organic matter and nutrients, overwhelming single-stage treatment.

Wet, saturated running of the wetland-fuel cell stage pushed open-circuit voltage to a peak of 539 mV, proof that microbes were generating current while cleaning. With pulsed feeding, that stage removed 83 percent of suspended solids and 69 percent of chemical oxygen demand in the reported figures. Cleaner outflow then grew the alga Tetradesmus obliquus to yields of 1.1 to 1.3 grams per litre, polishing the water further.
pmc-13399246:
Michael Chaim Sklar and colleagues surveyed international medical fellows at the University of Toronto about how the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic affected them, for a 2026 report. Fellows training abroad faced the usual pandemic strain plus distance from family, travel bans, and visa worries. The survey went out in June and July 2020 to 237 fellows in internal medicine and its subspecialties.

Eighty-eight fellows, a 37 percent response rate, described wide disruption. Training objectives were disturbed for 70 percent of respondents; among them, research was suspended for 60 percent and patient exposure shrank for 56 percent, per the survey tallies. Nearly half said they would rather be in their home country. Moderate or worse anxiety was reported by 64 percent, trouble concentrating by 59 percent, and burnout by 45 percent. Half felt their own wellness was affecting the care they gave. The authors argue institutions need stronger support plans for international trainees in future crises.
pmc-13399346:
Francisco Javier Romero-Expósito and co-authors studied how the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans keeps two developmental clocks in step, reporting in 2026. As the worm grows through four larval stages, its seam cells divide on one schedule while its skin is shed and rebuilt in molts on another. The team weakened insulin signaling, a pathway that senses nutrition, using the daf-2(e1370) mutant, and timed both processes.

Reduced insulin signaling slowed everything. It delayed the seam cell divisions much more than the molts, widening the gap between the two schedules. That mismatch then produced a knock-on effect. The start of the next molt was itself postponed, which pulled the programs back into alignment at the opening of the following larval stage. The authors describe this compensatory delay as a resynchronization mechanism. The authors suggest such buffering may be a general feature of how development stays reproducible when conditions vary.
pmc-13399446:
Mika Matsuzaki, Emma Sanchez-Vaznaugh, Joel Gittelsohn, and Jessica Fanzo argue in a 2026 commentary that school nutrition policy has a digital blind spot. Children now meet food through apps, delivery platforms, social media, and influencer marketing. The authors call this online layer the digital food environment. Their own 2025 survey found one in four United States teenagers had ordered food by phone app during school hours, traffic that cafeteria rules ignore.

The authors weigh two broad responses. The other is redesign. They point to trial evidence that making nutrition information and healthier options more visible on platforms reduced the calories, fat, and sodium in online orders. They propose partnerships with delivery companies to surface healthier choices for young users, plus classroom teaching that builds deliberate decision skills. Their aim is guidance that treats the phone in a student's pocket as part of the school food environment.
pmc-13399646:
Cheryl Marise Peilin Tan and colleagues present a simplified three-front-portal method for arthroscopic Latarjet surgery. Their 2026 technical paper addresses recurrent front shoulder dislocation, treated by moving a coracoid bone block to the socket rim. The arthroscopic version is technically hard, with risks of block misplacement, screw problems, and nerve injury.

The method places portals beside the coracoid process and conjoint tendon to lower nerve and vessel injury risk, and uses specific drill guides for socket and coracoid tunnels to improve block placement. The coracoid is prepared outside the joint after cutting, for better view and control. The authors call the technique safe and reproducible for recurrent anterior dislocation, while comparative outcome data remain to be gathered.
pmc-13399746:
Di Zhang and colleagues used the MIMIC-IV intensive care database to test whether a simple insulin resistance index predicts which ischemic stroke patients bounce back into intensive care. The work is a 2026 retrospective study. Among 2,929 stroke patients in the database, 24.0 percent were readmitted to intensive care during the same hospital stay.

Modeled as a continuous score, each step up in the index carried 17 percent higher odds of readmission, with an odds ratio of 1.17 in the adjusted logistic model. Split into quarters, the pattern rose in steps: the top quarter's odds ratio reached 1.53 against the bottom quarter's, in the reported trend analysis. Adding the index to conventional severity models improved their discrimination and reclassification statistics. The authors suggest the score could help flag stroke patients who need closer monitoring after they first leave intensive care.
pmc-13399946:
Wadha Mohammed and colleagues mapped the APOE gene landscape of the Emirati population to guide safer use of new anti-amyloid Alzheimer's drugs, in a 2026 analysis. The team combined Abu Dhabi health records of 2024 Alzheimer's diagnoses and antibody prescriptions with whole-genome data from 506,734 participants in the Emirati Genome Program, calling genotypes from the two defining variants.

In 2024, 1,285 Emiratis were diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease, and aducanumab had been prescribed to just eight patients across 2022 to 2024. In the genome cohort, the ε3/ε3 genotype dominated at 77.9 percent. The ε4 risk allele appeared in 14.7 percent of participants, and 0.9 percent carried two ε4 copies, the highest-risk group for ARIA. The protective ε2 allele was present in 7.5 percent of the population. The authors recommend building APOE results into the Emirati Genome Program's pharmacogenomic report so that antibody eligibility and risk counseling rest on local data rather than imported European frequencies.
pmc-13400146:
Mengmeng Jiang, Jing Qu, Moshi Song, and Guang-Hui Liu review how gene therapy could be turned against aging itself, in this 2026 article. Aging is the master risk factor behind most chronic disease. Instead of chasing each disease separately, the authors survey strategies that rewrite the genetic and epigenetic programs driving decline.

The toolkit they organize spans genome editing that permanently alters DNA, RNA modulation that adjusts gene output temporarily, and epigenetic reprogramming that resets a cell's age marks without changing its identity. Against the fourteen recognized hallmarks of aging, they map which genes push aging forward and which protect against it. They weigh each intervention class for durability against delivery difficulty, safety, cost, and ethics. Gene approaches promise longer-lasting effects than drugs or lifestyle change because they act programmably at the source. The review is candid that delivery efficiency and long-term outcomes remain unsolved.
pmc-13400646:
William Son Galanza and co-authors build, in 2026, a deep learning system that recognizes everyday activities of older adults from wearable sensors. Tracking daily routines at home can flag health changes early, letting support arrive in time. The aim was accurate recognition with as few sensors as possible.

In a small home-lab study, participants performed 14 everyday activities while wearing sensors in different combinations. Five models were compared. A two-sensor setup, at the pelvis and right hand, classified 12 activities with accuracy close to ninety percent. Five sensors covered all 14 activities at slightly lower accuracy, while a single sensor struggled. Sensor placement, the authors conclude, matters as much as sensor count.
pmc-13400746:
Saskia Kolb and a large team study, in 2026, the chromatin organizer SATB1 as a possible lever for improving engineered T cell therapy. SATB1 is essential for developing regulatory T cells, which calm immunity, and for helper T cell formation. Its effects in mature human T cells were poorly mapped.

Removing SATB1 changed gene programs in both regulatory and conventional T cells, with wider effects in the regulatory subset. Across both, cytokine production and a major signaling pathway were thrown off balance. Regulatory cells lost suppressive strength, while engineered tumor-targeting CD4 cells cleared tumors better in a humanized mouse model. Tuning SATB1, the authors propose, might simultaneously loosen brakes and press the accelerator in cell therapy.
pmc-13401146:
R S K Barnes examines, in 2026, whether the tiniest bottom-dwelling animals of the Knysna estuary in South Africa form a coherent group behaving differently from larger bottom fauna. The warm-temperate bay is the countrys top estuarine conservation site. Traditional indices treat meiofauna, animals passing through fine sieves, and macrofauna as distinct ecological units.

Five seagrass and five bare sediment sites were compared, using earlier macrofauna data from the same spots. Nematodes, copepods and ostracods made up almost all meiofauna numbers. Abundance tended to be equal or higher in seagrass and peaked in clean sands at the mouth. Each major group responded individually to estuary gradients, with no shared within-group pattern, undermining the idea of two neatly opposed faunas.
pmc-13401746:
Palak Satija examined the link between body mass index and asthma severity in children in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Nutrition shapes airway inflammation in both directions, since obesity and undernutrition can each worsen the disease course through different mechanisms.

At a tertiary paediatric centre between June 2020 and December 2021, 42 children aged 5 to 18 with doctor-diagnosed asthma were graded for severity by the Global Initiative for Asthma criteria. Their BMI was plotted on World Health Organization age and sex charts. About 60 percent had a normal BMI, while roughly 19 percent were overweight or obese and about 17 percent underweight. Rising BMI was strongly tied to greater asthma severity, and half of the overweight or obese children had moderate persistent asthma. The analysis also compared patterns between boys and girls.
pmc-13401946:
Gudly Nanda, Biswajit Mohanty, Sugyani Mohapatra, and Mamata Singh present a 2026 case of fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva, an ultra-rare genetic disorder where soft tissue progressively turns to bone, in a six-year-old girl. Mutations in the ACVR1 gene derail bone morphogenetic protein signalling and drive the process.

Painful inflammatory swellings flare and then ossify, joint by joint, until movement locks. Most patients are wheelchair-bound by their third decade, and chest restriction can prove fatal. Because the disease is so rare, it is often misdiagnosed, and biopsies or excisions done in error can trigger rapid worsening. The authors walk through the clinical and radiological findings that should raise the diagnosis early, using their young patient's presentation and imaging to show the characteristic pattern. They stress that early recognition is the main protection against harm caused by treatment itself.
pmc-13402046:
Khairy M Ali and co-authors asked whether the speed at which drug levels rise shapes how many Escherichia coli cells become persisters, the dormant cells that survive antibiotics. Working with the antimicrobial peptide pexiganan in small chemostats, they exposed primed and unprimed bacteria to slow and fast drug ramps. Their guess was simple: slow ramps keep cells longer at weak drug levels, which should breed more persisters.

The results matched that guess. Faster rises in drug level left fewer persisters than slower rises run in the same setup. Ali and colleagues frame the finding as proof of principle that dosing schedules, which doctors control, can change persister counts. Fewer persisters could mean fewer relapses after treatment and a slower path toward full drug resistance.
pmc-13402646:
Moran Hausman-Kedem and colleagues test whether sapropterin, sold as Kuvan for another condition, can help children with multisystemic smooth muscle dysfunction syndrome, an ultra-rare ACTA2 disorder. The fault, at position R179H of the actin gene, wrecks smooth muscle, bringing severe brain vessel disease, aortic aneurysms, and weak muscle action across organs. Computer simulations and virtual drug screening flagged sapropterin as able to restore the actin building that the mutation disrupts.

In skin-derived cells from a patient, the drug improved actin organization visibly. One child then received it off-label, and follow-up showed stabilized brain vessels and clinical improvement over time. The authors call the single-patient result first-in-human support, not proof: one case cannot separate drug effect from natural course. Still, with no gene therapy yet available, a repurposed, already-approved drug offers families a lead worth testing properly.
pmc-13402846:
Mariko Tsukagoshi and colleagues test whether a national risk tool built for short-term surgical danger also forecasts long-term fate after liver cancer surgery. They reviewed 210 patients who had first-time liver removal for the disease between January 2016 and December 2022 at their center. For each person they worked out a predicted death rate from the National Clinical Database tool.

Patients flagged at 3 percent or higher relapsed sooner and died sooner than the low-risk group. They also bled more, stayed longer, and had more severe complications. In adjusted models the 3 percent flag still predicted poor survival on its own, alongside male sex and tiny vessel invasion by tumor. The authors suggest the tool, already used for consent and planning, can double as a guide to long-term outlook when weighing liver surgery.
pmc-13403346:
Hafsa Malik and colleagues compute, entirely in theory, the promise of the double perovskite Ba2MnTiO6 for solar cells, hydrogen generation, and heat harvesting. Density functional calculations checked the lead-free crystal stability through formation energy, elastic traits, and lattice vibrations, and molecular dynamics runs showed no structural decay with heat. A direct band gap of 1.236 electron volts suits visible light work, and the magnetic ground state is antiferromagnetic with strong superexchange coupling.

The headline number is a spectroscopic efficiency limit of 32.28 percent, backed by an open-circuit voltage of 0.945 volts and a fill factor of 0.877 in the modeled device. Band edges also align for hydrogen production at higher pH, and at 1200 kelvin the thermoelectric figure of merit reached 0.63 in the reported figures. The authors present the compound as a versatile energy material awaiting synthesis.
pmc-13403946:
Hirokazu Kanegane, Dan Tomomasa, and Satoshi Okada set out in 2026 how they spot and treat a rare inborn immune fault called APDS. Faults in one of two genes leave a cell switch stuck on, which over-fires immune cells. Children with the fault face repeated lung infections, swollen glands, and higher cancer risk.

Unlike many immune faults, this one has targeted drugs, among them rapamycin and blockers of the faulty switch. Early spotting thus changes a child's outlook a great deal. Clues include airway damage that starts young and weak defenses against two common herpes viruses. The guide walks clinicians through signs, lab hints, and treatment choices.
pmc-13404646:
Yanqing Li and colleagues test a traditional Chinese formula, delivered in coated nanoparticles, against artery plaque in 2026 work. The Yiqi Huoxue formula was wrapped in macrophage membrane to form particles about 100 nanometres wide. The coating aims to steer the medicine toward diseased vessel walls.

Lab checks found round, evenly spread particles with a weak negative surface charge. About 59.4 percent of the formula was packed inside, and the particles did not poison rat vessel cells at the tested dose in the reported experiments. In cell tests, treated cells resisted turning into foam cells after exposure to oxidised LDL, the fat form that drives plaque. The pathway named involves KLF4 and NF-kappaB control of muscle cell behaviour.
pmc-13404846:
Ruth Hardman and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol to evaluate community paramedics working in rural Australian clinics. The CP@clinic programme began in Canada, where paramedics screen, teach and coordinate care for people with complex needs. Rural Australia faces ageing, disadvantage and staff shortages that such a role might ease.

A realist evaluation asks how the programme works, for whom and in which settings, rather than only whether it works. The team starts from an initial programme theory built from earlier evidence. Interviews and outcome data will test which local conditions trigger helpful mechanisms. Hoped-for gains include better health, stronger primary care links and fewer emergency visits.
pmc-13404946:
Yida Wu and colleagues benchmark tools that infer cell direction from single-cell gene data, reporting in 2026. RNA velocity estimates where a cell is heading by comparing new and mature gene messages. Dozens of methods exist, and earlier comparisons were narrow or incomplete.

Their benchmark covers 19 tools and 30 methods in total. Twenty-five RNA-only methods face eight tasks, including directional consistency, timing accuracy, resistance to false signals and stability at low sequencing depth. Five methods that add other data types are judged on integration. Tests span 34 datasets, mixing 26 real and eight simulated cases. Results expose a trade-off between directional consistency and robustness to negative controls.
pmc-13405046:
Hsi-An Yang and colleagues compare treatments for swelling at the centre of the retina in retinitis pigmentosa, in a 2026 review. Retinitis pigmentosa slowly destroys vision, and fluid swelling in the macula adds further loss. Many drugs are used, from water tablets to steroid implants, with little head-to-head evidence.

Twelve studies entered a network meta-analysis, which ranks treatments by combining direct and indirect comparisons. Options included oral acetazolamide, eye drops, steroid injections and implants, and immune cell infusions. At three to four months, oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors improved vision more than anti-VEGF injections in the reported analysis. By twelve months no treatment stood out as clearly best for vision.
pmc-13405646:
Cayuan Tadeu Brandão Pinto and Luciana Regina Meireles review beef parasites that can infect people, in a 2026 food safety article. Cattle carry Sarcocystis cysts in their muscle, and some species cause gut illness or painful muscle inflammation in humans who eat undercooked beef. New species with zoonotic potential are still being described.

Routine meat inspection relies on the naked eye, which misses microscopic cysts in carcasses. The review covers parasite biology, illness in people and animals, and how common infection is in herds worldwide. Molecular tests that identify species accurately are presented as the needed upgrade. The authors frame the issue as a neglected gap in slaughterhouse practice.
pmc-13406746:
Qian Wang and a large team review glowing carbon dots made by green routes, in a 2026 comprehensive survey. Carbon dots dissolve in water, shine stably and are gentle on living tissue, suiting them to sensing and medicine. Older recipes clash with green chemistry through harsh inputs and waste.

Newer methods start from plants, fruit peel or safer synthetic ingredients, using top-down and bottom-up routes the review compares. Machine learning now tunes recipes, predicting brightness and emission colour to cut trial and error. Uses span biosensing, imaging, drug delivery and light-based therapy, with scattered roles beyond biology. Scale-up and standard quality remain open challenges, the authors conclude.
pmc-13406946:
Jin-Hong Yoo, writing in 2026, sets out an ethics framework for AI-assisted scientific writing and peer review. Large language models are reshaping how papers get written and checked, so guarding against misconduct alone no longer covers the risks involved, Yoo argues.

Credit stays human: software cannot be an author, and named authors answer for accuracy in the end. Disclosure should scale with how heavily AI was used, following a tiered scheme. Reviewers may gain speed from AI tools, provided the work happens inside closed, secure systems that protect manuscripts. Yoo also flags newer hazards, including flattering, agreeable model output and hidden prompt attacks, and closes with a revision roadmap for authors, reviewers, and editors.
pmc-13407046:
Matylda Witkowska, Juliusz Huber, and Tomasz Kotwicki report a 2026 study of patients awaiting surgery for idiopathic scoliosis. That is a sideways spinal curve with no clear cause. They compared nerve and muscle function recorded before the operation. They contrasted Lenke 1 and Lenke 3 curve patterns, and patients braced alone against those who also received physiotherapy.

Testing covered muscle activity beside the spine and in the legs, nerve conduction in the lower leg, and responses evoked by magnetic brain stimulation. Deficits showed up more in Lenke 3 curves, and the brace-only group fared worse than the physiotherapy group, though a retrospective design cannot prove cause. Knowing which muscles weaken, and on which side, could shape targeted strengthening before corrective surgery.
pmc-13407246:
Nicoleta Dubei and co-authors offer prescribers, in 2026, a practical plan for preventing gut bleeding in patients taking direct oral anticoagulants, the blood thinners now widely used for atrial fibrillation. These drugs beat older thinners on convenience, yet bleeding in the stomach or bowel remains their most common serious side effect outside the skull.

Drawing on trials, real-world studies, and guidelines from 2004 to 2025, the review ties risk to existing gut disease, other illnesses, and companion drugs such as anti-inflammatory painkillers. Among the thinners, apixaban repeatedly showed the kindest gut profile, while rivaroxaban and high-dose dabigatran bled more. Suggested defences include treating Helicobacter infection, acid-suppressing medicine for high-risk patients, dropping needless companion drugs, and matching drug choice to the individual.
pmc-13407846:
Chia-Chen Chang and team weighed online team learning against simulation-based learning for teacher training in digital health education. Their 2026 quasi-experimental work enrolls 674 primary and secondary teachers in Taiwan, with 399 in team learning and 275 in simulation learning, each in a three-hour program. Digital learning is central to teacher growth, yet which online model best builds knowledge versus confidence had been unclear.

Both groups gained clearly in teaching knowledge and teaching efficacy, but patterns split: team learning gave greater knowledge gains, while simulation gave greater efficacy gains. Mixed models confirmed distinct change patterns, with mental load tied positively to knowledge gain but negatively to efficacy. The work suggests blending teamwork for understanding with simulation for applied confidence in teacher programs.
pmc-13408146:
Okutan and co-authors check, in 2026, whether harvesting the rectus femoris tendon from the front of the thigh to rebuild a torn anterior cruciate ligament weakens that muscle a year later. They use magnetic resonance volumetry, strength dynamometry, and hop tests in 54 patients whose operations ran from December 2024 to April 2025. Mean follow-up was 15.7 months in the retrospective series.

Patients scored a mean of 84.1 on the standard knee function questionnaire and showed a side-to-side laxity difference of just 1.8 millimeters on the arthrometer in the outcome battery. Every quadriceps muscle was smaller on the operated side, but the deficits were uniform, 9.63 percent for the harvested rectus femoris versus 8.52, 7.95, and 8.08 percent for its three partners, a spread that was not statistically significant, proving no selective harm to the donor muscle. Limb symmetry exceeded 90 percent on all strength and functional measures at one year.
pmc-13408346:
Zhiqi Guo and co-authors combine fermentation with light-driven chemistry in 2026 to build an unnatural amino acid from scratch. Engineered Escherichia coli first fermented a feedstock into indole-3-acetic acid, with gene copies and metabolic tweaks boosting output. A second, oxygen-free module then used light plus a redesigned enzyme to join that intermediate with serine, yielding the target compound in its mirror-image form. Because no purified enzymes or pre-made exotic substrates were needed, the design reads as a template for manufacturing other non-natural products inside living systems.
pmc-13408446:
Hui Wang, Jihong Tang, and colleagues present a 2026 deep-learning tool that infers protein levels from RNA measurements in brain tumours. Proteins do the actual work in cells, yet protein profiling is far scarcer than RNA profiling, and the two correlate only weakly. Their model, T2Pdecoder, learns a shared representation of both data types from paired examples.

Tested on glioma datasets, the model predicted measured protein levels somewhat better than RNA-only baselines and reproduced protein-level pathway patterns more faithfully. Applied to ordinary tumour RNA data, it separated patient groups with clearly different survival, and on single-cell data it reduced technical batch noise while sharpening cell-type markers. The tool offers cancer researchers a way to ask protein-level questions of the large RNA archives already available.
pmc-13410746:
Han Yan and a large team probe in 2026 whether gut microbes help cause kidney damage in diabetes, using genes as natural experiments. Watch-and-see studies had linked the two, yet cause could run either way. The method used compares people whose genes nudge microbe levels up or down across a lifetime.

Data came from genome studies of gut microbes, kidney disease, and immune cell traits. Five microbe groups and seven immune traits showed causal ties to diabetic kidney disease after strict corrections. Immune cells carried part of the effect for some microbes: one species raised risk partly by lowering a marker on regulatory T cells. The chain from gut to immune system to kidney is the paper's main message.
pmc-13410946:
Yuko Takeuchi and colleagues check in 2026 whether scan measures of rebuilt knee ligament bundles predict later graft failure in teenagers. The study followed 133 patients aged 15 to 19 for at least two years after surgery. CT scans a week after operation measured the shape ratios of both graft bundles. Both ratios linked to later non-contact failure and sorted patients with fair to good accuracy. In combined models, one bundle ratio, the front-inner one, kept its link. Scan-based sizing could help flag knees needing closer watch.
pmc-13411146:
Wenbin Rao leads a team describing in 2026 a case of genital herpes that hid for six months behind a wrong label. Herpes usually shows as clear blisters, yet this 59-year-old woman presented with raw, weeping, itchy, and painful vulvar skin. Repeated diagnoses of simple inflammation or contact allergy brought antibiotics and steroids without lasting relief.

Two biopsies showed only nonspecific inflammation, and microbe hunts came back empty. Gentle salt-water cleansing in hospital finally exposed pinpoint erosions, which prompted a DNA test that confirmed herpes simplex virus type 2. Blood tests suggested an old infection flaring again rather than a first one. Valacyclovir cleared the problem fully within eight days.
pmc-13411346:
Rachel Shelton and colleagues tested a contest-style method in 2026 for cutting back routine mammograms in older women where guidelines no longer back them. Stopping low-value screening is harder than starting a new habit. The team ran an Innovation Tournament across two New York City health systems, inviting clinicians and managers to pitch and refine stop-doing strategies.

Early work surfaced a core snag, since staff disagreed about the guidelines and found the very idea of de-implementation hard to discuss. The paper hands implementation teams a frank account of how to shape such contests, from user-centered design to handling clashing views in the room.
pmc-13411946:
Anupam Debnath and co-authors test, in a 2026 prospective study from Dhaka, whether a two-value blood score predicts problems after liver surgery. The albumin-bilirubin (ALBI) score combines two routine lab results to grade how much working reserve a liver has left. Seventy adults having part of the liver removed at a university hospital in Bangladesh were scored before surgery and followed for thirty days.

About 43 percent developed complications, and patients who did were older with lower albumin. Liver failure after surgery rose sharply across ALBI grades, from none in the best grade to every patient in the worst. The ALBI score separated the groups clearly, while the older MELD score did not.
pmc-13412546:
Niloufar Abdollahpour and colleagues test in 2026 whether two body-composition readings can signal anaemia risk in women with type 2 diabetes. Anaemia is common in this group and raises disability risk. Bioelectrical impedance gives a phase angle, reflecting cell health and muscle quality, and a water ratio showing how much body water sits outside cells. Records came from 1,381 diabetic women aged 35 to 65 in the MASHAD cohort.

Women with a higher phase angle had lower odds of anaemia and higher haemoglobin levels in adjusted models. A higher outside-cell water ratio pointed the opposite way, matching more anaemia and lower haemoglobin readings. The authors propose both readings as cheap early-warning markers worth adding to diabetes check-ups.
pmc-13412646:
Enrico Pompili, Martina Salvati, and Paolo Caraceni comment in 2026 on a trial of midodrine for patients with acute-on-chronic liver failure and ascites. Midodrine tightens blood vessels and is often proposed to counter the circulatory collapse of advanced cirrhosis. The double-blind MIDAS trial added the drug to standard care in 130 patients and measured transplant-free survival at one month.

Raising blood pressure, the commentary stresses, did not translate into better outcomes in that trial. Midodrine lifted mean arterial pressure yet failed to improve survival or cut complications and hospital stays. The authors use the negative result to argue that pressure alone is the wrong target in this syndrome, and that treatment development still awaits a shared definition of the condition.
pmc-13413946:
Bastian Estay Zamorano and co-authors review in 2026 how deep learning systems that read several data types at once are changing lung disease detection. Earlier reviews treated scans, breathing sounds, and health records separately, hiding how combined models behave. Their structured narrative covered peer-reviewed work from 2019 to 2024 across four databases, extracting architectures, dataset traits, performance, and stated limits.

Convolutional networks, and lately transformers, post high scores sorting chest X-rays in the studies surveyed. Sound-based systems using spectrograms or self-taught speech representations such as Wav2Vec 2.0 look promising but swing with the dataset used. Record-based and fused models remain the least mature. The authors catalogue translational barriers, from scarce shared data to uneven reporting, as the field's next problems.
pmc-13414046:
Matilde Carvalho and co-authors make cerium oxide nanoparticles from lemon juice and table sugar in 2026, in a hunt for a greener recipe. Jiting Wang leads a 2026 team that lets battery equalizer converters carry data on the same wires as power, using a talkative converter design. Separate communication hardware adds cables, cost, and failure points as module counts grow.

Their bidirectional flyback converter both moves energy between modules and encodes data into its switching ripple. A channel model, noise suppression plan, and tailored protocol support the dual role. Hardware tests sustained real-time communication at 8.33 kilobits per second alongside equalization. Shared-bus designs could slim wiring in vehicle and storage battery systems.
pmc-13507446:
Marius Trollmann, Paolo Rossetti, and Rainer Böckmann ask why fats used in lipid nanoparticles behave as if they were far less basic than they are on their own, in 2026 work. These particles carry RNA into cells, holding it at neutral conditions and releasing it when compartments turn acidic. The team ran long computer simulations at fixed acidity for five widely used fats. Each fat sat in membranes built from helper fats and cholesterol.

Across all systems, sitting in a membrane lowered the measured value into the range linked to good delivery. The shift reached up to 3.5 units for some fats. Fats also moved or grouped in distinct ways once they lost their charge, and firm helper fats made these effects stronger. The findings give makers a clearer way to tune particle formulas.
pmc-13508346:
Feng and colleagues published a 2026 study on a protein trio that fights stem cell aging. Mesenchymal stem cells are prized for therapy but age fast in lab dishes. Fluid from a broader-potency stem cell type slowed that aging visibly. The team fished out which proteins in the fluid did the work.

Three proteins together, GAPDH plus S100A8 and S100A9, carried the effect. Treated cells showed far fewer aging markers than untreated sister cells. Key aging genes, including p16 and p21, quieted after treatment. The trio also rescued cells aged early by a stress drug. A cell-free boost like this could extend stem cell usefulness. Dividing cells restarted dividing more briskly after the protein treatment.
pmc-13508446:
Natália Karla Bellini leads a twelve-author team producing the first full map of centromeres in the Chagas disease parasite, in 2026 work. Centromeres are the chromosome handles that ensure fair inheritance when cells divide. The parasite Trypanosoma cruzi has a highly repetitive genome that long blocked clean assembly. The team first improved a standard strain's genome using contact data that shows which DNA parts sit near each other in the nucleus. They then tagged two kinetochore proteins, the machinery that grips centromeres, and mapped where they bind.

Binding peaks numbered thirty-three across twenty-seven scaffolds. The sites sat in zones rich in jumping genes, near gene strand switches, and often at borders between conserved genes and virulence gene families. Contact maps showed these regions frequently separate neighborhoods with distinct interaction styles. The map suggests centromeres help organize the whole nucleus, not just divide chromosomes.
pmc-13508546:
Yang Liu and Zhiping Lv study a surface protein called MUC1 as a growth driver in lung cancer, in work published in 2026. MUC1 sits high in many cancers, yet its exact role in lung tumors was murky. The team measured it in tumor tissue and cell lines, then silenced it in two lung cancer cell types. A known signaling route, PI3K and AKT, was tracked, along with drug tools that block or force that route.

MUC1 ran high in lung cancers, and patients with low levels lived longer overall. Silencing it slowed cell growth, triggered cell death, and curbed movement and invasion. The signaling route dimmed in step with silencing, and forcing it back on partly restored the cancer traits. Tumors from silenced cells grew less in mice. The authors place MUC1 on the list of lung cancer targets worth drug development.
pmc-13509246:
Jinmei Tang and four co-authors track how the gills of a prized freshwater fish remodel during a day without enough oxygen, in 2026 work. Topmouth culter is farmed widely in China yet is unusually sensitive to low oxygen. Fish were held in water with low dissolved oxygen for up to twenty-four hours, with gills and blood checked at set times. Early on, the gill sheets twisted and thickened. Later, the tissue widened its blood spaces and packed in more red cells, changes that help grab oxygen.

Blood sugar spiked early and then fell away, while fat-carrying proteins kept climbing, hinting at a fuel switch from sugar to fat. Defense enzyme activity rose steadily, and the genes behind it switched on early then faded late. The authors read the pattern as a staged defense: quick chemical shields first, structural remodeling next, with costs mounting as stress drags on.
pmc-13510246:
Iamone and colleagues tested a 2026 set of enterococcus bacteria from dogs and cats for resistance to antibiotics reserved for human medicine. Enterococci live without harm in pet guts but also cause clinical infections, and resistant strains worry doctors and vets alike. Whether sickness-causing strains resist more than harmless gut strains was unclear.

Ninety-nine strains gathered between 2022 and 2025 were tested with three standard lab methods. One species, Enterococcus faecium, resisted far more drugs than the other and was resistant to many drugs in every clinical case. Clinical strains resisted common animal drugs more than gut strains did, matching drug use pressure in clinics. For human reserved drugs, though, Iamone found no gap between clinical and gut isolates.
pmc-13511246:
Cui and co-authors establish measurement standards for gene studies in elderberry. Their 2026 paper addresses a basic problem. RT-qPCR, the standard technique for measuring gene activity, is only as trustworthy as its reference genes. None had been validated for Sambucus nigra. That plant is a medicinal and edible species rich in anthocyanins. The team tested nine candidate reference genes across five tissue types at different growth stages.

Four stability algorithms were applied to the measurements. Across all tissues, the pair VAMP and Pol emerged as the most suitable normalising combination. Restricting attention to vegetative tissues, leaves and stems, a different pair, RPB2 and RPB5, proved most stable. The authors offer the rankings as the methodological foundation for reliable gene expression work in elderberry, supporting future functional genomics and molecular breeding in the species.
pmc-13511546:
Sadat and colleagues describe four patients with Knobloch syndrome, a rare inherited disorder that damages the eyes and sometimes the back of the skull, in a 2026 case series. The team worked at West Virginia University. The condition stems from faults in the COL18A1 gene and typically brings severe short-sightedness, degeneration of the retina and skull defects. Records covered 627 patients with inherited retinal diseases treated between 2010 and 2025.

Only four patients, or 0.64 percent of that clinic cohort, matched the syndrome with a matching gene variant. All four shared the core eye features: wobbling eyes, high short-sightedness, wasting of the central retina, and vitreous degeneration. Other problems ranged from seizures and kidney anomalies to developmental delay. Genetic testing found four COL18A1 variants, including two never reported before. Sadat argues the new variants widen the known genetic picture and may help link gene faults to symptoms.
pmc-13512246:
Carlo Maccheroni, Roberta Pace, and Giuseppe Venere map the geography of frail ageing across Italy, in 2026 work. Italians live exceptionally long lives, yet long life often arrives with disability, many coexisting conditions, and dependence on others for daily tasks. The study joins official demographic, health, and welfare data to show how those burdens spread unevenly across regions and between men and women.

North-south gaps stand out, with southern regions carrying heavier frailty and stronger pressure on care systems, and older women facing the greatest vulnerability. Longer survival, the authors show, does not mean healthier survival in much of the country. They argue that long-term care planning and assistance benefits should be shaped region by region, not by one national template. Joining health and welfare indicators can then steer resources more fairly.
pmc-13513646:
Tanya Beelders and Luna Bergh test how well the humor and rhythm of a Dr. Seuss classic survive translation into Afrikaans, in 2026 work. The study pairs a stylistic reading of Horton Hears a Who! and its Afrikaans version with an eye-tracking experiment. Readers worked through two passages in each language while their gaze was recorded, so ease and effort could be compared line by line.

Gaze behavior in both languages sat comfortably inside typical reading ranges, and readers showed no real difficulty with the invented words or playful tone. The meter of the translation did shift where longer fixations landed, and text features such as length, syllable count, and word position shaped gaze in both versions. The authors conclude the Afrikaans text keeps both the sly craft and the frivolous sparkle of the original, at least on the aspects tested.
pmc-13516346:
Michelle Kahn-John leads a fifteen-author team setting out a protocol for a mental health training programme built with an Indigenous community, in a 2026 article. The Fort Belknap Community partnered with the Johns Hopkins School of Nursing to close gaps in mental health knowledge and care coordination. A six-step participatory adaptation model guided the work, blending evidence-based teaching with Indigenous ways of knowing.

Four courses emerged: historical trauma, culturally informed screening and care, risks and protective factors, and the legal landscape of Tribal, state, and federal jurisdiction in Native health. The plan pairs the teaching with task shifting, so nurses, community members, and the wider workforce can spot concerns early and coordinate care. Piloting, evaluation, and decisions about wider rollout come next. Kahn-John's team offers the process as a template for academic-community partnerships serving Indigenous communities in other fields.
pmc-13517646:
Chang Liu and Zengyong Zhu ask how big a pig farm should be in a 2026 survey study from Heilongjiang, China. Bigger is not plainly better: scale trades output against disease risk, manure costs, and management strain. The authors surveyed eight hundred nine farms and scored three things together: production efficiency, disease prevention, and environmental management, grouped by yearly slaughter volume.

No single size won everything. Farms finishing five to ten thousand pigs a year ran the most efficient production. A smaller band, three to five thousand head, led on disease control and held manure costs down best. Weighing all three together, that mid band coordinated the whole operation most strongly. Liu and Zhu recommend it as the fitting scale for the province today, a data point for China's new push toward moderate-scale farming in its latest five-year planning.
pmc-13518846:
Zenghui Liu, Minjun Chen, and Feiyue Liu study in 2026 how rock around a coal mine roadway behaves as digging nears a fault-protected coal pillar. The pillar is a block of coal left unmined to guard against the fault, and its width decides how much stress and fracture reach the roadway. Horizontal ground stress dominates the study area.

Combining stress measurement, theory, 3D simulation, and field monitoring, the team tested pillar widths of 10, 20, 30, and 40 meters. Narrow pillars of 10 to 20 meters let fault disturbance swell roof sag, wall squeeze, and broken zones. Wider pillars calmed the response. Existing bolt-and-cable supports controlled deformation well in monitoring.
pmc-13520146:
Kusse Urmale Mare, Engida Yisma, and Zohra S Lassi pool population surveys in 2026 on whether caesarean birth raises the risk of acute respiratory infection in young children across poorer countries. Caesarean rates keep climbing, sometimes beyond medical need, and rich-country data hint at immune downsides. Demographic and Health Surveys from 47 countries supplied 534,423 singleton births.

Caesarean prevalence ranged from 1.3 percent in Chad to 44.9 percent in Bangladesh. Pooled analysis found children born by caesarean had an 11 percent higher prevalence of recent respiratory infection than vaginally born children, with little variation between countries. The link strengthened in the poorest settings and where caesarean rates were lowest. Residual confounding remains possible, the authors caution.
pmc-13520246:
Tesfahun Kassahun and Habtamu Admas test in 2026 which pairing of field pea variety and nitrogen-fixing bacteria works best in Ethiopia's Sinana District, where poor soils cap yields. Three varieties met two Rhizobium strains, their mixture, or no inoculation in greenhouse and field trials arranged in replicated blocks.

Strain EAL 302 survived better on seed and outcompeted its partner. In the field it raised nodule weight, plant mass, and nutrient uptake, reaching a grain yield of 2,900 kilograms per hectare and fixing 242 kilograms of nitrogen per hectare. The variety Wayitu yielded and nodulated best overall. Kassahun and Admas recommend the Wayitu plus EAL 302 pairing to lift yields and soil nitrogen together.
pmc-13520446:
Görkem Mümtaz and Beril Koyuncu test in 2026 how design software, resin choice and tooth preparation shape affect the fit of 3D printed permanent crowns. Poor fit at the edge or inside can cause seating trouble and biological problems over time.

Model teeth were prepared with three edge styles, while crowns were designed in two software systems and printed in two resin materials. Silicone replicas measured gaps under magnification. Edge style affected every fit measure, material affected edge and side gaps, while software affected only the biting-surface gap. Edge gaps stayed within accepted limits overall, although biting-surface gaps often ran high.
pmc-13522446:
Zhu and co-authors report in 2026 the first experimental observation of a discrete time quasicrystal, a phase of matter that keeps time order without repeating in a simple period. Ordinary time crystals respond at one steady rhythm locked to their drive. The team created the quasicrystal version in a gas of Rydberg atoms, atoms excited to very large, strongly interacting states, driven by two mismatched frequencies.

By applying a quasiperiodic drive with two incommensurate frequencies, frequencies whose ratio is not a simple fraction, they produced a robust subharmonic response. It appeared at several incommensurate frequencies, the signature of the new phase. They mapped the full phase diagram and showed the state stayed rigid when the radio-frequency field strength and laser detuning were perturbed. A cyclic group symmetry effect also constrained which symmetry combinations can form. The authors present the system as a platform for studying matter far from equilibrium.
pmc-13523146:
Phan Thao Nguyen and co-authors describe a protective strategy during catheter valve replacement in two high-risk patients in a 2026 case report. Both patients had severe narrowing of the aortic valve and anatomy that placed their coronary arteries at risk of blockage when the new valve opened. Protection was planned in advance using pre-procedure scans.

After valve deployment, standard imaging suggested flow was preserved in both cases. Ultrasound imaging from inside the vessel, however, revealed dangerous closeness between valve tissue and a coronary opening in one patient, while standard imaging caught ostial compromise in the other. A chimney stent, placed alongside the valve to keep the artery open, secured blood flow in both. The two patients recovered well with good follow-up results.
pmc-13523346:
Lærke Mygind and colleagues set out the protocol for a large Danish prevention study for youth mental health in a 2026 paper. Around fifteen percent of Danish young people receive a mental disorder diagnosis before age eighteen, and real-world evidence on prevention remains thin. The program spans schools and municipalities and targets eating problems, self-harm, internalizing difficulties, and parent support.

Five waitlist randomized trials form the first sub-study, with mental wellbeing as the shared main outcome measured at baseline, after the intervention, and six months later. Further sub-studies examine how change happens, how delivery works in practice, and whether the program offsets its costs elsewhere. The authors aim to give policymakers robust evidence on effectiveness, mechanisms, implementation, and economics in a single coordinated evaluation.
pmc-13525846:
Narththana Keerthinathan, Kanagasingam Arulmoly, and Ramanathan Ramesh present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 70-year-old patient. The patient had a sterile growth on a heart valve. Advanced lung cancer was also present. Symptoms included chronic cough, fever, and breathlessness. Weight loss was also reported. Scans showed fluid around the left lung. A central airway mass was confirmed as squamous cell lung cancer. It had spread to the liver.

Heart ultrasound found a growth on the mitral valve. It first suggested infection. But repeated blood cultures stayed negative. Antibiotics changed nothing. The team diagnosed non-bacterial thrombotic endocarditis. This is a clotting-related valve condition linked to cancer. Blood thinners were withheld. The tumour caused repeated coughing of blood, making them risky.
pmc-13526046:
Claudia Leslie and colleagues report a 2026 phase Ia dose-escalation study pairing a radioligand therapy with a radiosensitizing chemotherapy pill in metastatic prostate cancer that no longer responds to hormone treatment. The radioligand, lutetium-177 PSMA I&T, already works in this setting, and capecitabine sensitizes tumors to radiation in other cancers.

Twelve heavily pretreated men received the combination across four capecitabine dose levels in forty-two-day cycles, with the radioligand given on day ten. No dose-limiting toxicities appeared, so the maximum tolerated dose was set at the top level tested. Nausea, fatigue, and diarrhea were the common side effects. Half the patients achieved at least a fifty percent drop in prostate marker levels, and marker progression-free survival averaged 4.7 months. A dose-expansion cohort is underway.
pmc-13527046:
Rao and colleagues present a 2026 case report of swallowing trouble that a goiter seemed to explain, but did not. A 29-year-old woman had a benign multinodular goiter, yet her dysphagia, difficulty swallowing, was worse than the swelling size suggested. Thyroid tests showed a harmless gland, so the team looked further.

A barium swallow study showed the food tube being squeezed from outside. A CT scan of the aorta then found the true cause: an aberrant right subclavian artery. That artery takes a wrong route behind the food tube and presses on it, a condition called dysphagia lusoria. Removing the thyroid did not cure her swallowing, as expected once the artery was known. She was referred to vessel surgeons. The case warns against blaming the obvious lump when symptoms outsize it.
pmc-13529646:
Yogananthan Dhanapal and three colleagues test a medicinal herb against colorectal cancer in a 2026 study. The plant, Strobilanthes cusia, is a folk remedy for inflammation. Leaf extracts were made with four solvents in sequence. The alcohol extract killed two colon cancer cell lines best. Chemical scans found thirteen active ingredients.

One compound, andrographolide, was isolated from this plant for the first time. Network analysis pointed to a cell cycle guard, CHEK1, as its main target. Computer docking showed the compound gripping CHEK1 as well as a reference drug. Simulated motion kept the grip stable. Dish tests confirmed dose-driven cell death and slower growth. The authors back deeper study of the plant compound. Animal work would be the honest next step.
pmc-13530246:
R Anandhi and colleagues simulate in 2026 how radiation upsets memory chips built from ring-shaped transistors. A single radiation strike can flip a stored bit and hang or reset a system, a real risk in space electronics. Three transistor variants went through three-dimensional device simulation.

One variant with a buried oxide layer and light doping showed the best basic electrical behavior. Memory cells built from each variant were checked for stability in reading, writing, and holding states. The buried-oxide design with an inner drain contact tolerated the highest radiation dose, marking it as the toughest option.
pmc-13531746:
Clarissa Hsu leads a 2026 cluster trial testing whether materials designed with care-home staff raise COVID-19 booster uptake. Forty long-term care centers in Georgia and Washington were assigned to standard government materials or to a co-design path. Staff teams in the co-design arm met weekly online to build tailored promotion materials.

Booster uptake and scores for urging the shot on workmates showed no clear gap between arms after the materials went out. Doubt and confidence scores also matched. The authors share lessons on engaging leaders, sharpening message targeting, and customizing delivery for future campaigns in hesitant workforces.
pmc-13532446:
Pivot and co-authors contributed a 2026 Perspective on antibody drug conjugates, which are cancer medicines that link an antibody to a toxic payload. Such drugs are often told as simple carriers, yet antibodies like trastuzumab can fight cancer on their own. Attaching a payload can weaken that action, and Pivot names the loss an antibody exposure deficit.

Pivot traces the deficit to payload choice, how many drug units each antibody carries, and how water hating the linker and payload are. Designs built at one exact site with a single drug unit can shrink the loss, the authors argue. High load designs instead treat the antibody mainly as a delivery vehicle. The piece maps a spectrum between payload first designs and dual designs that keep both actions working.
pmc-13532846:
Anna Maxion and colleagues present in 2026 a lean computer model of how thin, unmyelinated nerve fibers remember their own recent activity. In these fibers, which carry pain signals, each impulse travels a little slower or faster depending on what the fiber did just before.

The model replaces heavy cell simulations with a memory function that blends past impulses, mixing a slow linear part with a fast nonlinear part. It was tuned on recordings from ninety-five human pain fibers gathered with fine needle electrodes. The model predicted later impulse speeds with low error and ran fast enough for real-time use during experiments. The authors say it can help researchers study long fibers and patient data without the cost of full biophysical models.
pmc-13533046:
Tuğba Çetin and colleagues report in 2026 results of catheter-based care for a narrowed aorta at one tertiary centre. The narrowing is present from birth and may stay hidden until adult life, when high blood pressure appears. Records covered adults treated from July 2017 to July 2023.

Twenty-nine patients had care, most with a stent placed through a vessel. The pressure gap across the narrowing fell sharply after care, and no deaths occurred in hospital. Problems arose in a small share, one case had a torn aorta, and narrowing returned in 14 percent of patients, so lifelong checks remain vital.
pmc-13535146:
Khajid Ullah Khan and colleagues report the first study of gut microbes in the scorpion Hottentotta tamulus from northeast Pakistan. Scorpions are key hunters with medical importance, yet their gut microbes were not known. Species identity was checked by body traits and a gene marker before long-read sequencing of gut samples.

The gut held low to moderate variety and was led by one large group, with Bacillus and Mycoplasma as top genera. Predicted roles spanned energy use, building block making, and breakdown of foreign compounds. The tight shared community may help this scorpion thrive where food and water are scarce.
pmc-13536546:
Phibion Manyanga and colleagues study in 2026 why women living with HIV in Zimbabwe accept or decline cervical screening as services shift toward HPV testing. Three public facilities surveyed 451 women about the older visual screening method and future preferences. Most had known their HIV status for five years or more and took antiretroviral therapy.

Over nine in ten accepted screening, mainly for reassurance and on health worker advice. Most women with screening history still preferred the older method for the future, while half of decliners favoured HPV testing. Fear of exam discomfort led reasons for declining.
pmc-13536646:
Samet Can Demirci and Ahmet Ozaslan study in 2026 what sets repeatedly jailed teenage boys with substance use disorder apart from first-time peers. The sample held 203 boys held in a closed facility, rated for addiction severity, resilience, and sense of meaning in life. About a third had been jailed before this stay.

Repeat cases showed heavier addiction and lower resilience and meaning scores than first-time boys. Family crime history was the strongest single predictor, raising repeat odds more than fivefold. The authors argue rehab must treat addiction, family strain, and lost purpose together.
pmc-13538046:
Cole C Sorensen and colleagues establish a vitamin B6 cofactor as a light-driven enzyme tool in a 2026 chemistry study. Light-driven enzymes can form bonds that standard catalysts struggle to make, yet many cofactors absorb light poorly and stay unused. The team used an energy transfer trick with an added light absorber and nonstandard starting materials to wake the cofactor excited state inside an enzyme.

Excited cofactor acted as a strong electron donor, generating a paired set of radicals together inside the enzyme pocket. Pairing radicals in one place enabled a lopsided radical joining between benzylamines and radical precursors without the usual sorting tricks. The authors present the route as a major widening of bond types open to this large enzyme family.
pmc-13539646:
L R Jessen and colleagues tested blood and urine markers for kidney infection in cats. Published in 2026, the study covered 71 cats: 22 with pyelonephritis, 35 with other urinary problems, and 14 healthy. Kidney infection is hard to pin down, since its signs overlap other urinary diseases and firm proof needs a tricky kidney urine sample.

A blood marker, serum amyloid A, ran clearly higher in infected cats with barely any overlap. At about 49 mg per liter it spotted infection with 95 percent sensitivity and 97 percent specificity, beating a white-cell ratio. The marker fell back to normal in 12 of 14 treated cats. A urine kidney-injury marker ran high in over half the infected and blocked cats, pointing to frequent tubule damage. The authors present the blood marker as a sharp tool for faster treatment calls.
pmc-13540246:
Aliye Aili and seven colleagues compare, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, gut bacteria in children with autism according to how severe their symptoms are. Signals passing between gut and brain have been proposed as part of autism's biology.

Eighty-one children aged three to twelve were split into mild-to-moderate and severe groups by a standard rating scale, and stool samples underwent gene sequencing. The severe group carried a less diverse gut community, with fewer Firmicutes and more Proteobacteria, including a near tripling of Klebsiella. Helpful fermenters such as Faecalibacterium ran lower. Eleven bacterial groups separated the two severity classes, most of them richer in the milder group.
pmc-13540846:
Rosebella Iseme-Ondiek and colleagues survey households in Kenya in a 2026 study. The topic is aflatoxin, a fungal poison in staple foods. Maize is the food of concern here. The poison links to liver cancer and weak immunity. It also links to stunted growth in children.

Interviewers questioned 17,813 household heads in a rural coastal area. The work ran from July to December 2022. Most households ate maize flour at least three times a week. Yet only about half had heard of aflatoxin. Fewer than twenty percent could name foods at risk. Fewer still could name signs of contamination or health effects. Wealth, schooling, sex, and rurality shaped the answers.
pmc-13540946:
Xin Ye, Hang Xu, and Man Zhang construct, in a 2026 study, an evaluation system for ideological and political education woven into basic nursing courses in China. Judging such teaching needs shared criteria rather than impressions, so the team built the framework on the CIPP model, which weighs context, input, process, and product.

A draft indicator set from literature and group discussion went through two Delphi rounds with twenty-one experts, whose response rates and authority scores were high. Weighting calculations produced a finished system of four first-level indicators, twelve second-level indicators, and fifty-five third-level indicators. The authors present it as a preliminary scaffold needing reliability testing in real classrooms.
pmc-13541946:
Borzelli and co-authors hang male and female climbers from a training board until their fingers give out. They record the electrical chatter of individual motor units in the forearm to learn why endurance differs by sex. Women often outlast men in such tasks, but whether the advantage sits in the muscle or in the nervous system's strategy was unclear. Their 2026 study used high-density surface electrodes on nine women and thirteen men, intermediate climbers, at two grip depths.

Time to failure did not differ between the sexes despite men's larger builds, which already says the outcome hides the story. Women's muscle signals fatigued more slowly on a standard frequency measure, direct evidence of tougher muscle fibres. Their motor units also fired more variably and intermittently, while men leaned harder on sustained early recruitment of their motor units, especially at the deeper, harder grip.
pmc-13543346:
Yaser Said Cetin and Semra Agirbas ran a 2026 study linking vitamin D levels to the severity of cervical dizziness, a balance disorder tied to faulty posture signals from the neck. They recruited 210 patients, checked blood vitamin D at entry, and sorted patients into deficient, insufficient, and sufficient groups. All got the same multimodal neck rehabilitation programme, with supplements for those low in the vitamin, while disability and dizziness questionnaires tracked symptoms and recovery time.

Patients with lower vitamin D showed clearly worse neck disability, dizziness handicap, and quality-of-life scores at the start. Vitamin D level also tracked recovery length strongly: the lower the level, the longer recovery took. A threshold near 17 nanograms per millilitre marked slower recoveries with high accuracy in early analysis. The authors suggest checking vitamin D when judging how severe cases are and planning rehabilitation for these patients.
pmc-13543546:
Xiaoya Chen and co-authors published a 2026 study tracing a three-protein chain behind age-related cataract, the clouding of the ageing lens. Death of lens epithelial cells is a central event, and the team compared cataract tissue with normal tissue and aged mice, then manipulated the proteins in cultured cells stressed with hydrogen peroxide. The proteins were DNMT3B, an enzyme that tags DNA, GJA3, a channel protein connecting cells, and the signalling enzyme GSK-3beta.

In cataract lenses DNMT3B ran high while GJA3 and the switched-off form of GSK-3beta ran low. Experiments showed the proteins regulate one another in sequence: GSK-3beta influences DNMT3B, which in turn controls GJA3, and together they steer cell death under oxidative stress. A green-tea compound, EGCG, eased the DNMT3B-driven cell death. The chain offers fresh drug targets for a condition now treatable only by surgery.
pmc-13547246:
Binoy Yohannan and a large team reviewed in 2026 the second blood cancers that arise after stem cell transplantation for multiple myeloma, a risk that grows as myeloma survival improves. Among 3,401 transplant patients treated at their institution between 1990 and 2022, 110 developed a second blood malignancy, most of them therapy-related myeloid neoplasms, with a smaller group developing lymphoblastic leukemia.

Such cancers became more common in the modern drug era than in earlier years. Mutations in the TP53 gene appeared in 40 percent of the myeloid cases, and certain drug exposures, including alkylator induction and lenalidomide maintenance, predicted higher risk. Patients who developed a second cancer survived less well overall. The authors urge monitoring and risk reduction as myeloma care extends lives.
pmc-13547346:
Olga Kędzia, Małgorzata Lubas, and Agata Dudek reported in 2026 the first part of a study on porous bone scaffolds. The scaffolds blend bioactive glass with recycled television screen glass and a bone mineral, hydroxyapatite. A foaming method created the pores, and four heating schedules were compared while the mineral share varied from 1.5 to 10 percent. The team mapped pore size and share, surface structure, and chemical phases.

Pores measured roughly 320 to 640 micrometers across, and the airiest samples, near 59 percent surface porosity, came from the highest temperature with the least mineral additive. More mineral shrank the pores. Microscopy showed a partly connected pore network, and chemical analyses confirmed glass phases plus strontium-bearing phases from the recycled glass. Mechanical and biological tests will follow in part two.
pmc-13548546:
Oğuzhan Karakaş and Gülce Gökgöz Özışık compare the eyes of people with amblyopia, often called lazy eye, against their fellow eyes and healthy eyes, in a 2026 imaging study. Whether the retina and its blood supply differ in amblyopic eyes has stayed unsettled. The pair used two scanning methods to measure layer thickness and vessel patterns in 65 patients and 65 control subjects.

The choroid, the layer beneath the retina, was thicker in both eyes of patients than in controls, and most macular measurements were thicker too. Some ganglion cell and nerve fiber sectors differed in either direction. Blood flow measures from angiography scans, however, showed no clear group differences, and one vessel index ran higher in controls. The authors conclude that amblyopia comes with structural differences in the back of the eye, while its microcirculation looks largely unchanged.
pmc-13548646:
Shining Cao and colleagues report one-year safety results for drug-eluting heart stents in a large Chinese registry, in a 2026 study. These stents prop open coronary arteries while releasing medicine, and Chinese outcome data at scale were thin. The registry covered 12,448 patients treated in three regions, about a quarter of whom had diabetes, comparing rates of a combined harm measure: heart-related death, heart attack, or a repeat procedure.

Under one percent of patients met that combined outcome within a year. Patients with diabetes ran a slightly higher crude rate, yet the difference was not statistically meaningful, and after adjustment diabetes showed no independent link to harm. The authors call the one-year results low and acceptable. They also warn that registry follow-up losses may hide events, so tighter tracking is needed, especially for older and sicker patients.
pmc-13549946:
Stijn De Schepper and colleagues read ancient DNA from Labrador Sea mud to track sea-ice effects on ocean life. Published in 2026, the study decoded tiny sea life groups across roughly 50,000 years. Today's Arctic ice is shrinking fast, yet how fully ocean ecosystems will answer remains unclear.

Warmer ice-free waters held higher variety than ice-covered waters, but group shifts lagged behind swift warmings 38,000 and 14,700 years ago. Surface ocean state, not air warming, steered group and variety patterns. The authors warn that further ice loss under global warming will likely remake sub-polar sea life sharply, with carbon-cycle and climate feedbacks to follow. Readers get a past-climate lens on the future Arctic.
pmc-13551946:

pmc-13554246:

pmc-13556046:

pmc-13558346:

pmc-13558646:

pmc-13560346:

pmc-13560746:

pmc-13569446:

pmc-13570146:

pmc-13570846:

pmc-13595746:

pmc-13596946:

pmc-13609746:
