Particles with the new ingredient produced nearly seven times more mRNA expression in the groin lymph node, the immune hub where responses are organised. Treated nodes swelled with immune cells, and vaccine effect rose with them. Sending the message and a brake release to the same address in one particle points toward cancer vaccines that work harder at lower doses.
pmc-13616346:
Ting Lu, Huangshui Ma, Mingquan Li, and Min Hong improve a heat-to-electricity material, germanium telluride, by doping it with both antimony and the rare earth lanthanum. The compound suits mid-to-high temperature waste-heat recovery, yet too many charge carriers and too little blocking of heat-carrying vibrations hold it back. Samples were made by melting, annealing, and hot pressing, then measured across scales.

Antimony trimmed the excess carrier count while keeping electric flow strong, which also cut the heat carried by electrons. Lanthanum stirred local strain and disorder into the crystal, scattering heat vibrations at several sizes at once. The pairing cut heat flow without hurting electric performance, lifting overall efficiency. Factories and engines throw off rivers of waste heat; materials tuned this way inch closer to harvesting it.
pmc-13617346:
Jennifer S Scholz and coauthors reviewed evidence on lentinan, a sugar compound drawn from shiitake mushrooms, for gut inflammation and gut cancer in a 2026 scoping review. Lentinan is used as an add-on cancer treatment in parts of Asia. It is credited with antioxidant and anti-tumor effects. Yet how it works and how best to use it remain unclear. The authors gathered preclinical and clinical studies on its effects in the gut and beyond.

Across studies, lentinan protected against colitis, gut injury from chemotherapy or immune suppression, infection models, and colorectal tumor growth. It acted through the gut lining, immune signaling, and gut microbes. It also interfered with cell death, self-cleaning, stem-like behavior, and blood vessel growth. It appeared to boost chemotherapy and CAR-T cell therapy while easing side effects and improving survival and well-being. Effects depended on size, dose, and route.
pmc-13618946:
Alp Özel and four colleagues run a randomized, double-blind trial of elastic therapeutic taping for pain after open-heart surgery through a breastbone incision. One hundred ninety-five elective bypass patients were assigned to real taping, placebo taping without tension, or sham taping elsewhere, applied once patients reached the ward. Pain at rest and while coughing was scored over forty-eight hours, alongside mobility, sleep, painkiller use, and hospital stay.

At forty-eight hours, resting pain in the taped group scored about nineteen on a hundred-point scale, against roughly thirty-eight for placebo and forty-one for sham. That gap exceeds the threshold patients can feel. Coughing pain also fell, tramadol use halved, and hospital stay shortened by about a day. Mobility test times and sleep quality also improved. The authors conclude the simple tape delivers real relief and speeds early recovery after sternotomy.
pmc-13619346:
Hiroki Wadati and Tetsuro Ueno ask whether two named patterns of ultrafast demagnetization can actually be told apart in real experiments. When a magnetic material is hit with a femtosecond laser pulse, its magnetism drops in either one step or two. Lab instruments blur the signal in time and add noise, so the two patterns can start to look alike.

Using computer-made datasets with varied blur and noise, the pair applied a Bayesian information criterion to judge which model fit better. Wide ranges of conditions left the choice statistically undecided. They also tested published data from nickel cobalt oxide films to show the method in action. Their warning is practical: a label given to a material's response may say more about the instrument and analysis choices than about the material itself.
pmc-13619446:
Hu and colleagues reported in 2026 a kagome metal that converts heat to electricity sideways, at room temperature and with no magnetic field, far more strongly than magnetic materials managed before. Kagome lattices, nets of corner-sharing triangles, host exotic electron states. Sideways, or transverse, thermoelectric devices suit curved heat sources, but the usual magnetic route gives weak output and stray fields that disturb nearby electronics.

The team used goniopolarity, where charge carriers switch sign with direction, in a lutetium-cobalt-germanium compound. Flat electron bands and sharp density peaks drove a transverse voltage of nearly twenty microvolts per kelvin. That is about triple the ceiling typical of magnetic systems, with matching strength in the reverse effect. The authors present goniopolar kagome metals as a new platform for waste-heat recovery and thermal control.
pmc-13620346:
Cécile Rousseau and colleagues reflect in a 2026 paper on how the Israel-Palestine conflict enters clinical care for young people in Quebec, Canada, during polarized times. Young people from many communities meet the conflict again at home, school, and online. Those encounters can shape trust in therapy, symptom patterns, and behavior in ways clinicians may miss. Drawing on clinical experience, the authors test cultural safety at three levels: the therapeutic alliance, symptom presentation, and acting out that may draw stigmatizing responses.

The paper argues for assessing the child within family, school, and community together. It also argues for naming distress and disagreement inside clinical and school teams rather than avoiding them. Silence, the authors warn, can itself harm, especially when institutional power already favors some narratives over others.
pmc-13620846:
Newton Nyirenda and nine colleagues examine how climate change is breaking rural primary healthcare in Zambia and what an equity-centered fix looks like. For most Zambians, a rural clinic is the front door to all care. The team synthesized national data, published studies, and regional cases, focusing on five pressure points: buildings, energy, water and sanitation, supply chains, and physical access.

Floods damage clinics while power and water failures shut services down. Broken supply chains leave shelves empty, and washed-out roads cut whole villages off during extreme weather. Women, children, and remote communities carry the heaviest burden from each failure. The authors argue climate adaptation must be written into health policy and district planning, not bolted on. Hardened rural clinics, they add, serve both climate readiness and the wider goal of universal coverage.
pmc-13621246:
Mehedi Hasan and nine colleagues screened wild plants growing in an industrial district of Bangladesh for species that can pull heavy metals out of polluted ground. Factories in Gazipur release lead, cadmium, chromium, and other metals that persist in soil and water. The team measured metals in soil and plant samples with atomic absorption instruments, then scored each plant by how much metal it gathered and how much it moved from roots to shoots.

One grass species moved nearly every metal upward with striking efficiency, a strong trait for harvesting contamination out of a site. Two other species concentrated lead heavily, one in its tissues and one by transport, while a chickweed gathered chromium best. Two more plants took up cadmium readily. The authors present the winners as candidates for planted cleanup schemes matched to each site's metal mix.
pmc-13621346:
Elham Khodaei and Amirali Abbasi built a reusable electrocatalyst that turns sulfides into sulfoxides, building blocks prized in medicines such as stomach acid blockers. Their design anchors a copper complex firmly onto graphene oxide sheets, a carbon support, using a chemical coupling step. Anchoring stops the metal from washing away while the support speeds charge movement.

A battery of structural checks, from X-ray crystallography of the copper site's exact geometry to electron microscopy, confirmed the hybrid's build. Run with hydrogen peroxide as a gentle oxidant in ethanol, the system reached full conversion with total selectivity in just over a minute. It then survived six reuse cycles with no detectable metal loss and a very high turnover count. The authors pitch the pairing of molecular precision with industrial toughness as a blueprint for greener chemical manufacturing.
pmc-13622346:
Qilong Wu and colleagues report a 2026 battery study aimed at making aqueous zinc-bromine batteries practical for storing power on the grid. These batteries are cheap and safe because they use water-based fluid, but a wandering bromine compound, called polybromide, leaks across the cell and shortens battery life. The team tackles the leak at two places at once.

Inside the carbon cathode, tiny charged pores trap the polybromide where it forms, blocking its drift. A second additive settles on the cathode surface and, during discharge, gathers into a layer that pulls stray polybromide back for reuse. Cells built this way cycled more than a thousand times at a very high capacity for their size. Larger pouch cells, at the ampere-hour scale, also ran steadily at room temperature and below freezing. The authors present the design as a step toward cheap storage for wind and solar power.
pmc-13624046:
Aline Weis and colleagues published a German-language ethics analysis asking whether steering patients through the health system clashes with patient autonomy. German reform debates promote steering tools, such as requiring a family doctor as the first port of call, to cut waste and guide people through a tangled system. Critics fear lost freedom of choice.

The authors use a wider idea of autonomy than mere absence of pressure: it also means being equipped to decide well, through clear information and support. Judged that way, formal freedom alone often fails patients, who can hold a legal right to choose yet lack the guidance to use it. Steering that structures choices can therefore serve autonomy rather than threaten it. For judging any scheme, they set three tests: it must keep value-based choices open, it must support proven and coordinated care, and it must share scarce resources fairly and openly.
pmc-13624546:
Ping Ni and fellow researchers ask whether losing both hearing and sight raises the risk of low mood in later life. They pooled three long-running aging studies from China, the United States, and England, covering 19,310 people in total. Mood was scored on a standard depression scale, and dual sensory loss meant reported trouble with both senses at once.

Across all three countries, people with both losses had higher odds of depressive symptoms, and a pooled review of earlier work agreed. Part of the link ran through two paths: people joined in less social activity, and their thinking skills scored lower. Supporting social ties and cognition, the authors suggest, may soften the mood cost of losing two senses.
pmc-13625446:
Manli Zhou and Sisi Feng, publishing in 2026, build a machine learning tool that flags kidney damage risk in multiple myeloma. Kidney impairment is a common, life-shortening complication of this bone marrow cancer, and catching it early changes care. At one center they gathered 1,029 patients, trained eight algorithms on 792 of them, and held back 237 patients from a later period to test the winner honestly.

A boosted-tree method, XGBoost, won, and their final tool, RI-Lab6, needs only six routine lab values, from inflammation and blood counts to calcium and a cancer marker protein. It sorted patients with and without kidney damage almost perfectly in training and nearly as well in the later test group. Such a cheap score could prompt earlier kidney checks in busy clinics.
pmc-13631246:
Ludmila Kasatkina and colleagues ran Ukraine's first country-wide survey of drug-proof germs in combat wounds. War damage, wrecked hospitals, flight, and broken hygiene fed drug-proof germs, yet national data were missing. Their 2023 to 2024 survey mapped drug-proof ESKAPE germs from combat wounds, checking about 1,000 multi-drug samples centrally.

About 60 percent of checked Klebsiella pneumoniae carried enzymes granting near-total beta-lactam proof. The survey, built on 40,823 strains with 18,848 flagged for study, confirms ward-caught drug-proof germs spreading under wartime strain. The authors demand joined-up drug rules and infection control fitted to war.
pmc-13633546:
Nujud Alamry and seven colleagues tested mouthwash ingredients against a germ that drives gum disease. The germ, Porphyromonas gingivalis, hides below the gumline and fuels the chronic swelling that destroys tooth support. The team grew it in the lab and challenged it with ten preparations. They tried the standard antiseptic chlorhexidine alone, a germ-killing drug, pomegranate extract, turmeric extracts, and several mixes, watching the clear zones where growth stopped.

Chlorhexidine paired with metronidazole produced the widest clear zone of all. Pomegranate extract alone ranked next among single agents, beating chlorhexidine by itself. Turmeric extracts, the antibiotic alone, and plain water produced no measurable zone at all. Pairings of chlorhexidine with the plant extracts landed in between. The results, from dishes rather than mouths, suggest pomegranate deserves testing in real patients as a partner rinse.
pmc-13638046:
Chanakan Suwanbongkot and five colleagues track what happens in the skin during a single feeding by a tick carrying spotted fever bacteria. Rickettsia parkeri, spread by the Gulf Coast tick, enters through skin, yet most research bypassed the tick itself by injecting bacteria with needles. The team built a one-tick feeding model in mice, sampling from one hour after attachment to six days, and profiling bacteria, immune cells, signaling molecules, and tissue damage.

Transmission was fast: bacteria reached the mouse within the first hour and spread quickly to lymph nodes and internal tissues. Delivered dose climbed steadily across the feeding period. Inflammation at the bite looked similar early on whether the tick was infected or not. By the late stage, infected skin shifted character, dominated by macrophages with stronger inflammatory signals and weaker calming ones. The authors read this as delayed immune activation at the true portal of entry.
pmc-13641046:
Glenn Gaston and five colleagues present a multicenter matched cohort study comparing two ways to bridge cut nerves in the arm. Surgeons can graft a patient's own nerve, which creates a second wound, or use a processed donor nerve graft instead.

The study matched twenty-four patients with twenty-five own-nerve repairs against twenty-three patients with twenty-five donor graft repairs for mixed and motor nerve injuries. Meaningful motor recovery was at least as common with donor grafts, and strong recovery was more frequent in that group. The authors support donor grafts as a reasonable alternative that avoids harvest-site problems.
pmc-13643446:
Subhasish Deb, Soumya Patra, Jayanta Roy, and Sujoy Das Thakur present a case report, published in 2026. It describes one 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis. She developed severe chest pain minutes after receiving iodinated contrast dye. The dye was for a chest scan. Her heart tracing showed ST-segment elevation. This is the classic heart attack pattern. Its distribution is named the South African flag sign by the authors.

Emergency angiography found no blocked artery. The tracing changes resolved rapidly. Blood tests and heart imaging showed a small area of heart injury. The timing supported type I Kounis syndrome. This is an allergic spasm of the heart arteries. Urgent angiography is still essential, the authors stress. A real blockage cannot be excluded without it.
pmc-13645746:
Shiqi Yang and seven colleagues investigate which sulfur compounds give soy sauce flavor baijiu, a Chinese liquor, its signature savory depth, in a 2026 study. Sulfur compounds are potent in tiny amounts, and their role in this liquor style was not well mapped. The team used advanced separation tools to catalogue the compounds. Machine learning then helped pick the ones that matter most.

Eighty-eight sulfur compounds were identified, and eight core ones were singled out by the combined analysis. Adding those eight back into the liquor clearly strengthened its two hallmark aroma notes. The effect depended on the liquor's age: in young liquor the boost spread to floral and fruity notes, while in aged liquor it focused on the core savory notes. The work gives distillers a clearer recipe-level grip on a prized flavor.
pmc-13646146:
Nargis Kaur Bali and five colleagues sequence the genomes of drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteria collected at a large hospital in North India from 2022 to 2024. This germ is a major cause of hospital infections and a driver of antibiotic resistance. Ninety-six samples underwent drug testing and whole-genome sequencing, with ninety genomes passing quality checks. The team mapped types, resistance genes, and family relationships.

Nearly every isolate resisted carbapenem drugs, the usual last line. One lineage and one capsule type dominated, and a resistance gene called blaOXA-232 appeared in three quarters of genomes. Eighty-two resistance genes spanning sixteen drug classes were found in all, alongside deep variety in the wider gene pool. No copies of two notorious virulence boosters appeared. The authors say this genomic portrait can guide infection control and treatment choices in the region.
pmc-13647746:
Bo Sun and eight colleagues build a skill list for lead investigators running novel drug trials in China, where trials have grown too complex for basic rules. Their multiphase study began with literature review and expert interviews that produced sixty-four candidate indicators. Two Delphi rounds, with a partly refreshed panel that added regulators, then compressed the list through content analysis. Agreement scores were tracked throughout.

The result is an early inventory of thirty skills, sorted into three bands by how tightly the experts agreed. Only four items reached high consensus, while seven remained divisive, a spread the authors report honestly rather than papering over. They stress the bands describe rating spread, not a ranking of importance or a training ladder. The framework is offered as a context-sensitive starting point for developing trial leads inside China's own setting.
pmc-13648146:
Ganguk Lee and three colleagues validate, in a 2026 study, two very short scales for measuring loneliness at work in Korea. Long questionnaires are impractical in large workforce surveys, so the team tested a single-item scale and a three-item scale, called SLAW-1 and SLAW-3.

A nationwide online survey of one thousand employees, with two hundred retested after four weeks, supplied the data. The three-item scale showed good internal consistency and a single-factor structure, while the single item proved moderately stable over time. Both scales related to stress, distress, engagement, and well-being in expected directions. The authors recommend the single item for rapid screening and the three-item version for fuller workplace assessment.
pmc-13648446:
Iasmim Lopes de Lima and six colleagues built a sorter for the immune paths breast tumours take during chemo. Chemo can wake the immune system to fight the tumour, a shift they call chemoimmunomodulation. It can also push the tumour into a stress mode that shuts immune cells out. No shared tool split these paths before.

Their tool reads gene shifts from before and after chemo in two patient sets and nine cell lines. Two paths stood out. The good path lit up fiery cell death, antigen display, and immune attack. The bad path lit up stress and repair, with fewer immune cells. In two large cohorts, start scores for the good path meant better odds, and bad-path scores meant worse odds.
pmc-13649446:
Weiwei Qian and two colleagues tracked how stroke patients' sense of their own risk of a second stroke changed over six months at home. How people view that risk may shape how well they recover. The team enrolled 240 patients in Nantong, China, and scored their risk views at discharge and at one, three, and six months.

Four paths emerged, from steady low concern to risk views that rose late. The late-rising group fared worst: more trouble with daily function, worse nerve scores, and lower quality of life at six months. That group also had the most repeat strokes, though such events were few. Steady or easing risk views showed no clear harm. The authors suggest watching risk views over time to spot patients who need more support.
pmc-13649646:
Cain and colleagues studied in 2026 how the body clock in airway club cells controls immune cell traffic in allergic asthma. Asthma symptoms swing across the day, and earlier work showed the molecular clock gates responses to allergens in mice. The team used mice whose club cells lacked a working clock gene, Bmal1, under chronic allergic inflammation.

In normal mice, eosinophils and helper T cells entered the lung in daily patterns tied to the clock. In clock-deficient mice those daily patterns in cell traffic were abolished. Airway barrier leakiness, which normally varies by time of day, also became flat, equally open at all hours. The authors link the club cell clock to both barrier control and immune timing in type-2 inflammation.
pmc-13649746:
Zewen Song and three colleagues set out a trial plan for stage three lung cancer that cannot be cut out. Standard care pairs chemo with radiation, then adds immune therapy, yet many patients never reach the last step. Their plan tests whether starting with immune therapy, a vessel-blocking drug, and chemo can shrink disease first and raise the odds of full care.

The trial aims to enrol 152 patients at many centres, split by chance into two arms. One arm gets two rounds of the lead-in trio, then chemo-radiation, then a year of immune therapy. The other arm skips the lead-in. The main measure is time with no disease growth. This is a protocol paper, so no results are reported yet.
pmc-13650546:
Adrianna Banach-Kopeć and five colleagues review chitosan, a sugar-based polymer from shells and fungi, as a building material for regenerative medicine. Its charge, solubility, and breakdown rate can all be tuned, which makes it attractive for scaffolds, gels, coatings, and printing inks meant to help tissue regrow.

That tunability is also the problem: products all sold as chitosan differ widely in chemistry, purity, contamination, and sterilization history, so results rarely transfer cleanly. The authors walk through sources, extraction routes, medical-grade purity demands, germ-fighting behavior, and combinations with growth factors, drugs, cells, and cell-derived vesicles. Their verdict is that chitosan is neither automatically body-friendly nor automatically germ-killing; performance depends on the exact formulation and use. They call for standardized reporting of key chemical measures and manufacturing that regulators can actually verify.
pmc-13651646:
Md Zakiul Hassan and colleagues warn in a 2026 correspondence that Bangladesh faces one of its largest measles resurgences. By May 2026 it had 49,159 suspected cases, 6,819 confirmed cases, and 336 deaths. The resurgence reverses long-standing immunization gains and reflects sustained community transmission. Routine vaccination gives measles-rubella doses at nine and fifteen months, yet many cases strike infants under six months, too young for vaccination, pointing to a widening immunity gap.

Coverage has reportedly fallen as low as 57 percent in some reports. No nationwide campaign has run since 2020, pandemic disruptions broke catch-up work, a planned 2024 campaign fell to political unrest, and procurement delays stalled a 2025 campaign. All this comes as the country shifts toward domestic immunization financing. The government has targeted campaigns at children six to fifty-nine months in high-risk districts, with expanded hospital support including low-cost bubble CPAP.
pmc-13651846:
Huan Ting Ong and thirty-nine colleagues, an international working group of reproductive biologists and ontology experts, standardize the names of cell types in the female reproductive tract. Single-cell and spatial studies of ovary, fallopian tube, and uterus have exploded, yet every laboratory labels cells differently, which blocks comparison across datasets.

Their harmonized terms enter the Cell Ontology with definitions for the major epithelial, stromal, and germ cell populations. Each term is backed by marker gene sets and links to the anatomy they inhabit. Egg cells, their supporting granulosa and theca layers, the hormone-making luteal cells, and the tract's epithelial, stromal, and immune residents all receive consistent classifications usable across the three tissues. The authors offer the framework as shared infrastructure: existing datasets can be re-annotated onto it, and future studies can label cells comparably from the start.
pmc-13672046:
Holly M. Poling led a 2026 study presenting a confined culture system that grows large human gut tissues with nerves for transplant, overcoming two limits of current organoids. Existing gut organoids mature incompletely and need complex assembly steps to add a functional nervous system. The team used a 3D-printed tray to restrict fusion of cell balls and growth, letting small gut, colon, and stomach tissues develop a new gut nervous system on their own.

Gene activity and electrical recordings showed selective nerve-muscle function with both activating and calming neurons present. Compared with traditional methods, the system sped maturation and produced tissues up to ten times larger, reaching eight centimeters wide after ten weeks, with better graft take. Transplanted tissues joined mouse gut while keeping barrier integrity and function. Transplant researchers get a simpler, faster route to useful gut tissues, with human testing still ahead.
pmc-2206446:
Mehta, Kellum, Shah, and co-authors report the work of the Acute Kidney Injury Network. Acute kidney injury is a complex, sudden loss of kidney function. At the time, the field had no accepted shared definition of the condition, which held back care and research.

The network sought a uniform standard for diagnosing and grading kidney injury. Common terms would let doctors manage patients more consistently and let researchers compare studies across hospitals. The report lays out an initiative for joint clinical and lab research aimed at improving outcomes for a common and dangerous problem.
pmc-3760646:
Witwer, Buzas, Bemis, and co-authors argue for standardisation in extracellular vesicle research. Publications on extracellular RNA and vesicles had highlighted their potential as disease biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Those findings created a paradigm shift, most prominently in cancer and diagnostics.

Yet labs collected, isolated, and analysed samples in very different ways, so results clashed. The authors propose shared standards for each step. Common methods would let the young field compare results honestly and speed the move of vesicle tests into clinics.  Funding for shared standards work followed, reflecting how seriously the field took it.
pmc-3995046:
Lopez-Calderon and Luck presented ERPLAB in 2014, a free toolbox for brain signal research. It works with event-related potentials, small voltage changes in the scalp signal that follow a sight, sound, or task. ERPLAB runs inside MATLAB and is built to work closely with EEGLAB, a widely used open toolbox.

ERPLAB handles the later steps of work, such as sorting trials, averaging signals, and measuring peaks and timing. Its screens let users run these steps without writing much code. Brain labs use it to study attention, memory, and language, with a shared tool that makes results easier to check and repeat.
pmc-4310146:
Methley, Campbell, Chew-Graham, and their co-authors compared search tools for qualitative reviews in 2014. Systematic reviews of qualitative research were growing in health care. Many teams reported trouble searching the literature with PICO, a tool built for clinical questions.

A newer tool, SPIDER, was designed for qualitative and mixed methods studies. The study compared PICO, its variant PICOS, and SPIDER for sensitivity and specificity in real searches. Knowing which tool finds the right papers without floods of junk saves reviewers weeks of work. The findings guide teams planning reviews of patient experience and other qualitative topics.
pmc-6259146:
Jin Dai and Russell Mumper reviewed plant phenolics in 2010. Phenolics are the most common secondary compounds made by plants. They drew attention for strong antioxidant action and possible roles in preventing disease.

The review covers how phenolics are extracted from plant material and measured in the lab. It then surveys evidence that they can slow oxidation and, in cell and animal studies, hinder cancer growth. Human proof was thinner at the time, and dose and absorption remain hard problems. Food and supplement researchers still use it as a broad survey of the field.
pmc-6323946:
Adam Frankish, Mark Diekhans, Anne-Maud Ferreira, and coauthors described GENCODE annotation for human and mouse in 2018. Accurate gene maps are a basic need for genome biology and clinical work. For over fifteen years the GENCODE group has produced reference annotation.

Their process blends computer prediction with human review to place genes and transcripts. Each release refines boundaries and adds newly found transcripts, including long non-coding RNAs. Most human genome studies align their results to GENCODE coordinates. The paper explains methods and quality checks so users know what the map rests on.
pretiosa-margarita-novella-de-thesavro-a:
Venice printers in 1546 issued this Latin alchemical treasury, the Pretiosa Margarita Novella, on the treasure and most precious stone of the philosophers, issued under a ten-year privilege from the Venetian Senate. The title page, preserved in the Wellcome Trust copy, announces the method: the art's types and method collected from Arnold of Villanova. Raymond Lull, Albertus Magnus, and Michael Scotus, and set in order by Janus Lacinius, now first published with an index. A preface by Pierius Roseus addresses the candid reader.

Behind the compilation stands the Margarita Pretiosa of Petrus Bonus, a fourteenth-century argument that alchemy is a true science with true authorities. The compilation dresses that argument for the Renaissance press, with its choir of named masters. The book is a landmark of printed alchemy: part anthology, part brief for the philosophers' stone, issued when alchemy and the new science still shared a cradle.
project-trinity-1945-1946:
Carl Maag and Steve Rohrer wrote an official history of the first atomic bomb test for the Defense Nuclear Agency, as part of a review of nuclear test staff. The report has since been declassified and covers the work of 1945 and 1946.

Chapters describe the Trinity site in New Mexico, the groups that ran the project, and the men and women who took part. Later sections cover work before the shot, the blast of July 16, 1945, and duties after that date. Readers get names, duties, and radiation-era records in one file.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave: Slave Narratives, a folk history of slavery in the United States from talks with former slaves, rests on typed records made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938. The Library of Congress project put the set together under the Work Projects Administration for the District of Columbia, with the Library of Congress as sponsor. One plate shows Uncle Willie, Uncle Sam, Uncle Charlie, Squire Sabagen, and Uncle Hick, grouped under the title The Old South.
state-of-the-union-addresses-pg5046:
Ronald Reagan gives seven yearly addresses in one set. Their dates run from January 26, 1982, to January 25, 1988. Three stars part each address from the next. The first marks his first such address to Congress. The duty is as old as the republic itself. Washington began the custom in 1790, Reagan notes. Washington warned of the sacred fire of liberty then. Its keeping rests on the trial in the people's hands.

Reagan adds a jest for the press at that point. He did not in fact hear Washington say it. The words are a matter of record, he grants. From this same stand, Churchill called the free world to stand as one. Roosevelt spoke of a day of infamy from it. MacArthur made his famed farewell in this chamber. Eisenhower taught that peace is bought at the price of strength. Kennedy spoke of the weight and glory of freedom here.
strauss-life-of-jesus-eliot-1846:
David Friedrich Strauss's Life of Jesus Critically Examined appeared in English in 1846, translated by Marian Evans, later George Eliot. The translation was her first book-length work. Strauss, a German theologian, had caused a storm in 1835 by reading the gospel miracles as myth, not history.

Strauss went through the life of Jesus scene by scene, testing each miracle against history and natural law. He argued that early Christians clothed Jesus in the myths their faith expected. German churchmen lost posts over the debate his book began. In English, the translation launched the Victorian crisis of faith, and it pushed its young translator toward the novels that made her famous.
summary-of-the-rosary-1546:
The Summary of the Rosary gathers extracts made by Giovanni Lacinius from the Rosarius of Arnold de Villa Nova, printed within his Pretiosa margarita novella at Venice in 1546. A head note adds that the text plainly shaped the Rosarium philosophorum of 1550, a cornerstone of later alchemy.

Lacinius arranges Arnold's remarks in chapters as a practical treatise on the Philosophers' Stone, holding that practice and theory correct each other. The first chapter argues there is one stone, one essence, and one method in the red and white medicines, the red being a further growth of the white. Later chapters ask where the stone is extracted from, and name the finding of the first matter of metals as the work's chief difficulty.
synopsis-of-phrenology-and-physiology-co: Only the opening leaves are present here. They give a title heading for a Synopsis of Phrenology and Physiology by L. N. Fowler. A catalogue of Fowler and Wells, No. 131 Nassau Street, New York, follows. It lists the firm's books for sale. Among them is Fowler's Phrenology in its thirtieth edition at one dollar. A two-in-one volume on education and self-improvement stands beside it. That volume covers physiology, health, and the training of children. No text of the synopsis itself appears in these pages.
the-constitution-of-japan-1946:
Japan's 1946 constitution was made public on November 3, 1946, and took effect on May 3, 1947. Its preamble speaks in the name of the Japanese people, acting through their elected members of the National Diet. It states that ruling power rests with the people and that government is a trust held from them.

The people pledge never again to suffer the horrors of war through the acts of government. They say they want lasting peace, trust the fair dealing of peace-loving nations, and hold that all peoples may live free from fear and want. Chapter I then takes up the emperor, making him a symbol of the state and of the people's unity, his place drawn from the people's will.
the-great-round-world-and-what-is-going-:
For September 23, 1897, The Great Round World and What Is Going On in It reaches its forty-sixth number. The paper is a weekly newspaper for boys and girls. Its lead item brings heartening news from India. London means to punish the tribes in revolt, and will send troops in strength to do it. Word comes that the Afridis have met in war council. They resolved to go back home and bring in their crops.

The paper then tells how the rising fell apart. Haddah Mullah, the priest blamed for stirring the tribes up, has yielded. He had called men out to strike at Peshawar, a strong British post, and ordered the Mohmands to join his march. At the meeting-place he found only a messenger waiting: the Mohmands would take no part in the revolt. The Mullah, disheartened, sent his Swati followers home.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
Number 394 of the Mirror, dated Saturday, October 17, 1829, illustrates Lord Grosvenor's gallery in Park Lane. The magazine recalls opening Volume 12 with the earl's Eaton Hall and his public-spirited patronage of the fine arts. The gallery forms the western wing of his spacious town mansion. Mr. Cundy designed it as a colonnade of the Corinthian order raised on a plain stylobate.

An isolated statue stands over each column, with an attic behind them after Palladio's Forum of Trajan. Vases crown the acroteria along a balustrade, and blank windows with balconies and triangular pediments fill between the columns. Mr. Elmes thinks those stopped-up windows disfigure the grand design, and the balustrade overpowers the statues. Even with these remedy-able drawbacks, he grants the building ranks near the metropolis's first class. Readers watch a private gallery judged like a public monument.

The Mirror's number for Saturday, November 21, 1829, No. 400, illustrates the Limoeiro, Lisbon's common jail. Locks, bolts, and bars open the piece, whose horrors the editors promise to describe lightly, in outline only. Their authority is Mr. W. Young, an Englishman who married a Portuguese lady at Leiria. In May 1828 he was arrested, suspected of disaffection toward Don Miguel's government.

Nothing was proved against Young, yet he suffered in jails at Leiria and Lisbon before his September discharge, granted on condition he leave the country. Back in England he promptly published Portugal in 1828, a narrative of his persecution and confinement. The prison stands on the highest ground of St. George's Castle, first on the south side toward the Tagus. Its internal divisions begin with the Saletta and the Salla Livre. Readers get prison reporting sourced from a man who ate its hard fare.
tob-0146:
A. P. Sinnett, editor and Theosophist in India, published letters he said came from hidden masters, Morya and Koot Hoomi. The Mahatma Letters, with Blavatsky as the claimed channel, instructed the young movement on the deep structure of things. Followers and skeptics have fought over their origin ever since.

The letters treat cosmic cycles, the afterlife, and the laws that govern adepts and chelas. Sinnett built his books on their teaching. Whether dictated by mahatmas or written nearer home, the letters shaped Theosophy more than any other papers. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry.
tob-10346:
Early Christian Gnostics of the Sethian school treasured the Apocryphon of John, a secret book in which the risen Christ teaches the apostle John. A copy survived among the Nag Hammadi books found in Egypt in 1945. Shorter forms of the same work also survive.

Christ tells how the highest God stands beyond all names, how Sophia fell, and how a lesser maker, Yaldabaoth, built this flawed world with his archons. The account then retells Genesis from that angle. No Gnostic text explains the Sethian system more fully, which is why scholars return to it first.
tob-13146:
Albert G. Mackey, an American physician and leading Masonic scholar, wrote a full History of Freemasonry in the nineteenth century. Mackey's encyclopedia and law books made him the craft's chief American authority. His history long stood as the standard work on the subject.

Mackey traces Masonry from its claimed ancient roots through the medieval building guilds to the modern lodges. He sifts legend from record, explains the degrees and symbols, and defends the order's principles. Masons and historians alike used his volumes for a century, and the work still frames how the fraternity tells its own past.
tob-4046:
Plutarch's Morals, the Moralia, collect the essays that stand behind his famous Lives. Written around 100 AD, the essays treat practical philosophy for educated readers: superstition, tranquility of mind, talkativeness, and how a young man should listen to lectures all receive warm, sensible treatment. Plutarch chats where other philosophers lecture.

Vegetarian arguments in On the Eating of Flesh, consolation letters, table talk, and advice on health and marriage broaden the range. Charming and quotable, Plutarch here resembles the ancient world's best advice columnist, learned without heaviness. Readers who know only the biographies will find the essayist equally companionable, and often more personally useful.
tob-4146:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli translated the Mahabharata into English prose in the 1880s and 1890s, the first complete rendering of the Sanskrit epic. The Mahabharata, ascribed to the sage Vyasa, is the longest poem in the world. Ganguli worked for over a decade with the support of Indian patrons.

The epic tells of the Bharata princes, the dice game that exiles the Pandavas, and the great war at Kurukshetra that destroys a generation. At its heart stands the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna's counsel to Arjuna. Ganguli's plain, full translation carried the whole vast story to English readers and remains the only complete one of its age.
un-ga-res-46:
Rebuilding the lands smashed by war was the great task facing the world in 1946. Resolution 46 of the General Assembly, passed on 11 December 1946, takes note of a first report on the rebuilding of devastated areas. It backs the plans of the Economic and Social Council. Those plans call for a survey of rebuilding needs in Asia and the Far East, and for study work in Europe to keep going.

All who can help are urged to act. Member states, the council, aid bodies, and world agencies should take every step in their power toward swift fixes. The Assembly also directs a word to the new World Bank: swift loans for rebuilding would serve the common good.
un-ga-res-a-69-46: Trust built close to home is the theme of Resolution A/69/46, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The vote recalls a chain of Assembly texts since 2003 on trust-building steps at the level of regions and sub-regions. It also recalls the 2003 call for states to settle their rows by peaceful means, as the Charter's sixth chapter sets out. Such steps, the Assembly has long held, work best when states craft them for their own ground.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 46, adopted on 11 December 1946, pushed the rebuilding of areas wrecked by war. The Assembly backed the Economic and Social Council's plans. Among them were studies of rebuilding in Europe and in Asia and the Far East. It urged members, councils, and agencies to do all they could toward a fast fix.

The text tells the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, through the Secretary-General, that it should reach full working order at the earliest date. That way it could lend for rebuilding early in 1947. It also backs a survey of raw material needs. It backs early thought to setting up economic commissions for Europe and for Asia and the Far East.

Resolution 69/46 of the General Assembly promotes confidence-building measures between neighboring states. It reaffirms the Charter's rules against the use or threat of force and for settling disputes peacefully. It restates the methods for confidence- and security-building set out by the Disarmament Commission in 1993. Member states are called on to pursue those methods through sustained talks and dialogue. They are called on to comply strictly with their arms agreements. They are called on to build bilateral and regional measures. Those measures prevent conflict and accidental outbreaks of fighting.
un-sc-res-1046: Entered in the record as Resolution 1046, this Security Council text is catalogued at 1996. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-1346:
UNAMSIL was enlarged to its peak strength on 30 March 2001. Fighting still burned along the borders with Guinea and Liberia, and its human toll was grave. The Secretary-General's report of 14 March set out a revised concept of operations. The Abuja ceasefire of November 2000 was being breached, and reports of abuses by the Revolutionary United Front troubled the Council.

The Council extended UNAMSIL's mandate for six months. It raised the mission's military strength to 17,500, counting the 260 military observers already in place. The new concept of operations was welcomed. Troop-giving states won thanks for the added soldiers and support. The Secretary-General had to report at regular times on the mission's progress with the core parts of its work. Deep concern was voiced at the RUF's abuses and at its breaches of the ceasefire. The bigger force was meant to hold the peace while disarmament finally began.
un-sc-res-1446: Entry number 1446 in the Council's official sequence is a resolution the catalog dates to 2002. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations. It sits in this library among other public records in the DECLASSIFIED group.
un-sc-res-146:
Belgium's troops in Katanga defied the Council in the summer of 1960. The Congo's richest province had broken away with Belgian support. On 9 August 1960 the Council confirmed the Secretary-General's authority under its July resolutions. It then called on Belgium to pull its troops out of Katanga at once. The pace and manner of the withdrawal were for the Secretary-General to settle. Belgium also had to help carry out the Council's decisions in every way.

The entry of the United Nations Force into Katanga, the Council declared, was necessary. At the same time, that force could not take sides in Congo's internal fights. It could not be used to sway any conflict's outcome. That line shaped the mission's hardest years.
un-sc-res-1546:
On the Council's agenda, Iraq drew Resolution 1546, adopted unanimously on 8 June 2004. The occupation authority was about to hand power to a sovereign interim government. That handover was set for 30 June 2004. Baghdad had asked the multinational force to stay on.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council endorses the interim government and the timetable that follows. Elections to a transitional assembly are due by January 2005. A permanent constitution and an elected government are to follow by the end of 2005. The force may take all necessary measures to keep security, working in partnership with Baghdad. The UN mission will lead on election advice and national dialogue.
un-sc-res-1646:
A new Peacebuilding Commission was taking shape at the end of 2005. Resolution 1645 had created it that same day, 20 December 2005. This companion text settled the Security Council's seats on its steering body. The Council decided that all five permanent members would sit on the Organizational Committee. Two elected Council members would join them each year. The Council would pick those two annually.

The Commission's yearly report would also go to the Council. The Council would hold an annual debate on it. The body was meant to help countries recover after war. Its steering committee mixed Council, Assembly, and other members. This resolution fixed the Council's share of that mix.
un-sc-res-1746: Resolution 1746, adopted in 2007, is a formal Security Council act kept here in its record text via English Wikisource. Fifteen delegations voted the words that follow in the full document; ten rotating members join the five permanent ones. The entry preserves their joint product whole, ready for citation as S/RES/1746 in UN usage.
un-sc-res-1846:
Piracy off Somalia occupied the Council on 2 December 2008, when it adopted Resolution 1846 on Piracy off Somalia. Growing ransom payments were fueling more attacks. Somalia's government could not patrol its own waters or guard the sea lanes. Many states and the European Union had sent warships to escort food aid convoys.

The Council renews the anti-piracy powers for twelve more months. States working with Somalia's government may enter its waters to stop piracy. They may use all necessary means there, as the law of the sea allows on the high seas. Pirate boats and gear may be seized. States should share news of attacks, help coastal states build patrol strength, and work together on trials for captured pirates.
un-sc-res-1946:
Côte d'Ivoire's sanctions were renewed on 15 October 2010, weeks before a long-delayed presidential vote. The voters list had been certified, and the first round was set for 31 October 2010 under the Ouagadougou Political Agreement. The Council noted the expert group's reports on the arms embargo. It also recorded continuing abuses against civilians, including sexual violence, despite a better overall human rights picture.

The Council renewed the arms, finance, and travel measures of resolution 1572 (2004) and the diamond ban of resolution 1643 (2005) to 30 April 2011. It promised a review tied to progress in the elections and the peace process. Ivorian parties and all states had to apply the measures in full and give inspectors free access. The Council underlined that it was ready to impose targeted measures on persons named by its committee. It also flagged media reports inciting violence and a return to civil war.
un-sc-res-246:
South Africa's trial of South West African detainees drew censure from the Security Council on 14 March 1968. Resolution 245 (1968) had ordered Pretoria to stop the illegal trial and free the men. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966 and taken direct responsibility for it. South Africa refused to comply and went on with the trial and sentencing.

The Council censured South Africa for flagrant defiance of resolution 245 and of the United Nations itself. It demanded that the South West Africans be released and sent home at once. Member states were called to help the Council give the resolution effect. The Council warned it would meet again to weigh further steps if South Africa still refused. The text treats the trial as an illegal act against people under direct United Nations responsibility.
un-sc-res-346: Resolution 346 stands in the official record of the United Nations Security Council, catalogued here with a 1974 date. Such texts can call for cease-fires, set up missions, impose duties, or settle points of UN procedure and membership. Its value lies in the primary wording: the decision as adopted, kept through the Wikisource transcription of the record. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-446:
Israeli settlements are the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 446, adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none, with three abstentions. Jordan had brought the matter to the Council. Building had spread across land taken in the 1967 war, including Jerusalem. The Council saw the growth of settlements as a block to peace.

The Council holds that the settlement policy and practice have no legal validity. It says the Fourth Geneva Convention of 1949 covers the occupied Arab lands. Israel must undo past steps and change nothing in the lands' status or makeup. Moving its own civilians into those lands must stop. A three-member panel will study the settlements and report by 1 July 1979.
un-sc-res-46:
Fighting between Arabs and Jews in Palestine brought a truce call from the Security Council on 17 April 1948. Resolution 43 (1948) had opened talks with the Jewish Agency and the Arab Higher Committee. Britain, as the Mandatory Power, still bore responsibility for peace and order. The Council said an immediate halt to the violence was of the utmost urgency.

The Council called on all persons and groups in Palestine to cease military and paramilitary action, violence, terrorism, and sabotage. No armed bands or fighters were to enter Palestine, and no weapons were to be brought in or bought. Both sides had to avoid political acts that might prejudice the other community's claims while the General Assembly weighed Palestine's future government. They were told to cooperate with the Mandatory authorities on law, order, transport, health, and food and water supplies, and to keep the Holy Places safe and open.
un-sc-res-746:
Somalia's famine and fighting drew the Security Council's first steps toward intervention on 17 March 1992. Cease-fire agreements had been signed at Mogadishu on 3 March, with a United Nations monitoring mission in view. The factions had not kept the truce, and aid still could not reach people in need. The Secretary-General had reported on 11 March on the scale of the suffering.

The Council urged the Somali factions to honor the Mogadishu cease-fire at once. All factions were told to work with the Secretary-General and clear the way for aid delivery. He was asked to press his humanitarian effort with every resource he had. Member states and aid groups were appealed to for contributions. The Council backed his decision to send a technical team to Somalia at once. The team would also plan safe aid delivery. All parties had to protect aid staff.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci: Security Council resolution 1046, adopted on 13 February 1996, adjusts UNPREDEP, the United Nations Preventive Deployment Force in the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia. Its mandate ran to 30 May 1996. The Council authorizes 50 more military personnel, so the force can keep its engineering work going. It backs the creation of a Force Commander position. It asks the Secretary-General for fresh advice on the makeup, strength and mandate by 20 May 1996.

Sierra Leone's fragile ceasefire frames Resolution 1346, adopted on 30 March 2001. Fighting ran along the borders with Guinea and Liberia, and refugees faced grave hardship. The UN Mission in Sierra Leone, UNAMSIL, was growing under a revised plan. The Council deplored abuses by the Revolutionary United Front, including forced recruitment of adults and children, and said the Abuja Ceasefire Agreement was not being kept in full.

The Council extends UNAMSIL for six months and raises its military strength to 17,500, including 260 observers already in place. It demands that the RUF free UN movement across the country, return seized weapons and gear, and rejoin the disarmament program. It urges the government to restore civil services across its land and pushes for quick setup of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission and the Special Court planned under Resolution 1315.

Rough diamonds from Sierra Leone stay banned for six more months under this text of 4 December 2002. Illegal diamond trading had helped fuel the country's civil war. Though the war had ended and security had improved, large volumes of diamonds still moved outside government control.

The measures stay in force from 5 December 2002, with one standing exception. Rough diamonds certified under the government's Certificate of Origin regime remain exempt from the ban. At the end of the period the Council would review the situation, including how far government authority reached over the diamond areas, before deciding whether to extend or change the measures.

Katanga's split from Congo pushed the young UN to a hard call. The rich province had broken away in July 1960. Belgian troops still stood on its soil. UN men had been kept out of Katanga though they stood ready to go in. The chief's new report told the tale. Resolution 146 passed on 9 August 1960 by nine votes to none. France and Italy held back.

Belgium had to pull its troops out of Katanga at once. The chief would set the pace and the way. The UN force's entry to Katanga was ruled a must. One guard rail was set down with care. The force would not take sides in Congo's own fights. It would not tip the scales of any home clash. All states were told to back the Council's word in full.

Resolution 1546 was adopted by the Security Council on 8 June 2004. It endorsed Iraq's return to full sovereignty after the occupation period. It welcomed the new Interim Government of Iraq, which was to take full authority on 30 June 2004. It also backed a set timetable toward elections and a permanent constitution.

The resolution gave the United Nations Assistance Mission for Iraq, known as UNAMI, a leading role in helping Iraq. UNAMI was to help with a national conference, elections, and talks on a constitution. The resolution also kept the multinational force in Iraq, at the new government's request, with power to act for security. It set that mandate to end once the political transition was complete.

A new UN body took shape at the end of 2005. The Peacebuilding Commission would help states heal after wars. It was born the same week as its twin text, Resolution 1645. Resolution 1646, passed on 20 December 2005, set the Council's own stake in the new body.

The five veto powers would sit on the steering group as of right. The Council would also pick two of its rotating members each year. Those picks would join the same group. One more rule was set. The body's yearly report would come to the Council too. Members would debate it once a year. The text is short and dry. It still fixed the Council's seat at the table of the UN's newest organ.

Afghanistan's assistance mission, UNAMA, is extended for a further year on 23 March 2007. The Afghanistan Compact, endorsed in 2006, set the shared plan for the country's security, governance, and development. A Council mission had visited Afghanistan in November 2006, and its report fed into this renewal.

UNAMA's mandate stays as laid out the year before, covering political support, human rights, aid coordination, and counternarcotics. Afghan parties are called on to join an inclusive political process, and the government to press ahead with reform, justice, and the fight against the drug trade. All sides are told to respect humanitarian law and protect aid workers, and donors are urged to deliver on their pledges.

Piracy off Somalia is fought at sea under Resolution 1846, adopted on 2 December 2008. Attacks threatened aid deliveries and shipping lanes. The Monitoring Group found escalating ransom payments were fuelling more piracy. Somalia's Transitional Federal Government asked for the Resolution 1816 (2008) powers to be renewed. The EU was about to launch a 12-month naval operation protecting World Food Programme convoys.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council decides that for 12 months, states and regional organizations cooperating with the Somali government may enter Somalia's territorial waters. They must have its consent, notified in advance. They may use all necessary means there to repress piracy and armed robbery, as international law allows on the high seas. It urges naval deployments, seizure of pirate boats and equipment, shared information, and cooperation on jurisdiction and prosecution. The authorization is limited to Somalia and sets no precedent in customary law.

Resolution 1946, adopted on 15 October 2010, renews the sanctions regime on Côte d'Ivoire on the eve of a long-delayed presidential vote. An arms embargo, a ban on rough diamond exports, and targeted travel and financial measures had been in place since 2004 and 2005. Experts monitoring the regime had reported in 2009 and 2010, and a certified voters list was finally ready.

The Council kept the measures in force and extended the mandate of the experts group, judging that sanctions still supported the peace process as the first-round election approached on 31 October. It pressed Ivorian leaders to hold the vote on schedule, in open and fair conditions. Weeks later the disputed result plunged the country into crisis anyway.

Namibians seized and tried by South Africa are the cause taken up in Resolution 246, passed by a full vote on 14 March 1968. Pretoria had seized men from South West Africa and tried them under its own laws. Yet the Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate in 1966. The UN had taken charge of the land on paper. A vote in January had told South Africa to stop the trial.

South Africa did not stop. The Council voiced its distress at this defiance. It treated the arrests, the trial, and the jail terms as unlawful acts. It pressed for the men to be freed and sent home. The case became proof of the UN claim that Namibia was not South Africa's to rule.

The buffer force between Egypt and Israel was reviewed by the Council in the spring of 1974. The United Nations Emergency Force had been set up after the October war of 1973. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 1 April 1974, held that the force was still required. Resolution 346 was adopted on 8 April 1974.

The Council thanked the states that had sent troops to the force. It also thanked those that had given money and material. The force was praised for its contribution to the search for a just and durable peace. The Council noted a shared view about the recent disengagement of forces. Pulling Egyptian and Israeli troops apart was only a first step toward a settlement. The plan to keep the force's size under review was welcomed, so it could be cut when conditions allowed.

Few Council texts on the Middle East are quoted as often as Resolution 446. It was adopted on 22 March 1979 by twelve votes to none. Norway, Britain, and the United States abstained. Jordan's ambassador had just addressed the members about Israeli settlements in occupied Arab land.

The Council ruled that building those settlements had no legal validity. It called them a serious block to a just and lasting peace. It said the Fourth Geneva Convention covers the territories taken in 1967, including Jerusalem. Israel was told to stop moving its own civilians into them. A three-member commission was created to inspect the settlement situation and report by 1 July 1979.

Resolution 46, adopted on 17 April 1948 by nine votes to none with two abstentions, tries to arrange a truce in Palestine. Britain still held the Mandate and was responsible for order, while fighting between Arab and Jewish forces was growing. The Council had already called for a truce two weeks earlier and now set out concrete measures.

All groups in Palestine were called on to stop military and paramilitary activity, violence, terrorism, and sabotage at once. Armed bands and fighters were not to be brought in from outside. The text pressed both leadership bodies in particular, the Arab side's Higher Committee and the Jewish Agency, to cooperate. The step was meant to guard the country's future while its political fate stayed undecided.

On 17 March 1992 the Council passed Resolution 746 by a full vote. It backs a truce in Somalia that was fraying at the edges. The warring clans had signed a ceasefire pact in Mogadishu on 3 March. It let a UN team watch the truce on the ground. A UN report of 11 March warned that the clans had not kept their word. Aid could not reach the starving in safety.

The Council deplored the broken pledge and the scale of the pain the war caused. It backed the UN chief's plans for help. A small team would go first to work out a watch force. Aid flights and food convoys would grow. In a month the Council set up its first Somalia force.
witches-of-huntingdon-1646:
Justices take down witch tales in The Witches of Huntingdon, a brief tract of 1646. In the shire town and its fields, poor folk were charged with pacts with the Devil, who, the tales say, tempts poor souls with coin, food, and ease. The tract prints the quizzes and words of guilt as the justices of the peace took them in the midst of the great war time hunt in the east.

Names, dates, and small grim facts crowd the pages. No scribe shapes them to a tale. The tract is the hunt's raw paper trail. Its plain, prim tone is its worth.
zoist-vol-04-1846:
The Zoist's fourth volume runs from April 1846 to January 1847. Elliotson's journal of mesmerism and cerebral physiology keeps its presses hot. Painless operations under mesmeric trance still headline the case lists. Ether, newly arrived in surgery, begins to shadow the journal's cause in these years.

Reports of clairvoyant somnambulists mix with sober hospital notes. Elliotson defends his methods against a hostile medical establishment. The movement's record grows volume by volume toward thirteen in all. Volume four catches mesmerism at a turning point in its fortunes. Anaesthesia by gas would soon steal its surgical crown. The pages hold the moment before that fall.
